retrieved_contexts: ['Research in polymer nanocomposites has been motivated by the opportunities to enhance or augment the physical properties of polymeric materials. Biomass-derived fillers, including cellulose nanofibers or lignin, have attracted particular interest in the context of ‘sustainable materials engineering’ as a means towards more benign (and low-energy) polymer materials. However, although the concept of reducing the environmental footprint of synthetic polymers by dilution with bio-sourced fillers appears to be straightforward, the loss of desirable physical properties, such as mechanical strength or optical clarity, that is often observed in biomass-based polymer composites limits the impact of the ‘nanocomposite approach’ for sustainable material engineering. The effect of filler addition on the physical properties of polymers sensitively depends on the morphology of the composite material and filler-matrix interactions. Aggregation of dispersed particle fillers is generally considered to be detrimental to physical properties of nanocomposites due to embrittlement of the material as well as the loss of optical clarity [1], [2], [3], [4]. This presents a particular challenge for biobased fillers - such as lignin - due their inherent chemical incompatibility with most engineering plastics [5], [6]. For example, blends of hydroxypropyl lignin in PMMA were found to exhibit a strain-to-fracture of less than 2% (about half of the value typically observed for pristine PMMA at moderate strain rates) - the embrittlement was attributed to weak polymer-filler interactions and the formation of micron-scale lignin aggregates [7]. A large number of studies involving both bio-sourced as well as inorganic particle fillers have corroborated the particular relevance of filler-matrix interactions as governing parameter that determines the physical properties of polymer nanocomposite materials [8]. A substantial amount of research - mostly on the phase behavior of inorganic particle-in-polymer dispersions - has established the sensitive relation between miscibility and architecture of polymer-tethered particle fillers (here the term architecture is used to describe the relevant structural parameters of polymer-tethered particle systems such as particle size, density as well as degree of polymerization and dispersity of grafted chains). For example, in the case of ‘neutral’ polymer grafts, in which the chemical composition of the grafted chains is identical to the matrix, miscibility has been shown to increase with the degree of polymerization of surface-tethered chains [8], [9], [10], [11], [12]. Parallel progress in surface-initiated controlled radical polymerization has established a range of synthetic methodologies to facilitate the tethering of polymer chains with precisely controlled degree of polymerization, grafting density and even modality of polymeric tethers [8], [13], [14]. Recently our group demonstrated that the application of surface-initiated atom transfer controlled radical polymerization (SI-ATRP) facilitates the efficient synthesis of polymer tethered kraft lignin with high molecular polymeric tethers [15]. SI-ATRP is a particularly interesting technique in the context of filler modification because of its applicability to a wide range of monomer chemistries, the high level of control over molecular characteristics of tethered chains as well as its proven economic efficacy and scalability [8], [16], [17]. Grafting of polymeric chains was shown to result in lignin-hybrid particles that could be assembled into ‘one-component lignin-hybrid materials’ with enhanced cohesive interactions as compared to the pristine lignin and polymer constituents - the latter was attributed to the occurrence of entanglements between tethered chains. The similarity of the effect of polymer-graft modification on the interaction between lignin fillers to those observed in inorganic particle brush analogs motivates the hypothesis that polymer-graft modification should be an effective method to facilitate the improved dispersion of lignin in polymer matrices and the fabrication of bio-sourced polymer composites with enhanced mechanical properties [18], [19].', 'Despite the potential benefits of incorporating lignin into traditional polymers to mitigate the shortcomings of composite materials, the utilization of lignin-based bioplastics is limited due to their inferior processability and mechanical properties [17]. The problem caused by poor processability of some types of lignin, such as Alkali lignin, can be solved by neutralization or acidification of lignin [18]. Moreover, it can only be blended in small amounts due to its immiscibility in the majority of polyesters. It was discovered that the organosolv lignin and its butyrate derivative were highly miscible with some polymers, such as PHB, and that lignin inhibits and delays the crystallization of PHB [19, 20]. Some researchers have tried synthesizing lignin copolymers, which is considered an effective approach to improve the compatibility of lignin and polymer matrix [21]. Moreover, using dicumyl peroxide as a crosslinker, which creates covalent bonds between lignin and polymer through reactive extrusion processing, and chemical modification of lignin through esterification are other techniques used to improve the compatibility of lignin into the polymer matrix [22, 23]. Organosolv lignin is a type of lignin extracted from biomass through the organosolv process. Lignin is a complex organic polymer found in the cell walls of plants, providing structural support. The organosolv process involves using organic solvents, such as ethanol, methanol, or a mixture of both, along with an acid or a base, to break down the lignin and separate it from the cellulose and hemicellulose components of biomass materials like wood, agricultural residues, or grasses. Organosolv lignin has been used by several researchers to address the poor properties of different polymers, especially polyesters [24,25,26]. Due to its structure, it can possess more complexity in the polymer matrix, resulting in higher resistance against biodegradation. Moreover, its low price, sustainability, and potential to be used as a reinforcing filler in polymer matrices make it a valuable additive [27, 28]. Since there is no discernible difference in the additive’s antibacterial and antioxidant activity between high and low lignin concentrations, the lower lignin concentration is seen to be ideal [29]. For example, based on phenolic chemicals in their structure, researchers found that 5% and 3% lignin in PLA-based composite may provide a high degree of antibacterial activity by inhibiting various bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli [30, 31]. However, a high lignin content would be more advantageous in terms of thermal and mechanical qualities like tensile strength; because of this aromatic polyester’s low aspect ratio, it can function as a filler.', 'Biomass-derived lignocellulose is the most abundant natural product on earth and has many potential applications as an additive for biodegradable plastics. Natural fibers have already been used as mechanical fillers for fiber-reinforced plastics (FRPs). With the recent introduction of nanocellulose, research on composite materials using nanocellulose as an eco-friendly binder or filler is being actively conducted [6,7]. On the other hand, lignin, a secondary component of lignocellulose, has recently been actively attempted to be used in the material industry based on its UV-blocking properties, antioxidant properties, and high organic carbon content [8]. However, when lignin is added to biodegradable plastics, it exhibits various disadvantages, such as self-aggregation of lignin occurring during the polymer melt process, low miscibility with the matrix polymer, and subsequent deterioration of the mechanical properties of the composite material strongly hindering its use [[9], [10], [11], [12]]. To overcome this problem, lignin fractionation, homogenization, and chemical modification have been proposed to increase the miscibility between lignin and a biodegradable polymer matrix [13]. A typical method for the chemical modification of lignin is acetylation, which has been reported to increase its hydrophobicity and compatibility with biodegradable polymers [14]. However, in the case of most biocomposites to which chemically modified lignin is added, the focus is on supplementing mechanical strength by enhancing the compatibility of the existing biodegradable matrix and demonstrating the UV-blocking effect of lignin [[15], [16], [17], [18]]. In particular, there are only a few studies reporting the effect of lignin addition on the biodegradation properties of manufactured biocomposites. Understanding the biodegradability and degradation mechanisms of bioplastics is important from an industrial and scientific point of view to predict their useful life and establish utilization plans. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the biodegradability of composite materials according to the addition of natural polymer fillers in biocomposite materials [[19], [20], [21], [22], [23]]. In fact, since general biopolymer fillers are hydrophilic, many studies have reported that most of them increase accessibility to the hydrolysis environment and accelerate biodegradation accordingly [24]. It has been also been reported that the addition of cellulose accelerated the biodegradation of PLA-based composites by 34 % and that the addition of microalgae-based biomass increases the degradation rate of PLA-based composites [[25], [26], [27]]. However, only a few additives have been designed to inhibit the degradation of these biodegradable plastics references [28]. The main purpose of this study is to prepare chemically modified lignin, improve compatibility with PLA, and use it as a functional additive to control the biodegradation behavior of PLA-based biocomposites. Firstly, AL was prepared through chemical modification to improve the low compatibility and dispersibility with PLA, which are the shortcomings of commercial technical lignin KL, and incorporated as an additive in PLA biocomposites. Changes in the physicochemical properties of lignin due to acetylation were investigated through Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR), gel permeation chromatography (GPC), phosphorus-31 nuclear magnetic resonance (31P NMR), proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). In addition, improved compatibility between PLA and AL was confirmed by observing the hygroscopic properties of AL, the dissolution and dispersion properties of AL in organic solvents, and the fracture surface morphology of the AL/PLA biocomposite. Ultimately, to investigate the effect of adding chemically modified lignin on the biodegradation characteristics of the lignin/PLA composite, a biodegradation experiment was performed for 45 days in a thermophilic composting environment above the glass transition temperature of PLA. Changes in physicochemical properties of lignin/PLA biocomposite according to biodegradation behavior were analyzed through GPC, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), TGA, and X-ray diffraction (XRD).', 'Formulation affects the hydrolysis mechanism. Biocomposites is a growing area of interest in the field of composite materials, due to the possibility to achieve materials that are fully biodegradable and cost-effective [[1], [2], [3]]. In this context, using agricultural or marine wastes represents an emerging trend in the perspective of developing materials possessing high level of sustainability both from an economic and ecological point of view [1,4]. However, a critical factor associated with manufacturing, application and end-use of biocomposites is the generally observed poor mechanical performance of such materials, as well as the prodegradant activity often exerted by some natural fillers during processing, which may determine further brittleness and may limit the possibility to use them in severe conditions [1,4]. Among the lignocellulosic fillers obtained by marine wastes, Posidonia flour (PF), resulting by grinding Posidonia Oceanica leaves, shows a promising potential as a filler for polylactic acid (PLA), although it presents the typical drawbacks of lignocellulosic fillers, in terms of poor toughness and pro-degrading effects [1,[5], [6], [7]]. Graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) belong to graphene family, and their use as fillers in PLA-based composites is widespread, due to the possibility to increase breaking properties of PLA and to preserve this polymer from thermal degradation and photo-oxidation, respectively occurring during processing and use [[8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]]. Furthermore, while the degradation paths of PLA can be extremely slow, depending on the conditions of degradation tests, with this issue representing an important concern in the case of plastic wastes disposal, recent studies demonstrate the possibility to achieve faster degradation of PLA when loaded with small amounts of GNP [16,17]. Similarly, the typical porous architecture of some lignocellulosic fillers together with their intrinsic hydrophilicity may facilitate water penetration, thus leading to faster degradation kinetics [[16], [17], [18]]. Anyhow, the effect of adding a hybrid reinforcement constituted by nano- and microfillers was marginally investigated in the scientific literature [[19], [20], [21]]. In particular, the effect of adding small amounts of GNP to a green composite based on PLA and PF have been never reported so far. Aim of this study is to investigate and model the effect of GNP/PF ratio on the mechanical properties of PLA-based composites and to assess eventual changes in the hydrolytic degradation kinetics of such materials in acidic, neutral and alkaline environments. Furthermore, the integration of GNP in PLA/PF systems is expected to enhance stiffness while improving the usually poor breaking properties of such materials. PLA 2002D was purchased by NatureWorks, is an extrusion grade having a content of D-lactic acid monomer equal to ~4%. Graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), trade name xGnP®, Grade C, were supplied by XG Sciences Inc., Lansing, MI, USA. Each particle consists of several sheets of graphene with an average thickness of approximately 2-5 nm, average diameter between 1 and 2 μm, and a specific surface area of about 750 m2/g [[22], [23], [24]]. PF, with particle size in the range 150-300 μm, was prepared according to a protocol reported in previous works [1,5].', 'Lignin, produced from papermaking and biorefinery industrial processes, is an interesting green substitute for petroleum-based derivative products with multiple functional properties, including bioplasticizing, bioadhesive, UV resistance and antioxidant properties. Although lignin is a major wood component (20-25 wt%) available in large quantities, it is seldom used industrially because of its difficult handling in the manufacture of high-value products. Controlling the lignin structural morphology in native and composite materials remains challenging because of the wide variety of chemical functional groups influencing its spatial organization and final network physicochemical properties. In thermoplastics applications, improving the interfacial interactions between the lignin charge and polymer matrix is essential. This work reports a combination of experimental approaches to investigate the chemical and adhesive properties of lignin at the molecular level, both in preparation of atomic force microscopy probes and in measurement at a nanometric scale through single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS), nano-infrared spectroscopy and imaging. The application of an original Langmuir-Blodgett (LB) deposition procedure produced homogeneous ultrathin coatings with controlled thicknesses in comparison with classical chemical deposition routes. Both procedures were verified for two synthetic lignins, guaiacyl and mixed guaiacyl-syringyl dehydrogenation polymers, before being applied to pine lignin as a proof-of-concept for the development of green lignin-based (nano)composites. Functionalizing the tip via the LB approach increased the adhesion force measurement resolution and provided new insights into the molecular affinity of lignin for other materials at the nanoscale, which prefers xylan polymers, such as those in native plant cell walls, and apolar/polar polymer matrices, such as those in composite materials, albeit to a lesser extent. Lignin plays a critical role in plant cell wall architecture since it is the last deposited polymer, forming numerous covalent bonds and noncovalent interactions (i.e., electrostatic and hydrophobic) with hemicelluloses, which results in the formation of a matrix that embeds cellulose.4,5 The complex hierarchical structure of lignocellulosic cell walls can inspire the design of smart nanostructured materials6-8 with improved performance under appropriate conditions. Nevertheless, lignin harnessing is still restricted by technical limitations, mostly due to its highly complex structure and difficult handling. Chemically, lignin is primarily composed of three phenylpropane units: p-hydroxyphenyl (H), guaiacyl (G) and syringyl (S). These units are formed from the free radical polymerization of p-coumaryl, coniferyl and sinapyl alcohols, resulting in multiple carbon-carbon and alkyl-aryl-ether cross-linkages.9,10 The composition and structure of lignin vary depending on taxa, tissue and cell type and environmental conditions. For example, softwood lignin is composed mainly of G-type units, whereas hardwood lignin contains both G and S units.11-13 Promising lignin-based coatings made of spherical lignin have shown interesting functional properties for food packaging and composite applications14 as antioxidant materials, antibacterial coatings,15 formaldehyde-replacing resins in composites and thermoplastic blends16-20 and cement plasticizers.21 The key to producing high-value products and efficiently integrating lignin into useable materials relies on the preparation of lignin-based materials to fabricate a new generation of innovative, multifunctional, competitive composites with high reactivity and chemical compatibility. The chemical groups, heterogeneity, ratio of lignin functional groups and the technical process used to develop (nano)composite materials (i.e., blending, multilayering, adsorption, plasma grafting, and self-assembly by evaporation) are of great importance in tailoring the final physicochemical and mechanical properties of these materials.22-24 Indeed, the amphiphilicity (exhibiting both hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity) of lignin, owing to the presence of various chemical groups (such as phenolic, aromatic, methoxy, alcoholic and carboxyl groups), induces locally variable affinity for matrix embedding through noncovalent interactions (dispersion forces, aromatic interactions, hydrophobic interactions, and H-bonds) either between lignin oligomers and other lignocellulosic polymers in native materials or between lignin and the polymer matrix in blends.25 Such variable affinity at the molecular scale endows lignin with differing adhesive properties, which may explain the difficulties encountered in homogeneously dispersing lignin into an apolar or polar matrix during blending, limiting the industrial applications of lignin with the aim of achieving final products with consistent and constant compatibility and mechanical and functional properties. Knowing that lignin can form strong noncovalent interactions with a wide range of polymers, estimating the adhesion forces between lignin and other components of the plant cell wall and between lignin and polar or apolar polymer matrices at the molecular scale can provide valuable information for the design of customized new lignin- and bio-based composites with the desired controlled, modular properties.', 'Lignin, a renewable macromolecule [17] and an abundant co-product of the pulp industry, was of particular interest as a possible filler for PLA-based composites [2]. It was estimated that only 2 % of the lignin was processed for non-energy application [18,19]. Lignin, the only non-petroleum resource capable of providing renewable aromatic compounds, had been the focus of particular attention by many researchers, who had sought to develop its rational and valuable use [20]. The molecular structure of lignin was composed of many aryl ring structures connected by ether bonds and carbon‑carbon bonds [21], which gave lignin high rigidity and high thermal stability [22]. At the same time, its phenol-rich structure gave interesting properties, such as antioxidant, ultraviolet adsorbent, antibacterial agent and so on [21,23,24]. As a result, the design of composites based on lignin and polymer materials not only added value to lignin, but can also lead to the design of high-performance polymer materials including 3D printed materials [24]. However, researchers [13,25,26] found that lignin can enhance the mechanical properties of PLA to a certain extent, but the compatibility between lignin and PLA was poor, and the strength of the composite cannot be further improved. At the same time, the performance of lignin/PLA prepared by blending was poor, which affected the feasibility of commercialization [26], mainly because of the thermal degradation of lignin during processing, and the uneven agglomeration and dispersion caused by its strong polarity, resulting in the decline of interface binding force [27]. So, chemical modifications were required to improve the composite interface. The Nam [28] team modified lignin by acetylation to improve the compatibility of lignin and PLA and prepared the bio-based lignin/PLA composite membrane by solvent volatilization. Polyethylene glycol was a non-toxic and biodegradable plasticizer, which made the processability of the polymer more convenient [26]. At the same time, PEG can be used as a modifier. retrieved_contexts: ['First published on 8th March 2023 Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting is an emerging manufacturing technology to print materials with cells for tissue engineering applications. In this study, we prepared novel ternary soft segment-based biodegradable polyurethane (tPU) using waterborne processes. The ternary soft segment included poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), polylactide, and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB). tPU2 with a soft segment of PCL, poly(D,L-lactide), and PHB in a molar ratio of 0.7:0.2:0.1 demonstrated lower stiffness (∼2.3 kPa) and a greater tanδ value (∼0.64) and maintained good vitality (91.3%) of neural stem cells (NSCs) among various tPUs. The bioprinted tPU2 constructs facilitated cell proliferation (∼200% in 7 days) and neural differentiation of NSCs. Meanwhile, tPU2 formed double network composite hydrogels with gelatin or agarose, and the composite hydrogels showed good biocompatibility and achieved high-resolution (∼80 μm nozzle) bioprinting. In addition, a new series of double network polyurethane-chitosan composite (PUC) hydrogels were developed by combining tPU2 with a self-healing chitosan hydrogel. The PUC hydrogel demonstrated self-healing properties and bioprintability without the need for a post-crosslinking process. The bioprinted PUC composite hydrogel promoted cell proliferation (∼300% in 7 days) and neural differentiation of NSCs better than the tPU2 bioink. This study revealed new formulae of a polyurethane bioink and a polyurethane-chitosan composite bioink for 3D bioprinting and tissue engineering applications. Several natural hydrogels are employed in 3D bioprinting, such as chitosan, alginate, agarose, and collagen.25-27 In general they lack appropriate mechanical properties and often need chemical modification or crosslinking to enhance their printability. The additional chemical processes may cause cytotoxicity.28,29 Synthetic hydrogels made of polyethylene glycol (PEG) have been used in bioprinting.30-32 The PEG-based hydrogels are not biodegradable and have low biological activities.33 Meanwhile, many bioprinted hydrogels are cured by UV light with photoinitiators before cell encapsulation. Either free radicals generated during the UV curing process or the residual photoinitiators may be harmful to cells.34,35 Therefore, it remains an interesting research topic to synthesize novel biodegradable materials with suitable mechanical properties and cytocompatibility for 3D bioprinting.', "Hydrogels are cross-linked three-dimensional (3D) networks of water-soluble polymers and large amounts of water, and structural similarities to some human soft tissues. Future research studies may focus on this frontier to fully utilize the synergistic combination of gelatin and HA in composite bioinks.', 'Increasing studies have provided abundant evidence that chitosan-based hydrogels can serve as scaffolds for cell growth and differentiation, but how they regulate the molecular signaling pathways during the entire process is still unclear. 3D bioprinting utilizes biodegradable hydrogels as bioinks to fabricate tissue-engineered constructs by leveraging their biocompatibility, structural mimicry of the extracellular matrix (ECM), and tunable mechanical and degradation properties. Key applications and mechanisms include:  

1. **Mimicking ECM and Supporting Cell Functions**:  
   - Hydrogels like **gelatin-alginate**, **polyurethane-chitosan composites (PUC)**, and **methacrylated gelatin (GelMA)** provide a hydrated, ECM-like environment that facilitates nutrient diffusion, cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation. For example, tPU2-based hydrogels promoted neural stem cell (NSC) proliferation (~200% in 7 days) and differentiation, while PUC hydrogels enhanced NSC proliferation (~300%) and neural differentiation [1, 9].  

2. **Tailored Printability and Mechanical Properties**:  
   - Hydrogels are engineered for **shear-thinning behavior** (e.g., alginate-agar blends) to enable extrusion through fine nozzles (~80 μm) and rapid post-printing stabilization via ionic crosslinking (e.g., Ca²⁺ for alginate) or chemical crosslinking (e.g., glutaraldehyde for gelatin). Biohybrid systems like **PU/gelatin** or **PEG/gelatin-RGD** combine synthetic polymers' mechanical strength with natural polymers' bioactivity, achieving high-resolution printing and structural stability [1, 6, 9, 10].  

3. **Degradation and Bioactivity**:  
   - **Ternary polyurethane (tPU)** with poly(ε-caprolactone), polylactide, and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) soft segments degrades controllably while maintaining cytocompatibility (91.3% cell viability). Composite hydrogels like **ADA-GEL-MBGNs-HPL** balance degradation rates with bioactive mineral deposition for bone regeneration [1, 3].  

4. **Self-Healing and Dynamic Networks**:  
   - **Polyurethane-chitosan (PUC)** hydrogels exhibit self-healing properties without post-crosslinking, enabling robust layer-by-layer printing. Granular hydrogels (e.g., **GelMA-hydroxypropyl chitosan**) leverage dynamic crosslinking for high permeability and self-repair, enhancing cell viability (~94%) [1, 13].  

5. **Functional Additives and Hybridization**:  
   - Incorporation of **mesoporous bioactive glass nanoparticles (MBGNs)** or **platelet lysate (HPL)** enhances osteogenic activity and vascularization. **Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs)** in chitosan hydrogels improve mechanical strength and osteogenesis, while **alginate/agar** hybrids minimize interfacial defects via double-network toughening [3, 5, 12].  

6. **Biocompatibility and Reduced Cytotoxicity**:  
   - Natural polymers (e.g., **chitosan**, **alginate**) avoid cytotoxic crosslinkers or UV initiators. For instance, **GelNB-PEGdiSH** hydrogels use photo-click chemistry for neural constructs with high cell viability (~68% at day 7) [8].  

In summary, biodegradable hydrogels in 3D bioprinting are optimized for printability, mechanical resilience, degradation kinetics, and bioactivity, enabling precise fabrication of functional tissues such as neural networks, bone, and cartilage.

For nearly a century, the conventional petroleum-based polymers have been applied in many fields and played increasingly important role in industry and daily life. In recent years, academia and industry are devoted to developing biodegradable and renewable polymers [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. Among these bio-based polymers produced from renewable resources, polylactide (PLA) is the most promising material for replacing the conventional petroleum-based polymers [5]. They found that with increasing TPP content, the size of PBSA dispersed phase reduced notably and the interface of PLA and PBSA exhibited fibrillated links, which resulted in a significant improvement in impact strength and elongation at break. These works mentioned above strongly suggest that the appropriate dispersed phase size and the suitable good interfacial adhesion are dominant influencing factors for achieving significant improvement of toughness, and the reduction of the dispersed phase size and the increased interfacial are commonly manipulated by reactive compatibilization.", 'PLA is a bio-based, biodegradable, and biocompatible polyester, which has strength and elastic modulus comparable to those of conventional petroleum-based polymers such as poly(ethylene terephthalate) and polystyrene [1]. PLA has attracted increasing attention in recent years as the environmentally benign and biomedical materials usable for agriculture, automobile, diary commodities, tissue engineering and controlled drug delivery etc. [2]. However, it exhibits brittle fracture behavior. It has also a low heat distortion temperature due to the low glass transition temperature (T g) (ca. 60 °C), and no back-up of the elastic modulus above T g due to a low rate of crystallization. Therefore, a great deal of efforts has been made to modify the properties of PLA in both industry and academia [3, 4]. Melt blending of PLA with some flexible biodegradable polyesters, such as poly(butylene succinate) [5-7], poly(butylene succinate-co-L-lactate) [8, 9], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [10-14] and poly(butylene adipapte-co-terephthalate) [15, 16] is an effective way to improve the ductility of PLA. Unfortunately, all the blending inevitably leads to a dramatic deterioration in originally poor heat resistance of PLA, which is not acceptable for many commercial applications. Interestingly, Oyama found the annealing induced crystallization of PLA matrix for the blends of PLA and poly(ethylene-glycidyl methacrylate) improves both heat deflection temperature and impact toughness [17]. Bai also reported the improvement of both heat deflection temperature and impact toughness for PLA/PCL blend is capable by the control of the PLA matrix crystallization and PCL particle size [18]. On the other hand, PLA-based polymer networks and semi-interpenetrating polymer networks (semi-IPNs) are promising strategies to improve the thermal and mechanical properties of PLA. Koo et al. reported that a crosslinked PLA by UV irradiation exhibits a little higher tan δ peak temperature and a higher toughness by 22.5 % in spite of a little lower elongation at break than PLA [19]. He et al. reported tough semi-IPNs composed of PLA and the crosslinked polyurethane prepared by reacting 4,4’-methylenediphenyl diisocyanate with poly(ethylene glycol) and glycerol [20]. In the past studies, simultaneous improvements of T g, toughness and ductility for the PLA-based polymer network and semi-IPNs compared with those of PLA have not been accomplished.', "The demand for bio-based polymers, i.e. derived from renewable resources, is continuously growing in many industrial sectors, in particular because of the willingness to reduce the dependency on petro-sourced materials, to improve the recyclability of products and to answer customer expectations for materials with lower environmental footprint. Among currently available bio-based polymers, polylactide (PLA) is undoubtedly one of the most promising alternatives to petro-sourced polymers. First, PLA is biodegradable and may also offer recycling possibility at product end-of-life [1], [2]. Above all, PLA has interesting mechanical properties, such as high flexural and tensile strength and rigidity, and can be processed using conventional equipment, in particular by injection molding [3]. Thanks to those interesting properties, PLA is now commonly used for some specific applications such as sustainable packaging. Recent breakthroughs allow the use of PLA for a wider range of applications (automotive components, electronic products, textile …) which require high performance materials [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Considering the particular case of the automotive industry, the use of polymers significantly increased over recent decades, thanks to appealing thermo-mechanical properties combined with low density and easy processing at high output rate and relatively low cost, generally by injection molding. Nowadays, many research projects aim to find sustainable alternative to conventional petro-sourced polymers. In that context, the use of PLA is undoubtedly appealing thanks to its high strength and rigidity, in particular. Based solely on the provided context, the Shape Memory Effect (SME) in biodegradable polyurethanes is described as follows:

1.  **Definition:** The SME enables a polymer to be deformed and temporarily fixed into a new shape under specific conditions (e.g., below a transition temperature) and then recover to its original, permanent shape upon exposure to a suitable external stimulus.
2.  **Stimuli:** The recovery stimulus is frequently heat (thermal-responsive), especially near body temperature for biomedical applications ([1, 2, 3, 9, 14]). Other stimuli mentioned include moisture, water/solvent, ions, pH changes, light, electricity, and magnetism ([1, 3, 7, 9]).
3.  **Molecular Mechanism:** The SME arises from the polymer's structure ([1, 3]):
    *   **Permanent Shape:** Provided by physical netpoints (hard segments formed by diisocyanate and chain extender, involving polar interactions, hydrogen bonding, and/or crystallization) or covalent netpoints (chemical crosslinking).
    *   **Temporary Shape Fixation:** Enabled by the switching domains (soft segments, often semicrystalline like PCL or PDLLA). Fixation occurs via vitrification (glass transition) or crystallization of the soft segments below their transition temperature (Tm or Tg). High crystallinity in the soft segment regions is crucial for shape fixity at room temperature ([10, 11]).
4.  **Biodegradable PU Specifics:** The biodegradable aspect is achieved by incorporating hydrolysis-prone segments like poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) diol, poly(D,L-lactic acid) (PDLLA) diol, or PLA diol as the soft segment ([1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 12, 13, 14, 15]). The semicrystalline nature of these soft segments (especially PCL) is vital for enabling the SME near body temperature due to their low melting point and biodegradability ([2, 9, 14]).
5.  **Design Challenge:** Balancing biodegradability, mechanical properties, and SME is crucial. Crystallinity in the soft segments aids SME but can slow degradation ([14]). Strategies to accelerate degradation while maintaining SME include introducing degradable groups into the hard segments (e.g., enzymatically cleavable chain extenders like PHP ([2]) or amino acid-based chain extenders ([14])). Decreasing crystallinity to speed degradation can compromise mechanical properties and shape fixity ([9, 14]).

**In summary:** The Shape Memory Effect in biodegradable polyurethanes is the ability to be deformed and fixed in a temporary shape (typically via crystallization/vitrification of a biodegradable soft segment like PCL below its Tm/Tg) and recover the original shape upon stimulus (often heating above the soft segment's Tm/Tg), driven by the permanent netpoints in the hard segments. The biodegradable nature comes from hydrolysable segments within the polymer structure.
reference: The Shape Memory Effect allows the polymer to be deformed and fixed in a temporary shape and then recover its original permanent shape upon heating above a transition temperature (Ttrans, usually Tg or Tm). In biodegradable polyurethanes, this is driven by the phase separation between hard segments (permanent shape fixation) and soft segments (switching transition).

The parameters of the printing process were:', 'In theory, a 100% interconnected rate and precise structure of the 3D printed scaffold can be produced by various combinations of the pore size and porosity.11,12 Nevertheless, in actual operation, the holes on the side of the polymer-based scaffold tend to collapse or even close under the influence of gravity, which weakened the penetration. Additive Manufacturing (AM) technologies have become a new standard in design due to product customization and fabrication [1]. The FFF form 3D geometries by layer by layer deposition of thermoplastics in form of extruded filament through nozzle for preparation of functional components [2]. So reinforcements are required for the enhancement of mechanical properties [3]. Also, recent studies reveal that mechanical properties can be improved with proper selection of optimal printing parameters in FFF [4-6]. It has been reported that reinforcement of almond skin powder (in different wt%) in polycaprolactone (PCL) leads to improvement in mechanical properties [7]. The significant gain in elastic modulus (17%) at 10 wt% particle loading was observed in comparison to 0% almond skin powder reinforcement. Thus, the study aims to address this gap by examining the influence of printing parameters on the impact strength and torque withstanding ability of biocompatible and biodegradable PLA-based LoBPs using an experimental design based on response surface methodology (RSM). Utilizing the 3D printing process, polymeric LoBPs were produced through six sequential steps (Fig. 1). Initially, the dimensions of the stainless-steel-based LoBP were replicated for the PLA-based LoBP in the first step. Subsequently, in the second step, a 3D model of the LoBP was created using SolidWorks software once the dimensions were obtained. Finally, in the third step, the LoBP was sliced using FlashPrint 5.8.3 software.', 'In vitro biodegradability of scaffolds Since the kinetics of drug release from drug-eluting scaffolds is particularly related to the biodegradability potential of the scaffolds, to optimize a 3D-printed drug-releasing scaffold, the structure of the system must be biodegradable. Therefore, it was necessary to investigate the biodegradability potential of the synthesized 3D-printed scaffolds by measuring the amount of weight loss in parallel with the pattern and rate of heparin release. Biodegradability is one of the significant features of cellular scaffolds. The rate of the scaffold degradation should be in accordance with the rate and time required for the differentiation of cells and the repair of that tissue [46]. The biodegradability of heparin-loaded 3D-printed scaffolds was measured under in vitro conditions in PBS buffer (pH 7.4). The results of weight change and weight loss (%) can be found in Fig. 3B. SA, Gel, and HA as biodegradable and biocompatible polymers have been previously described as having strong hydrophilic properties that could provide an effective dissolution rate for drug delivery systems and improve the bioavailability of various loaded drugs and agents [48].', 'Three-dimensional (3D) printing technology has advantage in gradient scaffold manufacturing due to its layer-by-layer deposition method [12, 13]. However, there still exist some disadvantages to be improved in the 3D printed osteochondral scaffolds, such as inadequate mechanical and insufficient integration between the layers [19, 20]. Proper mechanical properties are necessary for osteochondral tissue engineering scaffolds, especially the strength of bone for load-bearing and the toughness of cartilage for impact-absorbing. For example, if the strength of the scaffold is less than that of the surrounding bone, the scaffold will probably fail before it is replaced by ingrowing bone; while if the strength of the scaffold is higher than that of the surrounding bone, stress shielding will prevent the bone from being exposed to normal levels of mechanical loading, leading to bone resorption and lack of bone in growth into the scaffold [21]. Ceramic materials, such as HAp and β-TCP, have been widely studied for bone tissue engineering due to their good mechanical strength and similarity to the mineralized phase of native bone [22,23,24]. They also possess excellent biocompatibility, bioactivity and osteoconductive properties [25, 26]. On the other hand, biodegradable PCL is widely used in cartilage tissue engineering due to its good biocompatibility, shape retention properties and excellent toughness required for elastic tissues [21]. Therefore, HAp and PCL scaffolds, in combination with the mechanical behavior of the two materials, are expected to apply to osteochondral tissue engineering scaffolds. In this study, a biphasic osteochondral scaffold was prepared by 3D printing of PCL as cartilage layer and sintered HAp as subchondral layer. Finite element analysis was implemented to simulate the stress and strain process of the biphasic HAp/PCL scaffolds under compression. The mechanical properties of the scaffolds were also evaluated, and cell viability on the scaffolds was finally investigated for further applications.', 'Additive manufacturing is creating its presence in the current manufacturing sector more rapidly than any other manufacturing process. The technique of generating a three-dimensional object using CAD model data is known as additive manufacturing or 3-D printing. Additive manufacturing is a layer-by-layer material joining method that employs thermoplastic polymers such as Polylactic acid (PLA), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and others.3-D printing uses several methods for the printing purpose such as Selective laser sintering, Fused Deposition Modelling, Stereo Lithography, but the Fused Deposition Modelling is the most prominent ones because of its salient features such as durability, high strength and stability in producing parts. Several studies have been conducted to ascertain the mechanical properties of the 3-D printed parts and various research papers have been also published about 3-D printing. In this study we have found that the raster angle has the least influence on the sample’s mechanical properties. The mechanical properties of the samples are most affected by layer thickness and printing speed and they are the main parameters that influence the properties of the parts the most. This study helps in to determine the compressive strength of the parts and also guides on the selection of the best suitable printing parameters.', 'Porosity, crystallinity and architecture of poly(lactic acid) scaffold directly influence its compressive strength in dry state, while permeability and water content can affect load-bearing properties in physiological environment. Nevertheless, such mechanical property, depending on the implantation site, gives PLA/CHT-HA good potential in bone defect substitution.', 'A material often used in 3D printing is polylactic acid (PLA), which is a thermoplastic aliphatic polyester produced from renewable resources. Regarding the recycling of polylactic acid, technologies have already been developed for this operation, which shows that there are technologies available for each stage of the life cycle of products made of PLA. In the medical field, polylactic acid is used for stents, post-surgery stitches, and the medical implants in the form of anchors, screws, rod, pins, and plates. PLA medical implants disintegrate (break down) in the human body in a period of 6 months-2 years, depending on where they were used. Gradual degradation is beneficial for a supporting structure, as the weight is gradually transferred to the bone structure during the healing of that area. Information on polylactic acid and the 3D printed parts of it has been the subject of numerous scientific articles, from the study of which the following ideas emerge. Farah et al1 shows that polylactic acid is one of the most researched studied and utilized bio degradable aliphatic polyester in human history. retrieved_contexts: ['It has been widely known that PLA had poor oxygen barrier properties. Table 5 shows the oxygen permeability of neat PLA, f-CNF/PLA, and e-CNF/PLA nanocomposites. In this study, neat PLA showed about 32.26 ± 1.24 cc·mm/m2·day·atm of oxygen permeability value. There are several factors that affect the oxygen permeability properties; such as polymer internal structure, molecular weight, polymer crystallinity, molecular chain entanglement, and processing techniques.[40] In this study, CNF/PLA nanocomposites were produced into films using two step processing, therefore it could expected there would be some thermal degradation of polymer inducing slight increase of the oxygen permeability. Aulin et al.[41] reported an oxygen permeability value of 0.00006 cc·mm/m2·day·atm for 5 μm nanocellulose thin film at 23°C and 0% RH. Cellulose, which is a high oxygen barrier material, was distributed or dispersed in a PLA matrix to fabricate a nanocomposite, and it was confirmed that the oxygen barrier property was improved compared to neat PLA. On the other hand, the f-CNF/PLA containing about 1 wt% of CNF content showed an increase in oxygen permeability compared to f-CNF/PLA 0.5, and this could be due to the agglomeration of CNF creating a chink and crack in interface between PLA and CNF. Similar to the results of mechanical properties, it was found that the uniform dispersion of CNF in the PLA matrix tend to affects the oxygen barrier properties of the nanocomposites. On the other hand, the e-CNF/PLA samples showed a consistent reduction of the oxygen permeability with increasing CNF content. As shown in Table 5, t-PLA containing 12.5 phr of TEC shows increased oxygen permeability than neat PLA. The same trend was observed in mechanical properties, in that plasticization led a negative effect on oxygen barrier properties induced from disentanglement of the PLA chain. However, the oxygen barrier performance was improved due to the uniform dispersion of CNF in the PLA matrix. In addition, the CNF in the amorphous region in PLA restricted chain mobility and caused entanglement of the polymer chains, resulting in a decrease in oxygen permeability. These factors are confirmed by the results shown in Table 5, in which t-CNF/PLA sample containing 1 wt% of CNF were reduced by 47.3% compared to that of neat PLA. retrieved_contexts: ['As such, the emerging field of plastic degradation and recycling has attracted significant attention across the fields of microbiology,5-7 biocatalysis and directed evolution,8 synthetic biology1 and non-enzymatic catalysis.9-13 In particular, there have been significant developments in enzymatic PET degradation. The most promising enzymes discovered to date are variants of PETase from Ideonella sakaiensis14 and leaf-branch compost cutinase (LCC).15 Whilst PETase and its engineered variants16-20 operate at ambient temperature (30-37 °C) to release bis- and mono-(2-hydroxyethyl)terephthalate, the LCC derived enzyme is thermostable with maximum productivity at 72 °C and exhibits the highest PET to terephthalate (TA) degradation productivity reported to date (up to 16.7 g L−1 h−1).15 As increasingly efficient PET degradation methods are developed,16,17,21-23 the recycling of PET monomers TA and ethylene glycol has also been demonstrated. For example, TA from LCC catalysed PET degradation has been used as a feedstock for production of second generation PET,15 and as a building block for synthesis of value-added metal organic frameworks.24 Post-consumer PET has also been pyrolyzed and the TA produced used as a feedstock for bacterial production of polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs),25 a promising class of bioplastics with a superior biodegradability profile to PET26,27 (Fig. 1a). Chemically hydrolysed PET has also been used as a feedstock for protocatechuate (PC) derived small molecules using microbial co-cultures.28 However, to date there have been no examples of interfacing enzyme-catalysed PET degradation with biological upcycling pathways. To this end, we hypothesised that TA derived from PET waste could be valorised into the value-added product vanillin via a 5-step enzymatic pathway (Fig. 1b). Vanillin is the primary component of the extract of vanilla beans and is responsible for the characteristic taste and smell of vanilla. Consequently, vanillin is widely used across the food and cosmetics industries, as well as in pharmaceutical synthesis and formulation, herbicides, antifoaming agents and cleaning products, leading to a global demand in excess of 37000 tonnes in 2018.29 The demand for vanillin is growing rapidly and is projected to exceed 59000 tonnes with a revenue forecast of $734000000 by 2025.29 As the demand for vanillin far exceeds the supply from vanilla beans (‘natural vanillin’), methods for its synthesis (‘synthetic vanillin’) have been widely investigated. Biotechnological approaches are particularly attractive from a sustainability perspective owing to the inherently mild reaction conditions and use of renewable feedstocks.30 The most widely employed of these is the production of vanillin from lignin biomass,31 whilst methods for fermentation of vanillin using microbial and fungal hosts from ferulic acid,32,33 glucose, glycerol, L-tyrosine, xylose,34 curcumin,35 eugenol33 and isoeugenol36 have also been demonstrated (Fig. 1c). However, although conversion of TA to vanillic acid is known,28 direct access to the high value aldehyde vanillin from PET has not been reported. Herein, we demonstrate a novel enzymatic pathway using engineered Escherichia coli cells to synthesise vanillin from TA. This process falls within the ‘biotechnological vanillin’ sub-category of ‘synthetic vanillin’,30 namely vanillin produced by microbial fermentation via a non-natural, engineered pathway. After process optimisation, we obtain conversions in excess of 79%. Finally, we show that the pathway can be combined with LCC catalysed PET degradation to obtain vanillin directly from post-consumer plastic waste at ambient temperature and in aqueous conditions.', 'The establishment of infrastructure, such as commercial composting facilities, along with customer involvement in appropriate waste sorting, are prerequisites for the success of these initiatives. Moreover, new chemical recycling techniques are being developed that may decompose polymers into their monomers, providing a means of repurposing biodegradable waste to make new materials and thereby closing the loop. As a step toward a circular economy, sustainable woody-like composites derived from recycled Tetra Pak cellulose and poly(butylene succinate) were fabricated.320 McKeown et al.321 concentrated on PLA chemical recycling, highlighting how end-of-life disposal strategies of biobased polymers are vital for a successful transition to a sustainable circular economy. In the framework of a circular economy, the utilization of waste coffee trash as a renewable source for creating sustainable PBS biocomposites was highlighted.322 The creation of sustainable polymer materials in a way that improves sustainability through material design, waste management, renewable energy sources, biodegradability, biotechnological approaches, and enzymatic recycling within the framework of an international circular (bio)economy can foster efficient resource utilization and management.323 Biodegradability, while valuable in open environmental contexts where plastic leakage is inevitable, may not offer the same benefits in structured waste management systems lacking industrial composting infrastructure. In fact, in the hierarchy of circularity, recyclable materials are often prioritized because they better support long-term material retention and reuse.327,328 To align polymer blend development with circular economy goals, future strategies must go beyond traditional property enhancement. This includes designing blends with recyclability in mind through reversible chemistries, dynamic covalent networks, or advanced compatibilization techniques that allow effective reprocessing without compromising performance. Additionally, the concept of ‘design-for-recycling’ should be embedded from the outset, ensuring that material formulations account for their entire lifecycle, not just their immediate utility or degradability.328', 'Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) and poly(trimethylene terephthalate) (PTT) are examples of polyesters with partial biobased content, produced by combining fossil-derived terephthalic acid (TA) with renewable components such as 1,3-propanediol (PDO) or ethylene glycol. Bio-based PET (BioPET) typically has a biobased carbon content of around 30%, while bio-based PTT (BioPTT) has a biobased carbon content of approximately 37%. These percentages reflect the proportion of renewable carbon sources used in their production [158]. It is crucial to highlight the biodegradation potential of PET. Although PET is typically regarded as non-biodegradable or non-compostable, studies have shown that certain enzymes can naturally break it down, albeit at a very slow rate [81]. Recently, scientists have discovered a novel bacterium capable of utilizing low-crystallinity PET as a carbon source. This bacterium produces PET-hydrolyzing enzymes, such as PETase, which facilitate the breakdown of PET. This discovery presents new possibilities for the bio-recycling of PET, potentially leading to more efficient and environmentally friendly methods of recycling this widely used plastic. Polyamides (PAs) are a class of condensation polymers characterized by repeating amide groups in their molecular chains [56]. These amide groups facilitate the formation of inter-chain hydrogen bonds, which contribute to the material’s ordered microstructure and high degree of crystallinity. This structural feature underlies the polyamides’ excellent mechanical properties, including strong impact resistance, high hardness, and good abrasion resistance.', 'Another concept coming into focus and integrated into sustainability discussions is the circular economy, an economic system based on resource efficiency and the reuse and regeneration of materials or products.309 In a bio-based economy, economic activity involves the use of biological resources, technologies, processes and methods to provide value-added products, goods, services and energy in a sustainable manner to all economic sectors.310 In a circular bioeconomy, natural capital is renewable and sustainably sourced, produced, managed, recovered and reused as much as possible across its entire life cycle.311 Circular biopolymers are one probable pathway for decoupling economic growth from the consumption of finite resources by sustainably sourcing feedstocks and building end-of-life recovery pathways that recapture polymer material value after use.312 This approach includes bio-based material innovations sourced from renewable feedstocks that are waste byproducts and coupling material innovations with complementary end-of-life “waste” management and recycling systems that create added value in organics processing infrastructure. A circular bioeconomy is most effective when working symbiotically across the supply chain to create value. Connecting R&D activities with downstream entities provides opportunities for biopolymers to be kept in circulation as a resource and at an economic value, creating the demand pull for material integration into circular secondary markets (life extension pathways through high-value reuse and recycling, remanufacture, upgrading, etc.). A circular bioeconomy is not sustainable by default. Therefore, circular materials and innovations must be measured across the entire life cycle to ensure it does not offset social, environmental or economic gains. Hierarchical biopolymer-based materials provide a versatile platform for manufacturing new biocomposite materials with controllable mechanical performance and reduced environmental, social, and economic impacts. Structural biopolymers such as cellulose, chitin and protein-based β-sheet structured polymers, have been explored both as fillers in biocomposite materials, as well as main matrix materials, capitalizing on their vast network of macromolecular interactions. When used as a matrix, such biopolymers can effectively utilize their interactions to establish a hierarchical self-bonded backbone of exceptionally high stiffness, strength and toughness that is comparable to engineering polymers. Controlling the biopolymer morphology (aspect ratio), degree of polymerization, and orientation, allows tuning of their interactions at the molecular- and nano-scales, which ultimately governs the macroscopic behavior and fracture of those entirely biobased materials. Structural biopolymers are obtained from biomatter through extraction and homogenization processes, which often require excessive chemical and thermo-mechanical treatments, which need to be taken into consideration when discussing the environmental impact of such materials. In addition, the effects of each processing step on the composition and morphology of the extracted biopolymers are critical, and should be carefully evaluated. For example, we discussed literature-reported results which demonstrate that extraction processes effectively reduce the polymer chain length and aspect ratio, which leads to inferior performance, compared to the native biopolymer state.', 'Another concept coming into focus and integrated into sustainability discussions is the circular economy, an economic system based on resource efficiency and the reuse and regeneration of materials or products.309 In a bio-based economy, economic activity involves the use of biological resources, technologies, processes and methods to provide value-added products, goods, services and energy in a sustainable manner to all economic sectors.310 In a circular bioeconomy, natural capital is renewable and sustainably sourced, produced, managed, recovered and reused as much as possible across its entire life cycle.311 Circular biopolymers are one probable pathway for decoupling economic growth from the consumption of finite resources by sustainably sourcing feedstocks and building end-of-life recovery pathways that recapture polymer material value after use.312 This approach includes bio-based material innovations sourced from renewable feedstocks that are waste byproducts and coupling material innovations with complementary end-of-life “waste” management and recycling systems that create added value in organics processing infrastructure. For example, we discussed literature-reported results which demonstrate that extraction processes effectively reduce the polymer chain length and aspect ratio, which leads to inferior performance, compared to the native biopolymer state.', "In addition to a low carbon footprint, FDCA-based polymers offer substantial recyclability benefits, embodying circular economy principles through diverse green end-of-life options. Specifically, FDCA-based polyesters are amenable to mechanical recycling or chemical depolymerization for the recovery of FDCA monomers or derivatives. While mechanical recycling often results in downcycling or blending with virgin materials [36], chemical methods offer a more promising route. For example, PEF can be efficiently degraded into its constituent FDCA monomers or derivatives via alcoholysis or hydrolysis, facilitating closed-loop recycling and decreasing dependence on fossil feedstocks, thereby contributing to sustainable material cycling [37,38]. Alberti et al. [39] reported efficient methanolysis of waste PEF using zinc acetate catalysis under microwave irradiation, generating dimethyl 2,5-furandicarboxylate and ethylene glycol with a turnover frequency of 396 h-1. Crucially, these products serve as direct monomers for PEF re-synthesis, enabling true closed-loop recovery. This chemical recycling approach offers a significant technological advancement for the circular transition of FDCA-based polymers. Biodegradability serves as a critical metric for assessing the life cycle environmental impact of polymeric materials. For FDCA-derived polymers, such as PEF, their inherent biodegradability and compliance with mainstream industrial composting standards, alongside their degradation rates in natural environments, have been a focal point of research and remain a subject of debate. Although PEF exhibits faster degradation in certain environments compared to traditional PET, it is not classified as compostable according to ASTM D6400-04, even when demonstrating superior degradation performance under industrial composting conditions. However, chemical structure modification, particularly through copolymerization with aliphatic polyesters, has been shown to enhance the degradability of FDCA-based polymers [36]. For instance, through ecodesign principles, Bianchi et al. developed an aromatic-aliphatic multiblock copolymer based on polylactic acid (PLA) and FDCA, which achieved complete biodegradation within 60 days of composting [40]. This work exemplifies a successful strategy for imparting degradability to FDCA-containing materials. The planar nature of the furan ring and the regularity of the polymer chains enable the formation of a dense chain packing structure, which effectively impedes the permeation of gas molecules, such as O2 and CO2. This characteristic endows furan dicarboxylic acids with significant potential in the realm of food and beverage packaging [[40], [41], [42]]. Burgess et al. [[43], [44], [45], [46], [47]] conducted a systematic investigation into the gas/water transport behavior of PEF. In terms of physical properties, amorphous PEF exhibits significantly superior gas barrier properties compared to PET: the CO2 permeability and diffusivity were reduced by 19-fold and 31-fold, respectively, and the O2 permeability decreased by 11-fold. Microstructural mechanistic studies reveal that the polarity and asymmetry of the furan ring are key factors. The enhanced polarity of the furan ring leads to improved CO2 adsorption (a 1.6-fold increase in solubility). However, the asymmetric structure restricts chain segment mobility, resulting in a substantial decrease in diffusion coefficients, a phenomenon not fully explicable by traditional free volume models. In terms of water adsorption, PEF demonstrates a 1.8-fold increase in water uptake due to the polarity of the furan ring, but the diffusion coefficient is reduced by fivefold, further confirming the constraint on chain segment motion. The furan ring's intrinsic characteristics provide a theoretical basis for designing bio-based barrier materials by enabling multi-scale regulation of chain segment mobility and free volume distribution.", 'Despite these benefits, the expansion of bioplastic production must be matched with the development of effective end-of-life strategies for managing bioplastic waste. Without proper waste management systems, the environmental benefits of bioplastics could be compromised. It is crucial to implement comprehensive recycling and disposal methods tailored to the specific types of bioplastics, ensuring their environmental benefits are fully realized. This includes enhancing recycling technologies, developing standards for compostability, and increasing public awareness about the proper disposal of bioplastic products. As the bioplastics industry grows, these measures are crucial to prevent new forms of pollution and capitalize on the sustainable promise of bioplastics. Non-biodegradable bioplastics, such as bio-PET, bio-PE, and bio-PP, can be efficiently processed within existing recycling systems alongside conventional petrochemical plastics. However, the end-of-life treatment for biodegradable bioplastics, such as PLA and PHAs, is more complex. While biodegradation is often considered the standard disposal method, these materials can be processed through mechanical, enzymatic, and chemical recycling. PLA, one of the most widely used biodegradable bioplastics, degrades very slowly in natural and marine environments, potentially causing environmental pollution if not managed properly. Therefore, evaluating PLA’s recyclability is essential, starting with the development of an efficient waste collection strategy and considering the establishment of a dedicated recycling stream. As the production of bioplastics continues to grow, these materials will coexist with traditional plastics for many years. Therefore, it is essential to identify the most effective end-of-life strategies for each significant type of bioplastic, irrespective of their biodegradability, to facilitate a comprehensive transition toward sustainability in the entire plastics value chain. This gap can lead to inefficiencies and increased costs, which may deter investment in recycling technologies specifically tailored for bioplastics. Significant investments in advanced sorting technologies, such as those utilizing machine learning and robotics, are necessary to segregate different types of plastics and address these challenges accurately. Furthermore, fostering partnerships between bioplastic producers, recyclers, and policymakers can help establish a circular economy framework, ensuring that bioplastics are effectively reintegrated into production cycles, thereby minimizing waste and conserving resources. In conclusion, a multi-faceted strategy that incorporates financial incentives, regulatory support, and technological innovation is necessary to optimize the recycling of bioplastics, thereby supporting the broader goal of sustainability in the plastics industry.', 'The escalating global reliance on petroleum resources has intensified research efforts toward renewable-processable bio-based polyesters as sustainable alternatives. FDCA-derived polyesters and copolyesters, leveraging their balanced physicochemical stability, tunable mechanical properties, and inherent sustainability, are positioned as leading candidates to displace conventional petroleum-derived plastics (e.g., PET) in diverse applications. Addressing these limitations requires synergistic advancements in three domains: strategic optimization of polymerization protocols, development of innovative catalytic systems, and implementation of advanced process engineering strategies. Such multidisciplinary integration is imperative to establish FDCA-based polyesters as industrially competitive materials for a sustainable plastic economy. These versatile polymers have gained industrial prominence in textiles, automotive components, and electronic packaging applications owing to their exceptional mechanical robustness, thermal stability, wear resistance, superior gas barrier properties, and chemical durability [[94], [95], [96], [97]]. This context underscores the strategic imperative to develop circular lifecycle solutions for PAs through innovative monomer sourcing, green synthesis protocols, and advanced recycling technologies. As non-food lignocellulosic feedstocks ubiquitous in plant cell walls, cellulose and hemicellulose offer strategic valorization pathways to decouple biomass utilization from food chain competition. In light of the aforementioned context, bio-based polyamides have been initially industrialized as substitutes for petroleum-based materials, with products such as PA11 (castor oil-based) and PA610 (castor oil/sebacic acid-based) being introduced in succession. Although current market penetration remains limited, global R&D investments in bio-based polyamides maintain an upward trajectory, driven by advancements in biotechnological processing and green chemistry principles. Particularly noteworthy are FDCA-derived furanic polyamides that exhibit superior thermal resilience, enhanced mechanical integrity, and exceptional chemical resistance, positioning them as next-generation candidates to overcome critical performance limitations in bio-based polyamide systems.', 'The review paper explores the innovative utilization of recycled polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste in synthesizing advanced polyester resin-based composites, particularly through integrating metallic nanofillers. PET, a highly durable and versatile polymer, poses significant environmental challenges due to its non-biodegradable nature and extensive use, especially in consumer packaging. The paper examines chemical recycling methods such as glycolysis, methanolysis, hydrolysis, and aminolysis, which depolymerize PET into monomers that can be repolymerized into unsaturated polyester resins (UPRs). These UPRs, reinforced with metallic fillers like iron oxide, alumina, nickel, and copper, exhibit enhanced mechanical, thermal, and magnetic properties. The incorporation of these nanofillers significantly improves composite matrices, increasing tensile strength, thermal stability, conductivity, and magnetic responsiveness, thus making them suitable for applications in electronics, automotive, and structural industries. This study highlights the synergistic effects of multi-filler systems, which provide superior reinforcement by altering thermal conductivity and electromagnetic absorption properties. Furthermore, this review promotes the circular economy, demonstrating how PET waste can be transformed into high-performance, sustainable composites, thereby reducing environmental impact and conserving resources. Future research is directed toward optimizing nanoparticle dispersion and developing multi-functional composites tailored for specific high-performance applications. This paper contributes valuable insights into sustainable materials science by advancing Recycling Technologies and Hybrid Nanocomposites Development. Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) and Unsaturated Polyester Resins (UPRs) represent two pivotal categories of polymers with substantial applications across diverse industries, driven by their distinct properties and functionalities. PET is a saturated polyester characterized by its thermal stability, clarity, strength, and moldability, making it an ideal material for manufacturing films, bottles, and fibers. However, the escalating production and consumption of PET have resulted in a corresponding increase in PET waste, presenting significant environmental and economic challenges. Efficient recycling methods exist for clear PET bottles, such as washing and remelting; yet contaminated or colored bottles pose greater difficulties. To address this issue, lower-quality PET can undergo chemical recycling processes that involve purification and conversion into new PET, thereby facilitating its reintroduction into the production cycle.', 'It is important to position plastic wastes as low-cost, abundant raw chemical materials and consider them as the beginning rather than the end of value chain.16 To this end, high-purity monomers or chemicals obtained from chemical depolymerization of plastic wastes can be recombined into new plastics via closed-loop recycling or other value-added products via upcycling.11 Primarily, it is difficult to adapt the design of traditional polyolefins into closed-loop recycling. Polyolefins (Fig. 2), such as polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS), are the most widely used petroleum-based polymer materials, with a global market size of USD 240 billion in 2020. Generally, polyolefin monomers are joined by C-C bonds, with the monomer skeleton structure also composed of C-C bonds. Thus, the selective recovery of monomers by polyolefin depolymerization is challenging under moderate reaction conditions, as the bond energies of the different C-C bonds are basically the same.11,17 Although some recent advances have been made in polyolefin depolymerization, with the capture of fuel additives such as alkanes and aromatics through the catalytic pyrolysis of waste polyolefins, this cannot solve the recycling issue.17,18 Therefore, there is still a need to produce new plastic from non-renewable resources including petroleum and coal.19 Moreover, if plastic waste is converted to fuel, the carbon atoms in the plastic will still end up in the atmosphere, which is not conducive to carbon neutrality in terms of carbon footprint. Compared with polyolefins, polyesters can be more easily depolymerized to their monomers via highly selective breakage of the ester bonds.20-23 More importantly, most polyesters, such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), polycaprolactone (PCL), poly(ethylene-2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF), and PET, can be produced from a variety of sources, including non-renewable and renewable resources, and have become more attractive due to their good thermal and mechanical properties, processing versatility, and degradability (Fig. 2).24-27 Among these, PET is the most important and abundant one, and is widely used as thermoplastic polymers with excellent properties, including thermal stability, transparency, high strength, low density, chemical resistance and low cost.28 PBT and PEF are structurally and functionally similar to PET, and possess unique advantages in physicochemical properties.29,30 For example, PBT can be a viable substitute for the crystalline thermoplastics (e.g., PE and nylon) because of its lower melting point, lower strength and stiffness, lower glass transition temperature, and better impact resistance. PLA is a cornstarch-based biodegradable polymer and exhibits mechanical properties comparable to those of polystyrene. Though some grades of PLA are semi-crystalline, they generally crystallize slowly during processing, resulting in PLA products of low crystallinity [1], [2], [3], [4]. Therefore, HDT is largely dictated by the glass transition temperature (Tg) of PLA. The low HDT limits the current applications of PLA to those disposable goods that do not require high heat resistance. Apparently, it is essential to enhance the HDT of PLA to expand its applications at elevated temperatures [5]. Various methods have been explored to improve the HDT of PLA. One method is to incorporate heat-resistant reinforcing fillers into PLA to increase the HDT. Additions of wood fiber [6], [8], glass fiber [7], cellulose fiber [9], wheat straw [10], [11], corn stover and soy stalks [11] to PLA, were all noted to increase HDT; however, the improvement in HDT is limited (within 20 °C). Another method is to add a nucleating agent to increase the crystallinity and hence improve the heat resistance of PLA. Talc [12], montmorillonite [13], and bismaleimide [14] were studied as nucleating agents for PLA, and behaved differently in improving the HDT of PLA. While addition of 9.1 wt% talc brought about an increase of 1 °C in the HDT of PLA [12], incorporation of 8 wt% montmorillonite to PLA resulted in an increase of 28 °C in HDT [13]. A further increment is limited mainly due to aggregation of the nucleating agents.', "Figure 12 shows the heat deflection temperature (HDT) of PLA and the polymer blends. PLA showed an HDT of around 53°C, a value close to that reported in the literature.91 Incorporating 30% AES into the PLA matrix did not increase the HDT, producing a similar value of 52.6°C. Although the acrylonitrile in the AES molecular structure often confers thermal and chemical resistance, it did not improve HDT. Therefore, the structural stability of the PLA matrix was maintained in the PLA/AES blend. Similarly, the 0.2 phr DCP did not improve the HDT of the PLA/AES/DCP blend. In the 0.4-1 phr DCP range, the HDT results of the PLA/AES/DCP blends stabilized between 53.2 and 53.8°C, a minor and insignificant improvement. Even though the degree of crosslinking increased in PLA/AES/DCP blends, it could not significantly increment the HDT. The annealed PLAT, PL/AEST, and PLA/AES/DCPT samples presented an increment of around 11°C in HDT. This behavior suggests that PLA and the polymer blends gained structural stability upon annealing, explained by the higher degree of crystallinity shown in XRD and DSC. The effect of crosslinking on PLA/AES/DCPT blends was insignificant, bearing that the HDT of all samples was within the margins of experimental error. The most prominent factor positively influencing HDT was the development of higher crystallinity in the PLA matrix. The HDT results of the PLA/AES/DCP blends are of technological relevance, especially for the composition containing 0.8 phr of DCP that retained a high impact strength. For the first time in the literature, AES has been applied as an impact modifier to PLA under the combined effect of the crosslinking and annealing heat treatment. The direct addition of AES improved PLA's ductility and impact strength, possibly due to polar interactions. Crosslinking increased proportionally to the DCP content used in PLA/AES blends, as evidenced by torque rheometry, resulting in higher molecular entanglement in the PLA/AES/DCP blends, increased viscosity, and reduced fluidity according to MFI. However, the 0.2 DCP could not effectively crosslink the PLA/AES blends, giving similar results to the non-crosslinked base system. Adding 0.8 phr of DCP maximized the impact strength and elongation at break, with gains of 505.6% and 264.8%, respectively, compared to PLA. From the standpoint of annealing, FTIR and XRD showed the formation of crystalline materials for PLA and the polymer blends. However, there were improvements in elastic modulus, Shore D hardness, and HDT. The data collected suggests that the PLA/AES/DCP (0.8 phr) system promoted the optimum mechanical and thermomechanical properties balance, as it remained tough and had good thermomechanical stability by HDT. Therefore, data suggests that new semi-biodegradable materials can be produced with the potential for application in additive manufacturing. The typical heat deflection temperature (HDT) of amorphous PLA is **50–60 °C**, as this range is dictated by its glass transition temperature (Tg). This is supported by multiple contexts:  
- PLA inherently exhibits low crystallinity due to slow crystallization during processing, and its HDT is closely tied to Tg ([1], [5]).  
- Experimental measurements in the literature report HDT values of ~53 °C ([2], [3]) and ~55 °C ([5], [11]) for unmodified PLA, consistent with the Tg range.  
- While some studies mention lower HDT values (e.g., 39 °C in [6]), these likely reflect specific formulations or testing conditions, whereas the majority of evidence confirms the 50–60 °C range for amorphous PLA.  

Thus, the HDT of amorphous PLA remains near its Tg due to limited crystallinity, restricting its use in high-temperature applications without modifications.
reference: Amorphous PLA has a low HDT, typically around 55°C (near its Tg). This limits its use in applications requiring thermal resistance (e.g., hot coffee cups) unless it is crystallized (raising HDT to ~100°C) or composited with heat-resistant fillers.
