retrieved_contexts: ['In situ injectable hydrogels can be formed by either chemical or physical crosslinking methods. Chemically crosslinked hydrogels, prepared through photopolymerization [4], disulfide bond formation [5], or reaction between thiols and acrylate or sulfones [5], undergo significant volume changes during the phase transition. In contrast to chemical hydrogels, physically crosslinked hydrogels, formed by the self-assembly of polymers in response to environmental stimuli (for example, temperature, pH, or both) display sol-gel transitions without marked volume changes. The hydrogels systems are relatively low viscosity aqueous solutions (sol state) prior to injection, but rapidly convert into a gel under physiological conditions post-injection [1], [6], [7]. Physical hydrogels have several advantages over chemical hydrogels, because they do not require photo irradiation, use of organic solvents or crosslinking agents, and do not release heat at the gelation site, which may denature incorporated proteins and damage embedded cells and surrounding tissues. Thus, the physical systems have recently attracted increased attention. For use in drug/cell delivery and tissue engineering, hydrogels should be low-viscosity solutions (free-flowing) prior to subcutaneous injection, and should rapidly gel in the human body, where ultimate degradation of the hydrogels is desired. Injectable hydrogels that are sensitive to temperature are useful for both in vitro and in vivo applications, because temperature control is generally easy. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)/Polyester copolymers, as an injectable biodegradable temperature-sensitive physically crosslinked hydrogel, of hydrophilic biocompatible PEG with biodegradable biocompatible aliphatic polyesters, for example polylactide (PLA) [8], [9], poly(d,l-lactic acid-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) [10], [11], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [12], [13], or poly[(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate] (PHB) [14], have received increasing attention as promising biomaterials. Among those thermogelling systems, block copolymers of PLGA and PEG are very important owing to their high adjustability of biodegradation and good properties to encapsulate and release biological substances [15], [16], [17], [18]. However, the appropriate composition region, such as block ratio and block length, is narrow, which limits its application to a large extent. Recently, Yu’ group has found a facile approach to prepare a thermogelling system by simply blending two similar block copolymers with different block ratios [19], [20]. One specimen was water-soluble and the other was just a precipitate in a broad temperature region. Although neither specimen possessed the thermogelling property, the aqueous solution of the copolymer mixture with a certain mix ratio showed a reversible sol-gel transition with the increase of temperature. On the basis of this good idea, thermogelling property of mixed star-shaped block copolymer hydrogels is investigated by us in order to develop applications of pure star-shaped block copolymer hydrogels. Our study effectively enlarges the applicable window of the pertinent polymers for designing injectable biomaterials. In this paper, a new kind of copolymer, 3-arm or 4-arm star-shaped poly(d,l-lactic-co-glycolic acid)-b-methoxy poly(ethylene glycol)(3sPLGA-mPEG or 4sPLGA-mPEG), is synthesized via the arm-first method rather than the core-first method reported in the literature [21], [22], [23]. We will present a systematic study of sol-gel transition behavior, micellization behavior and degradation behavior of the two-component thermogelling mixture and examine their in vitro and in vivo biocompatibility. Comparing with plenty of reports of biodegradable biomaterials, the detailed research of the degradation profiles of injectable temperature-sensitive hydrogels, particularly of physical hydrogels, is very limited. As such, our study effectively enlarges the applicable window of the pertinent polymers and puts forward a new strategy to design injectable biomaterials.', 'Stimuli-sensitive injectable hydrogels, composed of biodegradable copolymers, have emerged as prominent candidate materials for the sustained delivery of therapeutic drugs. In this study, we developed a biodegradable and temperature-sensitive injectable hydrogel system based on heparin-bearing poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide)-b-poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide) (Hep-PCLA) as the carrier system for lysozyme. Hep-PCLA conjugates are capable of undergoing temperature-induced sol-to-gel transitions in an aqueous solution. The gelation rate, mechanical strength, and viscosity of Hep-PCLA conjugates are controllably tunable by varying the graft density of PCLA copolymers to heparin. The gel window in which Hep-PCLA forms a gel covers the physiological conditions (37 °C), i.e., free flowing Hep-PCLA in aqueous solutions (25 °C) could form a hydrogel at body temperature. Using an in vitro cytotoxicity test, Hep-PCLA conjugates were found to be non-toxic to fibroblast cells, even at high concentrations. Lysozyme, chosen as a model protein, was effectively loaded into Hep-PCLA conjugates using ionic and hydrophobic interactions. The lysozyme-loaded conjugates readily formed a hydrogel when implanted in the back of Sprague-Dawley rats, and retarded the initial burst of lysozyme release, exhibiting sustained release. In recent years, numerous injectable hydrogels have been developed that are responsive to various stimuli including temperature, pH, and enzymes.10-13 Stimuli-responsive injectable hydrogels, also termed smart hydrogels, are able to switch sol-to-gel phase transitions in response to various stimuli. Of these stimuli, temperature is the most widely used stimulus in injectable hydrogels.14,15 Polymers exhibiting lower critical solution temperatures (LCSTs) with ideal phase transitions between room and body temperatures are attractive candidate materials for injectable formulations.16,17 Such polymers are soluble at room temperature and form hydrogels after administration. For instance, various copolymers including Pluronic, poly(phosphazene), and poly(N-isopropyl acrylamide) exist in the sol state at room temperature and transform into gels at body temperature.14,18-20 Although these copolymers exhibit sharp temperature-responsive transitions, their biological usage has been limited due to non-degradability and limited biocompatibility. To surmount these issues, poly(ester)-based biodegradable and biocompatible polymers that are capable of exhibiting LCSTs have been developed.21 In particular, poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide)-b-poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone-co-lactide) (PCLA)-based copolymer hydrogels are promising candidates for injectable delivery systems.22 In addition to the PCLA copolymers, thermosensitive injective hydrogels based on poly(ethylene glycol)-b-poly(ε-caprolactone)-b-poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG) have been developed for biomedical applications.23 The PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG-based thermosensitive gels combined with curcumin have been proven to enhance anti-tumor activity in a colorectal peritoneal carcinomatosis model as well as wound healing in an excision wound model.24,25 Furthermore, PEG-b-PCL-b-PEG/acellular bone matrix composite hydrogels have been used for bone regeneration in cranial defects.26 Although PCLA-based amphiphilic copolymer hydrogel systems could load proteins and enable their sustained release, the neutral nature of hydrogels severely restricts the loading of some proteins, as most therapeutic proteins are ionically charged.27,28 It is noteworthy to mention that the integration of the PCLA-based polymers with cationic or anionic charged polymers may provide a useful hydrogel system for the delivery of ionically charged proteins. Natural polysaccharide-based ionic polymers including hyaluronic acid, heparin, chitosan, and dextran derivatives have been extensively investigated in biomedical applications mainly because of their biocompatibility, non-immunogenicity, biodegradability and cell-adhesion properties.29-37 Among the variety of natural polysaccharides, heparin is a negatively charged linear polysaccharide composed of alternating units of sulfated glucuronic acid and glucosamine derivatives.38 Heparin is clinically used as an anticoagulant. The presence of negatively charged functional groups (sulfate and carboxylate) endows a high negative charge to heparin, which facilitates ionic interaction and complexation with various proteins, growth factors, and chemokines.39 Given its unique structure, hydrogels and nanoparticles composed of heparin exhibit attractive properties in biomedical applications.40 For example, photo-cross-linked alginate-heparin hydrogels allowed the sustained release of various therapeutic proteins.41,42 It is known that heparin could form complexes with various growth factors.43 The heparin present in the photo-cross-linked hydrogels binds to various growth factors and allows the sustained release of growth factors.44 Although numerous attempts have been made to develop heparin-based hydrogels, no significant attempt has been made to develop heparin-based biodegradable and injectable hydrogels for protein delivery.', 'To form the adhesive hydrogels, biocompatible and biodegradable natural or synthetic polymers can be cross-linked physically or chemically, or a combination of both. (74) have modified the gelatin with methacrylic anhydride to synthesize methacrylate functionalized gelatin (GelMA). (75) have prepared HA hydrogel by the method of photoinitiation, in which methacrylate modified HA was obtained by the reaction of HA and methacrylic anhydride. (77) reported a new drug encapsulation strategy to achieve the sustain release of small molecule ionic drug from hydrogel platform. Based solely on the provided context:

1.  **Crystallinity Impact:** Stereochemistry (L vs D isomers) directly influences the crystallinity of PLA.
    *   Optically pure PLLA (L-form) and PDLA (D-form) are semicrystalline polymers ([2], [4], [5], [9], [12]).
    *   The racemic mixture PDLLA (DL-form) is amorphous ([2], [4], [5], [9], [12]).
2.  **Degradation Rate Correlation:** Crystallinity is a key factor controlling degradation rate.
    *   **Amorphous PDLLA degrades faster:** Due to its amorphous structure, PDLLA has a higher degradation rate compared to the semicrystalline PLLA or PDLA. The amorphous regions are more accessible to water penetration, facilitating hydrolytic degradation of the ester bonds ([1], [4], [5], [6], [9], [14]).
    *   **Semicrystalline PLLA/PDLA degrade slower:** The crystalline regions in PLLA and PDLA are more resistant to hydrolytic attack, leading to a slower overall degradation rate ([4], [5], [9], [14]).
3.  **Stereocomplexation Effect:** Blending PLLA and PDLA can form stereocomplex (SC) crystallites.
    *   SC crystallites have a higher degree of crystallinity, higher melting temperature, and **increased resistance toward hydrolytic degradation** compared to homocrystallites of PLLA or PDLA alone ([3], [8], [10], [15]).
    *   Materials with a higher degree of stereocomplexation exhibit **slower mass loss** (degradation) ([3]).
    *   Factors affecting stereocomplexation (like oligomer architecture, end-groups, blend ratio) consequently affect the degradation rate. For example, star-shaped d-LA oligomers with alcoholic end-groups promoted stereocomplexation and slowed degradation, while carboxylic end-groups reduced stereocomplexation and accelerated degradation ([3]).

**In summary:** The L/D isomer ratio (stereochemistry) determines the crystallinity of PLA. Amorphous PDLLA (DL-form) degrades fastest. Semicrystalline PLLA (L-form) or PDLA (D-form) degrade slower. Blending PLLA and PDLA to form stereocomplex crystallites further increases crystallinity and provides the greatest resistance to hydrolytic degradation, resulting in the slowest degradation rate.
reference: Poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) is semi-crystalline and degrades slower due to the difficulty of water penetrating the crystalline regions. Poly(D,L-lactide) (PDLLA) is amorphous (due to the random distribution of L and D isomers inhibiting crystallization) and therefore degrades much faster due to higher water uptake and easier hydrolysis.

retrieved_contexts: ["Hydrogen bonds hold the starch chains together, making them insoluble in cold water. Additionally, these hydrogen bonds lead to a high glass transition temperature, which makes starch difficult to process. This disadvantage can be overcome by converting raw starch into thermoplastic starch (TPS). This conversion is achieved through a process called “gelatinization,” which is performed in the presence of excess water, using a plasticizer and heat. As a result of this irreversible process, the crystalline structure in the starch granules is eliminated, resulting in a completely amorphous structure [6, 7]. The selection of plasticizers plays a pivotal role in determining the mechanical, thermal, and biological properties of TPS. Among various options, the combination of glycerol and D-sorbitol offers significant advantages over conventional plasticizers such as urea, glycols, and citrate esters [7-9]. Glycerol, due to its high hydrophilicity, disrupts intermolecular hydrogen bonding between starch chains, thereby improving processability. In contrast, D-sorbitol, with its longer molecular structure, contributes to enhanced thermal stability and water resistance [10]. Furthermore, its low volatility reduces plasticizer migration, thus improving the long-term stability of the material [11]. The synergistic use of these two plasticizers can effectively address common issues associated with TPS, including starch retrogradation, plasticizer migration, brittleness, and elevated glass transition temperatures, while allowing for precise tuning of water resistance and mechanical performance [9, 10]. Li and Huneault [7] reported that while glycerol alone produced TPS with low thermal stability and excessive hydrophilicity, the incorporation of sorbitol improved expansion resistance by 30%. Similarly, Sanyang et al. [10] found that combining glycerol and sorbitol doubled the Young's modulus of palm starch films compared to systems plasticized with glycerol alone. However, these studies primarily focused on corn or potato starch, leaving a significant knowledge gap in the plasticization behavior of wheat starch-a variant particularly rich in amylose. In a recent study in which glycerol was used as a plasticizer, it was reported that the tensile strength and Young's modulus of TPS films obtained from wheat starch were higher than those of other conventional starches [4]. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to systematically investigate the physicochemical properties and cellular interactions associated with varying glycerol-to-sorbitol ratios in wheat starch-based TPS formulations. Based solely on the provided context, the role of glycerol in TPS production is:

1.  **Disruption of Hydrogen Bonds:** Glycerol, due to its high hydrophilicity, disrupts intermolecular hydrogen bonding between starch chains ([1], [2]). This is essential because native starch's strong hydrogen bonds make it insoluble and difficult to process.
2.  **Facilitation of Gelatinization:** Glycerol acts as a plasticizer during the gelatinization process (performed with excess water and heat), which converts raw starch into TPS by eliminating the crystalline structure and resulting in a completely amorphous structure ([1], [2], [3], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10])
3.  **Reduction of Glass Transition Temperature (Tg):** Glycerol lowers the high glass transition temperature (Tg) of native starch, making it processable like a thermoplastic ([1], [2], [4], [5], [9], [10]). For example, it can decrease Tg from around 87°C to 25°C ([4], [5]).
4.  **Formation of Hydrogen Bonds with Starch:** Plasticization occurs because glycerol molecules form hydrogen bonds with the hydroxyl groups of starch, replacing the strong starch-starch bonds with plasticizer-starch bonds ([9], [10]). This is evidenced by FTIR spectroscopy showing shifts in the OH band ([11], [12]).
5.  **Improvement of Processability:** By disrupting hydrogen bonds and lowering Tg, glycerol significantly improves the processability of starch, allowing it to be shaped using techniques like injection molding, extrusion, and blow moulding ([6], [7], [8], [14], [15]).

**(Additional notes from context on glycerol limitations):**
*   Alone, it can lead to TPS with low thermal stability and excessive hydrophilicity ([1], [2]).
*   It is known to leach out during aging and humidity exposure ([3]).
*   It has a higher retrogradation rate compared to some other plasticizers like sorbitol ([9], [10]).
*   Therefore, it is often used in combination with other plasticizers like sorbitol ([1], [2], [4], [5], [9], [10], [13]) to overcome these limitations.

The access of water molecules from the external environment is indeed easier when the particles form a continuous path that connect the surface and the interior of the composite. The **lag phase** in the biodegradation of plastics in compost refers to the initial period during which abiotic degradation mechanisms (e.g., **chemical hydrolysis**) dominate over biotic enzymatic processes. This phase is characterized by microbial acclimatization to the environment and the time required for **water diffusion** into the polymer matrix and enzymatic cleavage of polymer chains. 

1. **Mechanism**:  
   - For synthetic polymers like PLA, the lag phase arises due to their resistance to immediate microbial assimilation. Water penetration initiates hydrolysis, breaking ester bonds and reducing molecular weight to a threshold (~10–20 kDa) accessible for microbial enzymes.  
   - In contrast, natural polymers (e.g., cellulose, starch) bypass this phase as their biodegradation starts immediately via extracellular enzymes.  

2. **Duration**:  
   - The lag phase varies with material composition and environmental conditions. For example:  
     - **Cellulose** (readily biodegradable) exhibits a negligible lag phase (~10 days) in compost.  
     - **PLA** typically shows a lag phase of ~20 days in compost, shortened by additives like graphene nanoplatelets (GRH) or blending with thermoplastic starch (TPCS).  
     - Natural fiber-PP composites (e.g., pineapple leaf fiber) have extended lag phases (~30 days) due to their recalcitrance.  

3. **Environmental Influence**:  
   - In compost, the lag phase is affected by microbial diversity, temperature, and organic matter. A priming effect (over-degradation of indigenous carbon) can mask the lag phase in materials like TPCS.  
   - In controlled systems (e.g., inoculated vermiculite), the lag phase is more distinct due to the absence of background organic carbon.  

4. **Significance**:  
   - The lag phase determines the biodegradation timeline. Polymers with shorter lag phases (e.g., DH4T cassava starch sheets) achieve faster mineralization (>80% in 45 days), while longer phases delay biodegradation, impacting compost facility timelines.  

In summary, the lag phase reflects the transition from abiotic breakdown to microbial-driven depolymerization, critical for designing compostable plastics with aligned degradation rates.
reference: The lag phase is the initial period where no significant mineralization (CO2 evolution) occurs. During this time, microorganisms colonize the surface and secrete extracellular enzymes to begin fragmenting the polymer chain. Only after the molecular weight drops sufficiently to produce water-soluble intermediates does rapid assimilation and mineralization begin.

To resolve these limitations, many research groups developed copolymers of PHB with longer side chains monomeric units like 3-hydroxyvalerate (3-HV) and 3-hydroxyhexanoate (3-HHx) [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. Chemical structures of PHB, PHV, and P(HB-co-HV) are shown in Fig. 1.', "First, PHAs are very difficult to convert into packages with conventional plastic processing techniques. In addition to their low viscosity and melt strength, PHA thermal degradation occurs upon melting;5 this depresses the final structural and mechanical properties of the plastic part or package. The crystallization of PBS could be pronouncedly enhanced by partial crosslinking, resulting in higher strength, elongation at break, and impact toughness.15', 'AbstractPolyhydroxyalkanotes (PHAs) are biobased and biodegradable polymers, of which poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV, 3 %mol HV) and poly-3-hydroxybutyrate-co-4-hydroxybutyrate [P(3HB,4HB), 10 %mol 4HB] are currently commercialized. To understand the influence of chemical structure on the biodegradability of PHA, the biodegradation behavior of poly(hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), PHBV (40 %mol HV), PHBV (20 %mol HV), PHBV (3 %mol HV) and P(3HB,4HB) (10 %mol 4HB) were investigated under the controlled composting conditions according to ISO 14855-1. It was found that PHAs with different chemical structures can be biodegraded under the controlled composting conditions. The order of biodegradability was P(3HB, 4HB) (40 %mol 4HB) ≈ PHBV(40 %mol HV) >PHBV(20 %mol HV) >PHBV(3 %mol HV) >PHB. IntroductionPoly (hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is one type of polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) that can be produced by bacteria from agricultural raw materials. The chemical structures of several PHAs are shown in Fig. 1. The biobased PHBV can be processed to form a variety of useful products and has attracted the attention of academia and industry due to its good biodegradability, biocompatibility and thermoplasticity. Compared with poly (hydroxybutyrate) (PHB), PHBV has good toughness and ease of processing. However, its poor thermal stability, low elongation at break, slow crystallization rate and high degree of crystallinity still remain problematic. Therefore, it has been subject to chemical and physical modifications.In the chemical modifications, the HV content of PHBV can be adjusted by controlling the amount of propanoic acid during the biosynthesis process [1], [2], [3]. Other chemical methods, such as grafting and reactive blending have also been used to modify its properties [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. It was found that the melting temperature of PHBV decreased with increase of HV content when the total molar content of HV was less than 28%, but increased when the molar content of HV was more than 28% [11]. The toughness of PHBV was also affected by the HV content in the molecular chains. It could vary from rigid to flexible with change of HV content, for example, it could behave like polyethylene, polypropylene and polyvinylchloride when the HV content is high, medium and low, respectively [12].Obviously, the modification of PHBV should not destroy its biodegradability, which is its most important advantage, regardless of the aims of modification. Therefore, broad investigation of biodegradability of different modified PHBV systems is important.Hermida et al. [13] found that the biodegradation of PHBV proceeded via a surface erosion mechanism resulting in the formation of pits by microbial attack, and the crystallinity and molecular weight of PHBV specimens remained virtually constant after 45 days of degradation in a liquid medium inoculated with a 2% v/v fresh spore suspension of Somiyaensis SSM 5670. Li et al. [14] studied the enzymatic degradation of microbial copolyesters consisting of 3-hydroxybutyrate and medium-chain-length 3-hydroxyalkanoates. They found that the crystallinity of PHAs decreased in the order of PHB > PHBV (19 %mol HV)> PHBHHx (19 %mol HHx)> PHBA (15 %mol HA), while the degradation rate increased in the order of PHBV > PHB > PHBHHx > PHBA in a medium with PHA depolymerase. They proposed that the length of side chains in the PHA structure would affect the depolymerase degradation rate, that is, PHA with longer side chains, including PHBHHx and PHBA, are less favorable for depolymerase degradation than PHA with shorter side chains. Weng et al. investigated the biodegradation of PHBV (3 %mol HV) on both pilot and laboratory scale composting conditions and found that its degradation occurred from the surface erosion to the interior [15].Although there have been some investigations on the biodegradation of PHA, the effect of HV content on the biodegradation of PHA has not been reported in open literature. Therefore, in this paper, the biodegradability of PHA with different chemical structures PHBV (40 %mol HV), PHBV (20 %mol HV), PHBV(3 %mol HV), P(3HB, 4HB) has been investigated by the controlled composting conditions according to ISO 14855-1 [16].', 'Many attempts were carried out to improve the performances of PHB, mostly by copolymerization of PHB with other monomers such as β-hydroxyvalerate (β-HV), 4-hydroxybutyrate (4-HB) and 3-hydroxyhexanoate (3-HHx). However, the copolymerization route compromises on the strength and E-Modulus of PHB, and results in even slower crystallization of the copolymerized materials. Alternatively, another approach by blending PHB with other (co)polymers such as ethylene propylene rubber (EPR) [13], poly(ethylene-co-vinyl acetate) (EVA) [14], epoxidized natural rubber (ENR) [15], poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) [16], poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) [17, 18], poly(propylene) (PP) [19], poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) [20] and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) [21, 22] was applied in literature. Among these polymers, the PVAc, PEO and EVA with >85 wt% of vinyl acetate were reported to be miscible with PHB while the others are immiscible with PHB. Another polymer used to blend with PHB is poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), which is biodegradable under aerobic conditions and is a condensation polymer of succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol [23]. Commercial grade of PBS, currently, is synthesized from oil-based feedstock, however, both of the two monomers, i.e. succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol, can be derived from renewable resources via fermentation [24, 25]. Thus, PHB/PBS blends can potentially retain both biocompostable and renewable characteristics. Qiu et al. [26, 27] blended poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) with PHB and PHBV in solution. They reported that PHB and PHBV were immiscible with PBS except the PHB/PBS (20/80) blend which showed limited miscibility. The incorporation of PBS restricted the crystallization of PHB and PHBV to a certain extent. In our previous work, the toughness and the strength of the PHB and PHBV were remarkably enhanced by incorporation of PBS in combination with an in situ compatibilization using dicumyl peroxide as a free radical initiator [28]. However, to the authors’ knowledge, the morphology and crystallization behavior of melt-blended PHB/PBS which are more environmentally friendly and more industrial feasible have not been widely studied yet. The prime objective of this paper is to increase the over all crystallization of the PHB by melt blending with PBS. The results of an investigation concerning of the phase morphology of the blends, the crystallization and melting behavior of the PHB in the presence of PBS are discussed.', 'Similar to PLLA, poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is also an aliphatic polyester with similar applications and mechanical properties, which is synthesized by bacterial fermentation from renewable resources like sugar and vegetable oil [4], [5], [6], [7]. When PHBV is implanted to animals intramuscularly, the tissue reaction is similar to the reaction to silk and less severe than the reaction to catgut [8]. Despite of its potential application in clinics, PHBV has major issues of narrow processing temperature window and polymer chain scission during melt processing, which have significantly restricted its application [9]. Much effort has been paid in the past decades to improve the mechanical properties, particularly the impact resistance of the PLLA and PHBV materials. Blending with other polymers has been widely considered as an easy and cost-effective way to improve their mechanical properties and processibility of polymer materials. Although they both have the problem of brittleness, it is very interesting that the PLLA/PHBV blends have been shown to exhibit a balanced stiffness and toughness [10], [11]. Ferreira et al. [12] reported that adding PHBV to PLLA led to tougher materials compared to the neat samples, and the blend films showed yield behavior. In addition, the studies of Nanda et al. [10] and Modi et al. [13] also showed that the tensile elongation of the poly(lactic acid) (PLA) and PHBV blends was improved by blending compared to the neat polymers. Very recently, the low-cost and easily prepared, biocompatible and biodegradable PLLA/PHBV fibers were developed [14], [15]. The composite fibers show decreased shrinkage in boiling water, indicating that the heat resistance property of the PLLA was improved by blending with PHBV. Moreover, the softness of the composite fibers was also enhanced compared to that of pure PLLA fibers. Although previous studies have shown that the PLLA/PHBV blends exhibit improved toughness and tensile properties, the two components showed rather poor compatibility and were phase-separated in a wide composition range [13], [16]. A common way to improve the compatibility in immiscible polymer blends is to introduce a compatibilizer between the two phases. In general, the compatibilizer should have good miscibility with both of the components in the immiscible polymer blends. For PLLA/PHBV blends, the main compatibilizers include poly(vinyl acetate) (PVAc) [17] and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) [18]. El-Hadi et al. blended PVAc (9.1 wt %) with poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) and PLLA, and found that the blends with PVAc were miscible [17]. In parallel to this study, Wang et al. reported that the elongation at break of the PLA/PHBV blends was greatly improved from 2.1% to 237.0% by the addition of PEG (20 wt %). Polyester plasticizer (Lapol 108) has been also applied to improve the miscibility of PLA/PHB blends [19]. The above compatibilizers effectively improved the miscibility of PLLA/PHBV or PLA/PHB blends, however the contents of the third component were relatively high. Therefore these methods may significantly increase the producing cost, and meanwhile the ‘3B’ nature of the materials will be compromised.', 'Poly(hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) has become an inevitable bio-plastic. It has gained the focus of present researchers due to effective awareness campaigns for environmental sustainability [1]. Many types of bacterial genera, like Micrococcus, Pseudomonads, and Ralstoniaeutrophs, etc., are capable of synthesizing PHB as their intracellular inclusions-useable as energy sources under nutrients strive conditions [2]. Once isolated from the cell biomass, the PHB exhibits brittleness, low mechanical strength, hydrophobicity, and mild degradation rate which makes it incompatible for diverse biomedical applications [3]. Therefore, PHB-based bio-composites with other materials like poly(caprolactone) (PCL), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), and cellulose, etc., have been practiced for improved mechanical properties [4]. The PHB/PCL composites had been reported viable scaffolds’ formation for possible biomedical applications [5]. The 3-hydroxy butyric acid is a monomer produced by hydrolytic degradation of PHB which has also been natively found in blood serum although at low concentrations [6]. Poly(caprolactone) (PCL) is a low-cost linear biodegradable aliphatic polyester, usually obtained through ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone in the presence of catalyst stannous octanoate. It is easily degradable through hydrolysis of its ester linkages in the physiological environment of the human body and producing no toxins. The PC, therefore, qualifies as an implantable biomaterial, and as a drugs/proteins carrier and deliverer [7]. The tensile strength of PCL is around 23 MPa and its elongation-at-break is comparable to plastics which shows its potential as a precursor in composite formation. Moreover, the thermal stability of PCL-based composites is usually high. The PCL can be fabricated into thin membranes with appropriate mechanical strength for biomedical applications [8]. The pure PCL films are also hydrophobic like that of pure PHB [9]; thus, there is a need to chemically modify their surfaces to impart hydrophilicity and to tune the degradation profile [10].', 'Major applications of PHB in different sectors PHB/polysaccharide blend-like pectin-PHB is used in making nanofibers. These nanofibers are used in retinal tissue designing [114]. The PHBV (polyhydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) and chitin blends have a porous texture with different macro- and micropores and serve different purposes (migration, transportation, etc.) in tissue engineering [115]. Chitosan PHB blend acts as an ideal matrix in drug delivery applications. The controlled drug delivery is possible as PHB/chitosan blend possesses a porous texture due to cross-linking [116]. The mix of PHA/PHB is used in food packing and medical implantation as it has better mechanical properties [117]. On blending of PHB with PEG (polyethylene glycol), the increase in the hydrophilic property of PHB is reported [118]. For the safety from bacterial infections post-operations, the micro- and nanospheres of PHB with PEG loaded with antibiotics are used. PEG/PHB blends promoted the growth of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs). The presence of different-sized pores leads to MSCs growth with a slow rate of differentiation [119]. FDA has approved the use of PHB/PEG films for tissue engineering. Polyhydroxybutyrate and poly-ε-caprolactone (PHB/PCL) are used to manufacture fibrous membranes by the electrospinning method. These membranes possess antibacterial properties (N-halamine quaternary ammonium salt (HQAS) as an antibacterial agent) and hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties when treated with HCl and NH4OH [120]. These hydrophilic membranes possess enhanced antimicrobial properties together with thrombogenicity with a blood clotting index of 60.6%. These pH-responsive membranes generated from PHB and PCL have better stability, durability, and improved storage. With these properties, the membranes offer a great potential application in the biomedical sector. Polyhydroxybutyrate/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PHB/PCL) scaffolds and PHB/PCL/solgel-derived silica (SGS) scaffolds are used to incorporate a model drug, levofloxacin (LFX), and MG-63 osteoblast-like cell cultivation on both scaffolds have shown that there is no effect on biocompatibility from LFX inclusion [121]. These multifunctional scaffolds are showing promising results in bone tissue engineering applications.', 'Copula-Based Data Augmentation and Machine Learning for Predicting Tensile Strength of 3D-Printed PLA Under Anisotropic Conditions In recent years, the growing concern over environmental pollution and the excessive use of non-biodegradable materials has driven significant research efforts toward the development of sustainable and eco-friendly alternatives. Biodegradable polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), have garnered considerable attention as promising candidates for various applications due to their renewable origin, biodegradability, and compatibility with industrial processes. PLA, a thermoplastic polymer derived from lactic acid, is widely recognized for its mechanical strength and transparency [1], while PHAs are a family of microbial biopolymers, endowed with excellent biodegradability and tunable thermal and mechanical stability depending on PHA composition [2]. In particular, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), polyhydroxybutyrate-co-valerate (PHBV), and polyhydroxybutyrate-co-hexanoate (PHBH) are among the most studied members of the PHA family, offering a versatile range of properties that can be tailored for specific applications through variations in their monomer composition or post functionalization reaction [3, 4]. The use of these polymers as matrices for advanced composite development offers opportunities to optimize their individual properties and expand their application potential. A key aspect of advancing the functionality of biodegradable polymeric films is the incorporation of functional additives, such as titanium dioxide (TiO2), which can impart unique properties to the material [5, 6]. TiO2 is well-known for its photocatalytic activity, which makes it particularly effective for applications in environmental remediation, self-cleaning surfaces, and antimicrobial materials [7, 8]. For this reason, TiO2-based polymer composite materials have gained much interest in applications in many fields, such as catalysis, bioengineering, food packaging, biotechnology, and biomedical sector [9-12].', 'Blending poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) and poly(butylene adipate-co- terephthalate) (PBAT) presents an effective approach to fabricate fully biodegradable polymer blends with tailored mechanical properties. This study investigated the composition on the mechanical properties and structure of PHBV/PBAT blend. The remarkable enhancement in elongation of the PHBV/PBAT blends was shown due to the ductile PBAT. The fracture behavior of the PHBV/PBAT specimens transited from brittle to ductile with the increase of the PBAT in the blends. Two different phases as a co-continuous microstructure with a large interpenetrating structure indicate immiscibility between PHBV and PBAT in the PHBV/PBAT (50:50) specimen. The miscibility, intermolecular interaction, and mechanical properties of PHBV/PBAT blends were also investigated by molecular dynamics simulation. The results showed the immiscibility of PHBV and PBAT. The degradation temperature increased from 277 to 356°C with the increase of PBAT content in the PHBV/PBAT blend. Whereas the crystallinity ability of the PHBV component in the blend was confined by the PBAT phase, leading to a decrease in the overall crystallinity of PHBV. Many efforts have been made to develop sustainable bio-based and biodegradable polymers for packaging, automotive, electrical & electronics, household, agriculture, and biomedical application. Commercially available poly(hydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) has gained much attention due to its comparable mechanical properties as compared to polyolefin along with excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability.1-5 As one of the members of the PHA family, PHBV is a copolymer of PHB with randomly arranged 3-hydroxybutyrate (HB) groups and 3-hydroxyvalarate (HV) groups and synthesized by various microorganisms.6, 7 It can be efficiently degraded into carbon dioxide and water by microorganisms in the most biologically active environment.8, 9 Consequently, PHBV has been considered to be one of the good alternatives for petroleum-based synthetic polymers. However, the applications of PHBV are limited by its brittleness, low impact strength, low thermal stability, and low melt elastic strength.10-13 The mechanical properties of PHBV need to be improved to widen its applications.', 'The poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) is a natural, nontoxic, semicrystalline, linear chain copolymer, with fewer hydroxyvalerate (HV) units than hydroxybutyrate units. Furthermore, it is biodegradable, biocompatible, has a high degree of polymerization.1-3 Its high crystallinity provides good barrier properties1 and as a rigid and brittle material, it bears low deformations. Its compatibility with biological systems and biodegradability allows the PHBV to be applied in controlled drug delivery and tissue engineering.4, 5 It also can stimulate bone tissue growth and be used for biodegradable packaging.6 Many studies propose the combination of PHBV with other polymers or reinforcing agents, forming polymer blends, composites and nanocomposites in order to improve its properties.6-12 The plasticizers are considered processing additives and properties modifiers, because they change processing parameters and the thermal and mechanical properties of polymers. These additives are selected in order to enhance polymer attributes, such as processability, elongation capacity, flexibility and can even lower the glass transition temperature and tensile modulus.13-15 Plasticizers make the polymers flow easier when they are melted, due to lower viscosity, and the higher the plasticizer concentration, the lower the hardness, tensile strength and modulus, and the higher the elongation at break.13, 16, 17', 'Biopolymers are envisioned as the potential substitute of petroleum-based polymers. retrieved_contexts: ['Biodegradable materials based on magnesium alloys have a huge potential for bone fracture fixation devices due to their adequate mechanical properties and biocompatibility. (8) for a review), which provide information regarding material safety, biodegradability, bone formation stimulation, and inflammatory response, among others. Then, the interference screw with the best mechanical performance was used as the sample to be tested in an in vitro degradation experiment.", 'The biocompatibility of the biomaterial is not compromise by the process. Additionally, PLA/Mg has been tested in vivo [18] showing that composites with a 10 % Mg loading exhibited optimal osteogenic properties, whereas a 20 % Mg composite group showed angiogenic effects and promising osteoinduction properties.', 'Although natural polymeric coatings have demonstrated the superiority for protecting Mg substrates from quick corrosion and supporting cell activity (cellular adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation) simultaneously, their degradation behaviors are more or less unpredictable due to the potential enzymatic degradation in vivo. Moreover, the risk of stimulating immune response and carrying microbes or virus can still not be absolutely eliminated when using natural polymer-based biomaterials.13 In contrast, biodegradable synthetic polymers show a more controllable degradation process and lower risk of immunogenicity in physiological environment, the physicochemical properties of which can be designed and modified to meet specific needs in biomedical applications.41 Hence, the biocompatible and biodresorbable synthetic polymers, including poly (lactic acid) (PLA), poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), poly (-caprolactone) (PCL) and polydopamine (PDA), have been proposed as promising alternatives to modify biodegradable Mg-based implantable materials for hard tissue engineering (Figure 4). Traditionally, permanent metallic materials have been used in orthopaedic applications due to their high strength and inert nature. Therefore, it is vital to design and construct Mg-based implants with a good balance between mechanical properties and corrosion resistance.', 'Besides performance limitations, another drawback of PLA is its slow biodegradation rate [t1/2 > 45 days; Figure 1(a)] as compared to other biodegradable polymers such as PHB, polycaprolactone (PCL), and polybutylene succinate (PBS), which have been reported to undergo near-complete biodegradation within two weeks10 implying half-lives of a week or less.11 The formation of microplastics during PLA degradation, particularly in aquatic environments where biodegradation is slow, remains a viable concern.12 When degradation does occur, it generally proceeds through acid-catalyzed hydrolysis or photo-degradation of the ester backbone, resulting in a decrease of molecular weight.12, 13 Theses oligomers can then be consumed by microorganisms, and several microbial enzymes capable of PLA degradation have been reported.14-16 The rates of hydrolysis in PLA and its composites increases with increasing water content temperature17, 18 and are enhanced by the unrestricted carboxyl groups of the hydrolyzed PLA ends. Natural fibers from coconut, cotton, bamboo, kenaf, flax, nettle, hemp, jute, sisal, and wood were used as reinforcement material.", "Export citation and abstractBibTeXRIS In orthopaedic surgery, bone screws, often in combination with plates, are routinely used implants for fracture fixation in weight-bearing bones [1]. After the healing and reorganization of the bone in the fracture gap, common implants made from stainless steel or titanium alloys have to be removed in a second surgery [2-4]. In addition, stress-shielding effects can lead to an implant-induced osteopenia and an increase in cortical porosity [5]. retrieved_contexts: ['As noted earlier, bioactive glass is an ideal material for osteoconduction due to its ability to promote bone formation and degrade over time, releasing soluble calcium and silica ions in the process which are assumed to act as the activators of bone growth. Bioglass® is produced by a melting process, however scaffolds can also be formed using a sol-gel foam process which avoids any issues of crystallisation during sintering as with the melt-derived glasses and enhances the bioactivity of the resultant material [237-242]. It has been found that using a variety of particle size ranges and fibre diameters and foam textures allowed for the ideal dissolution properties of the bioglass to be attained [242-245]. The interconnected macropores (in excess of 100 μm) allow for bone ingrowth and the nanoporosity allows for the attachment of osteoprogenitor cells. In fact, there is evidence which indicates the biological and mechanical benefits of having a nanostructure in biomaterials since they are able to guide cell attachment, migration and differentiation [246, 247]. The formation of nanopores, such as those which are inherent to the sol-gel methods of glass fabrication, can be used to tailor the degradation process of the scaffold, since they dramatically increase the surface area available for cellular interaction [248]. However, as with CNTs, there remain concerns regarding the use of nanostructured materials in the body [249, 250]. As with bulk glasses and glass-ceramics, the development of glass-ceramic scaffolds are to try and overcome the limitations of glass scaffolds in terms of mechanical properties and to widen their applications beyond small defect sites and minor load-bearing applications [251-254]. These bioactive, biodegradable glass-ceramic scaffolds exhibit oriented microstructures and mechanical properties which can be tailored and are in the lower range for cortical bone along with controlled porosity [252-259]. The 3D foam-like glass-ceramic scaffolds are formed using polyurethane sponge as the sacrificial templates and silicate glass powders (produced via a melt-quenching process) as the final scaffold material. The scaffolds have great potential for bone reconstructive surgery, including load-bearing applications, due to the ease with which they can be produced and how their strength, bioactivity and bioresorption can be tailored. More recently, a study has been performed by this group observe the effect of adding silver ions to the surface of the scaffold to install antibacterial properties and broaden the effectiveness of the glass-ceramic scaffold [260, 261]. Alongside ceramic, glass-ceramic and bioglass scaffolds, composite scaffolds are also being investigated. Prior to the formation of composite scaffolds, degradable polymers were extensively researched for tissue engineering applications. They were selected due to their biological acceptance and controllable degradation rates. A recent review discussed the benefits and limitations of degradable polymer systems for use as scaffolds in tissue engineering [262]. The ability to seed and grow cells on the surfaces of such biodegradable polymers was shown to be vital to promoting tissue growth and bone remodelling. Therefore, in an attempt to mimic the natural system and provide enhanced bioactivity, biodegradation and mechanical properties, bioactive composite scaffolds based on bulk bioactive composites were developed [242]. Composites of degradable polymers reinforced with bioactive and biodegradable materials would ensure total resorption and replacement of the material by natural bone cells.', 'Among all of the bioactive inorganic phases, bioactive glass nanoparticles (BGn) have some advantages over other bioactive ceramics. For example, the osteoinductivity of BGn resulted from the CaO and SiO2 components of BGn, stimulates the osteoblastic cells gene expression, which in turn modifies osteogenesis and promotes bone formation [13]. Besides, BGn can bond more strongly to hard tissues than other bioactive inorganic nanoparticles and facilitates cell migration and differentiation [14]. The superior osteoconductivity, osteoinductivity and biodegradability of bioactive glass nanoparticles (BGn) makes them well known as proper fillers in PDLLA/PCL biodegradable polymer blends [15]. In a study focused on the mechanical properties of highly porous PLLA, PCL and PLCL scaffolds, the effect of bioactive particle content as a filler was studied by means of model approaches [16]. In another paper, the effect of inorganic filler presence in the PLLA/PCL scaffolds on long term hydrolytic degradation was investigated [17]. Adding bioactive glass nanoparticles to the polymer matrix could provide composites with suitable mechanical properties, which has made them useful as ligaments reconstruction screws. However, in this regard, there are some problems. One of the main challenges is the filler agglomeration due to incompatibility of the second phase and the matrix, resulting in an inhomogeneous composite. These phase inhomogeneities may influence the mechanical behavior of composite and cause an early failure at the interface [18], [19].', 'Collagen (COL), the most abundant protein in mammals, offers a wide range of attractive properties for biomedical applications which are the result of its biocompatibility and high affinity to water. However, due to the relative low mechanical properties of COL its applications are still limited. To tackle this disadvantage of COL, especially in the field of bone tissue engineering, COL can be combined with bioactive inorganic materials in a variety of composite systems. One of such systems is the collagen-bioactive glass (COL-BG) composite family, which is the theme of this Review. BG fillers can increase compressive strength and stiffness of COL-based structures. This article reviews the relevant literature published in the last 15 years discussing the fabrication of a variety of COL-BG composites. In vitro cell studies have demonstrated the osteogenic, odontogenic, and angiogenic potential of these composite systems, which has been confirmed by stimulating specific biochemical indicators of relevant cells. Bony integration and connective tissue vessel formation have also been studied by implantation of the composites in vivo. Areas of future research in the field of COL-BG systems, based on current challenges, and gaps in knowledge are highlighted. The calcification capacity of bone-substituting materials is generally referred to as “bioactivity” and materials exhibiting this capacity, such as hydroxyapatite (HA),1-3 calcium phosphates,2, 4 and bioactive glasses (BGs)3, 5-7 are called bioactive material.4, 8 These types of materials possess the capacity to promote the nucleation and subsequent growth of calcium phosphate crystals on the surface. Generally, most polymeric materials do not exhibit this capacity but the addition of inorganic phases can render the resulting composites bioactive by providing nucleation sites for the formation of HA or precipitation of other calcium phosphates.2, 9 The addition of an inorganic bioactive phase can also provide cell adhesion sites that facilitate integration with surrounding bone tissue.10, 11 There are many inorganic materials that can be used to impart bioactivity to the resulting polymeric composites, usually HA and other CaP particles in addition to silicate BGs are used.2 These inorganic materials are able to create a firm bond with bone at the site of implantation by forming an intermediate layer of HA on their surface.9, 12 The bioactivity level of BGs, given their high surface reactivity, is superior to that of HA or CaP, as discussed in the literature.3 Indeed rapid deposition of HA layer on an implant surface appears to be essential to allow the formation of a high-strength interface between host bone tissue and biomaterial.13 Incorporation of inorganic filler particles into soft polymer matrices affects also the mechanical properties.2, 14, 15 In particular, compressive strength and stiffness can be increased by incorporation of inorganic fillers.', "Bone is a multifunctional tissue which has organic mineral phase. Bioactive glass (BG) fillers enhance the function of biodegradable bone scaffolds through multiple mechanisms, as derived from the context:

1. **Bioactivity and Osteogenesis Promotion**:  
   - BG releases soluble calcium (Ca²⁺) and silica (SiO₄⁴⁻) ions during degradation, which stimulate osteoprogenitor cells at the genetic level, enhancing osteoblastic differentiation, bone formation, and mineralization [1, 5, 13].  
   - These ions promote the rapid formation of a hydroxyapatite (HA) layer on the scaffold surface, crucial for bonding with native bone and creating a high-strength interface [3, 6, 14].  

2. **Mechanical Reinforcement**:  
   - BG fillers, particularly nanosized particles (nBG), increase compressive strength, stiffness, and structural integrity of polymer matrices (e.g., PCL, PDLLA, gelatin) by providing a high surface area for interfacial bonding and load transfer [2, 9, 14].  
   - Composite scaffolds mimic natural bone's mechanical behavior, combining polymer toughness with ceramic stiffness, enabling load-bearing applications [5, 9].  

3. **Degradation Control**:  
   - BG incorporation tailors the scaffold's degradation rate to match bone regeneration kinetics. The release of ions from BG buffers acidic byproducts of polymer degradation, stabilizing pH and reducing inflammatory risks [6, 10].  

4. **Porosity and Cellular Interaction**:  
   - BG scaffolds feature interconnected macropores (>100 μm) for bone ingrowth and nanopores for osteoprogenitor cell attachment, migration, and differentiation [1, 9].  
   - Nanostructured BG enhances surface roughness, mimicking natural bone ECM, which improves cell adhesion and osteoconductivity [3, 14].  

5. **Enhanced Biocompatibility and Functionality**:  
   - BG-doped composites exhibit antimicrobial properties (e.g., with Ag⁺ or Sr²⁺ doping) and angiogenic potential, supporting vascularization and reducing infection risks [4, 12].  
   - Hybrid systems (e.g., BG-gelatin) synthesized at ambient temperatures retain bioactivity while enabling covalent bonding for controlled degradation and mechanical stability [15].  

6. **Drug Delivery and Bioactivity Synergy**:  
   - Mesoporous BG in composites enables sustained drug release (e.g., growth factors, antibiotics) while maintaining bioactivity, enhancing therapeutic outcomes [10].  

**Challenges**:  
- Agglomeration of BG nanoparticles in polymer matrices can lead to inhomogeneity and mechanical weaknesses, necessitating optimized dispersion techniques [2].  
- Balancing bioactivity with degradation kinetics requires precise compositional control to avoid premature ion release or scaffold collapse [1, 15].  

In summary, BG fillers synergistically improve mechanical properties, bioactivity, and degradation profiles of biodegradable scaffolds, making them versatile for bone regeneration, particularly in load-bearing and complex defect applications.

The value of C∞ is higher than the actual amount of degraded starch in Fig. 5B, as it is the corresponding amount of starch degraded when the reaction was stopped, which may be not actually be 100% complete.', 'Characterization of Residues from Partially Hydrolyzed Potato and High Amylose Corn Starches by Pancreatic α‐Amylase There is growing global impetus for a transition away from fossil fuel-based materials to enhance sustainable development, protect ecosystems, and reach net-zero targets. Synthetically derived, non-renewable polymers such as polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyvinyl chloride are particularly problematic due to their poor biodegradability,1 and carbon-intensive production methods. The remaining 40% is used for pharmaceuticals (tissue and drug carriers), cosmetics, fertilizers, coatings, packaging, textiles, bioplastics, building materials and oil drilling (as an additive).7 Most starches used in industry are modified to improve structural properties and functionalization.4 Unmodified starch has the tendency to adsorb water at higher temperatures (typically insolubility in cold water) leading to expansion and eventually swelling of the crystalline region which disrupts the formation of hydrophobic colloids (gelatinization).1 After cooling, the molecules of starch reorganize and restructure leading to an increase in viscosity and gel-like structure (retrogradation).8 Amylose in particular has a greater tendency to retrograde, resulting in the formation of hard gels and strong films as opposed to soft gels and weak films produced by amylopectin.9 Raw starches also tend to have unfavorable properties required for product development; with poor processability, low shear stress resistance,3 poor cohesive qualities when heated up, and unwanted gel-like properties when cooled.4 Reiterating, the hydrophilic nature of starch introduces the problem that comes along with the commercial use of native starch in industry, as the product is unstable and difficult to process.10, 11 Instability of the product during storage is mainly caused by starch being sensitive to moisture which affects its average molar mass due to hydrolytic degradation. Additionally, starch can be removed from the composite by microorganisms, decreasing the mechanical strength of the final product and increasing permeability.14', 'Enzyme and starch concentrations and grains size determine encounter statistical probability, meaning accessibility of enzyme to starch. Specific surface area conditions access to amylopectin and amylose of the starch grain. It has to do with grain surface state, variable according to botanical origins. Glucosidic bonds type and structure determine starch grain degradability. Additive effects indeed explain different cements behaviours.', 'Starch is the second-most abundant natural polymer after cellulose. It is produced as a storage polymer in several granular plants such as corn, cassava, cereal, rice and potato. It is an odorless and tasteless white powder, and insoluble in cold water or alcohol. Starch is a semi-crystalline polymer, with a crystallinity varying from 15 % to 45 % depending on the plant species from which it originates (Vall zabala, 2020). Morphologically, starch is composed of mostly microscopic spherical granules with diameters ranging from 2 to 100 μm, depending on the botanical origin. Chemically, starch molecules are composed of two main macromolecular components: amylose and amylopectin. Amylose has a linear or slightly branched structure consisting of 2 × 105-106 glucose units per molecule, which are joined together by ∼99 % α-D (1 → 4) glucosidic bonds and ∼1% α-D (1 → 6) glucosidic linkages. Amylopectin has a highly branched structure with approximately 106 glucose units per molecule, which are connected with α-D (1 → 4) linkages and 5-6% of α-D (1 → 6) glucosidic side chains (Wu et al., 2018). Generally, amylose and amylopectin constitute ∼20-25 % and ∼75-80 % of a starch granule, respectively. There are three reactive hydroxyl groups on the glucose unit of the starch chain: one primary and two secondary hydroxyl groups. These hydroxyl groups serve as anchoring platforms for surface modifications or cross-linking reactions (Ojogbo, Ogunsona, & Mekonnen, 2020). Starch molecules have two critical features that make them a unique and promising material for the production of composites. First, starch is naturally biodegradable in soil and water and can be easily degraded into sugars and organic acids, which is of utmost importance from an environmental viewpoint. Second, owing to its unique chemical characteristics, starch is amenable to a variety of chemical and enzymatic modifications that provide many opportunities to confer new functionalities on starch polymers. To meet the necessary requirements of green chemistry, renewable resources are increasingly in demand to enable the manufacture of sustainable composites. Starch, which seems to meet these expectations, can be employed as a green polyol component for the synthesis of PU-based materials. Thermoplastic starch (TPS) has also attracted considerable attention during the past two decades as an interesting alternative to synthetic polymers (Gironès et al., 2012). PUs are a diverse class of polymeric materials that possess urethane linkages within their backbone. PUs are generally composed of hard and soft segments. The soft segment consists of a polyol, such as a polyester or polyether, which renders flexibility to the PU’s structure; the hard segment is composed of a wide variety of isocyanate-based components that impart mechanical strength to the PU network. The use of a varying range of hard and soft segments with different chemistries gives rise to the development of PUs with a broad range of physical and mechanical properties (Costa et al., 2015; Sáenz-Pérez, Laza, García-Barrasa, Vilas, & León, 2017). For example, PUs can be either thermoplastic or irreversibly thermoset depending on the ratio of hard and soft segments in their structure. The versatile PU chemistry and its ability to form different types of molecular architectures enable PUs to meet the highly diversified demands of modern technologies, including coatings, adhesives, foams and thermoplastic elastomers (Dandeniyage et al., 2018; Kausar, 2018). It is worth mentioning that almost all traditional PUs are non-degradable; however, they can be specifically designed to show some degrees of degradation. Biodegradable PUs have recently gained great interest because of their sustainable features and potential for use in different biomedical applications. Biodegradable PUs can be devised with a simple manipulation of PU structure and/or its composition, particularly modification of the soft segment (Dou et al., 2019). Soft segments, which are composed of polyester or polyether polyols with a hydrolysable backbone, are more susceptible to microbial attack. Thus, the incorporation of a biodegradable unit (particularly an ester group) into the PU backbone is a pragmatic approach to impart higher susceptibility to microbial action under natural environmental conditions. The potential to introduce biodegradability and tailor a multitude of structures and mechanical properties makes PUs versatile polymers for developing starch-PU composites or hybrids (Mahajan & Gupta, 2015). Conventional PUs are synthesized through a step-growth polymerization reaction between isocyanate and polyol molecules in the presence of either a catalyst or UV light irradiation (Fig. 1a). Polyols that are commonly used for PU synthesis often have two or more OH groups. Isocyanates are another essential component for PU synthesis. They are often di-functional in nature, containing two NCO groups per molecule. They can be classified as aliphatic or aromatic isocyanates. Aromatic isocyanates, such as toluene diisocyanate (TDI) and diphenylmethane diisocyanate (MDI), tend to be more reactive towards polyols than their aliphatic counterparts, such as isophorone diisocyanate (IPDI) and hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI) (Akindoyo et al., 2016). Isocyanates can react with OH groups to produce PUs at room temperature (and up to 50 °C), while, they generate allophanate, biuret, and isocyanate linkages at higher temperatures above 100 °C. If linear PUs are desired, the use of the low temperature is required. If high cross-linked PUs are desired, higher temperatures (100-150 °C) are indeed required (Engels et al., 2013). Synthesis of PUs can be carried out as one- or two-step reactions. In one-step synthesis, all required ingredients are mixed at the beginning; in two-step synthesis, the polyols are first reacted in excess with a diisocyanate component to prepare NCO-terminated PU prepolymers, after which a chain extender is added to produce a final long-chain PU (Janik, Sienkiewicz, & Kucinska-Lipka, 2013). The two-step reaction method is generally preferred because it allows more control over the reaction, and yields PUs with well-defined structural and physical properties (Akindoyo et al., 2016). Even though these PU materials are highly durable and safe, the main drawback of classic PU synthesis is the use of isocyanates, which are classified as carcinogenic and mutagenic. Prolonged exposure to isocyanate substances in the workplace can have dramatic impacts on health, such as asthma, dermatitis and acute poisoning. Therefore, despite the continuous efforts of the PU industry to improve the quality of PU raw materials (e.g., using bio-based diisocyanates derived from natural resources), the need for more environmentally friendly processes that address both the renewability of the starting material and the sustainability of the synthesis is urgent (Llevot & Meier, 2019). NIPUs, which are mainly synthesized through a ring-opening reaction between poly(cyclic carbonates) and polyamines, have been shown to have substantial green credentials (Fig. 1b). The phosgene-free and isocyanate-free reactions represent a suitable greener alternative for PU synthesis, with structures comparable to those produced by the polyaddition of diisocyanates and polyols (Ghasemlou, Daver, Ivanova, & Adhikari, 2019). The isocyanate-free reactions can be carried out at ambient temperatures although a moderately high temperature (ca. 60-80 °C) can achieve high conversion rate of NIPU (Cornille et al., 2016). More importantly, due to their hydrophilic nature, NIPUs tend to be more compatible with hydrophilic native starch in composites. We have recently reviewed the various green routes that have been used to synthesize NIPUs and their precursors to pave the way for their application in the PU industry (Ghasemlou et al., 2019a).', 'The degradation of biomaterial implant or scaffold is a challenging factor because the FDA approved synthetic polyesters would take more than 2-3 years to degrade in the living systems. Degradation profile of the prepared membranes', 'Among the biopolymers that can be used to produce biocomposite materials, starch is highly promising because it has many advantages, such as renewable and biodegradable properties in addition to being relatively inexpensive [129]. 1. **Primary cleavage**: The enzyme α-amylase initiates degradation by performing the primary cleavage of long starch polymers, breaking them into shorter fragments.

   - PCL's inherent hydrophobicity [4,9] can impair **layer adhesion** during printing, potentially causing delamination or weak interlayer bonding. Surface modifications (e.g., plasma treatment, alkaline treatment [2,4]) are often required to enhance adhesion.  

3. **Mechanical Limitations**:  
   - PCL has a **low elastic modulus** [9], which may compromise the structural integrity of printed scaffolds, especially in applications requiring mechanical robustness. Blending with stiffer polymers (e.g., PLA, TPU) is common to address this [1,6].  

4. **Process Parameter Sensitivity**:  
   - Achieving high-resolution prints with PCL is challenging due to its viscosity and flow characteristics. Parameters like **layer thickness, raster angle, and infill density** must be optimized to ensure dimensional accuracy and functional performance [5,14].  

5. **Post-Printing Modifications**:  
   - While not directly a printability issue, PCL's lack of biological recognition sites [3,9] often necessitates post-printing surface functionalization (e.g., electrospinning bioactive agents [2,8]), adding complexity to the fabrication workflow.  

In summary, PCL's printability in FDM is constrained by its thermal behavior, surface hydrophobicity, and mechanical properties, requiring tailored processing parameters, material blending, or surface treatments to overcome these challenges.
reference: PCL has a very low melting point (~60°C) and retains heat for a long time (slow crystallization). In FDM, this can lead to poor dimensional accuracy as deposited layers may not solidify quickly enough to support subsequent layers, causing sagging or structural collapse unless active cooling is used.

retrieved_contexts: ['Alginate, a biocompatible polymer naturally derived from algae, is widely used as a synthetic analogue of the extracellular matrix in tissue engineering. Integrin-binding peptide motifs, including RGD, a derivative of fibronectin, are typically grafted to the alginate polymer through carbodiimide reactions between peptide amines and alginate uronic acids. However, lack of chemo-selectivity of carbodiimide reactions can lead to side reactions that lower peptide bioactivity. To overcome these limitations, we developed an approach for copper-free, strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC)-mediated conjugation of azide-modified adhesive peptides (azido-cyclo-RGD, Az-cRGD) onto alginate. Successful conjugation of azide-reactive cyclooctynes onto alginates using a heterobifunctional crosslinker was confirmed by azido-coumarin fluorescent assay, NMR, and through click reactions with azide-modified fluorescent probes. Compared to cyclo-RGD peptides directly conjugated to alginate polymers with standard carbodiimide chemistry, Az-cyclo-RGD peptides exhibited higher bioactivity, as demonstrated by cell adhesion and proliferation assays. Finally, Az-cRGD peptides enhanced the effects of recombinant bone morphogenetic proteins on inducing osteogenesis of osteoblasts and bone marrow stromal stem cells in 3D alginate gels. SPAAC-mediated click approaches for peptide-alginate bioconjugation overcome the limitations of previous alginate bioconjugation approaches and potentially expand the range of ligands that can be grafted to alginate polymers for tissue engineering applications. Hydrogels, due to their high water content and tissue-like elasticity, are commonly used to encapsulate cells and study cell interaction with various natural extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins. Many hydrogels which are used as synthetic analogues of the ECM are generated using bioinert polymers like alginate and are accordingly modified with the ECM, mimicking peptides such as RGD to favor integrin-mediated cell adhesion. (1−7) Cells in their natural environments interact with multiple ECM ligands. (8−10) However, the ability to present multiple peptides-ligands in combination within hydrogel-based ECM analogues is limited by the availability of chemical schemes that allow orthogonal-simultaneous conjugation of multiple peptides with high specificity. (11−14)', 'Synergistic effect of graphene oxide on the properties of poly (vinyl alcohol)/carboxymethyl cellulose electrospun nanofiber mats Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a linear polyester with good biocompatibility, a relatively slow degradation rate (it remains up to 2 years without shape modifications in vivo)1 and ease of processability.2 These characteristics are suitable for the usage of this polymeric material in tissue engineering applications.3, 4 However, surface cell attachment and wettability of the structures are limited because of its hydrophobic character.2, 5, 6 Surface modification has been proposed as a strategy to overcome this restriction. The procedures can be based on plasma treatment of the structure to introduce functional groups7 or the coating of the surface with bioactive compounds, such as RGD peptides (peptides based on the sequence arginine-glycine-aspartic acid),8 collagen,9 or gelatin.10 However, surface treatments have the disadvantage of being effective for a short period of time: as long as the degradation process does not affect the outer layer of material. Alternatively, in this study, the feasibility of obtaining bulk PCL-based hybrid material with tunable hydrophilicity is proposed. This tailored hydrophilicity can be achieved by introducing different amounts of a highly hydrophilic biocompatible material, as carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC).', 'Initiating a positive healing response from the vascular implant requires modification of the surface-binding peptide MP with bioactives that help guiding the regeneration process. An on-resin modification protocol combining the Diels-Alder reaction with inverse electron demand with the copper(I)-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition was recently identified as an optimal strategy for the orthogonal introduction of two cell-adhesive peptides.11 The generated bifunctional coatings MP-RGD-HBP and iMP-RGD-HBP2 were tested for their ability to enhance the adhesion of HUVEC cells to PCLLC scaffolds. Both peptides were found to be superior over alkaline hydrophilization, which only provides a generally more favorable interface for unspecific adsorption.38 Coatings with unfunctionalized MP do not compromise endothelial adhesion in comparison to PCLLCNaOH, HUVECs attach equally well owing to its positive surface charge introduced by a free lysine residue. In contrast, cell viability on MP-RGD-HBP and iMP-RGD-HBP2 is significantly enhanced, HUVEC display more organized actin fibers and improved spreading. The presented cyclic RGD peptides specifically address cell surface integrins, promoting the formation of more stable anchor points and linking the surface with the cytoskeleton, causing actin rearrangement.39 Herein, a cooperative action between the proteoglycan-binding HBPs and the RGD peptide is conceivable, as syndecans and integrins synergize to promote focal adhesion contacts and receptor crosstalk.40 While syndecans have a higher potential reach and mediate the initial attachment to distant adhesion ligands,41 integrins finally take their place to form tight interactions necessary for focal adhesion formation.42 Subsequently, adhesion-dependent processes including wound healing and angiogenesis are modulated by the synergistic signaling.43 By trend, iMP-RGD-HBP2 binds more HUVEC cells to coated glass slides than MP-RGD-HBP, possibly due to an enhanced affinity towards heparin and heparan sulfates by HBP sequence elongation. Under physiologic conditions, exposure to shear stress is a crucial factor in shaping endothelial morphology.44 During microfluidic culture, we observed dramatic changes in HUVEC morphology in comparison to static adhesion studies and the observed differences between coatings intensified. The presentation of cell adhesion peptides by MP-RGD-HBP was found critical for the development of parallel actin stress fibers and a more cobblestone-like cell morphology. This is in agreement with literature, where a combination of integrin- and proteoglycan-binding peptides was identified to induce the alignment and spreading of endothelial cells under flow.31 Notably, collagen I, a standard coating in cell culture, was unable to promote spreading and cytoskeleton organization, even though it likewise displays both binding sites.45 This can be rationalized by the high affinity of the cyclic RGD peptide for integrin αVβ313 which results in an enhanced adhesion strength in comparison to linear sequences and the full-length protein.46 Additionally, anchor strength is enhanced in mussel-derived peptides compared to unspecific protein adsorption. Small peptides combine a number of advantages over structural proteins as they reach a higher packing density, provide receptor selectivity and display ligands in a defined orientation and spacing.47 Nevertheless, dynamic mediators like growth factors, cytokines and chemokines exert substantial roles in orchestrating cell recruitment, proliferation and matrix remodeling during wound healing. Therefore, specific implant coatings should mediate the immobilization and release of such factors. Incorporation of heparin-binding peptides into biomaterial coatings allow the immobilization of heparin and subsequent delivery of heparin-binding cytokines.17 Herein, the interaction between peptide and GAG is based on the electrostatic attraction of negatively-charged sulfate and carboxyl groups of the heparin with basic amino acids within the peptide. Consensus sequences include alternating motifs of basic and hydrophobic amino acids matching the charge density of heparan sulfates.48 Elongating the motif increases the number of potential ionic bonds and can, therefore, retain significantly more heparin. This, in turn, enables an adjustment of the amounts of chemokine bound and released by the implant.', "A considerable problem related to the biomaterials is how hydrophobicity and lack of biological recognition sites on the surface of the material provide an unfriendly environment for cell adhesion.[12] To improve cell adhesion, previous functionalization studies focalized on modifying biomaterial surfaces have been developed. Further, surface modifications play a role in cell migration, proliferation, and differentiation of stem cells.[13] Therefore, cell adhesion enhancement would improve cell-biomaterial interaction.[14] Several functionalization methods were used based on the interaction of different components with cell membrane proteins. For example, the surface can be functionalized with the peptide RGD (Arg-Gly-Asp),[15] with 1-pyrene butyric acid (PBA),[16] or with different components present in the extracellular matrix (ECM) like fibronectin or collagen.[17] Synthetic polyesters, like 1,4 butanediol thermoplastic polyurethane (b-TPUe), have received considerable attention for cartilage TE, due to their appropriate mechanical properties such as the highly elastic recovery capacity.[18] However, its hydrophobicity does not provide the desired environment for cell adhesion and proliferation. Hence, the aim of this study was the set-up of two different functionalization methods, based on the biomaterial coating with collagen type I and PBA, probing how it is possible to reduce the hydrophobicity of b-TPUe improving cell-biomaterial interaction. Two methods were selected due following the objective of comparing a traditional coating method (Collagen type I) adapted from literature[17] with a new methodology (PBA) with reduced costs and good results obtained from making graphene biosensors.[16] Both methodologies are compared by evaluating the efficacy of functionalization by atomic force microscope (AFM) and ninhydrin reagent. Then, the biological efficacy of both functionalization methods was analyzed by seeding mesenchymal stem cells obtained from Hoffa's fat pad (infrapatellar mesenchymal stem cells (IPFP-MSCs) and performing the subsequent metabolic activity and viability studies. Together with cellular studies, extracellular matrix (ECM) secretion was analyzed through PCR, Glucosamine Glycans (GAG) quantification, and, finally, by SEM, to verify the chondrogenic potential of both functionalized methods.", "A considerable problem related to the biomaterials is how hydrophobicity and lack of biological recognition sites on the surface of the material provide an unfriendly environment for cell adhesion.[12] To improve cell adhesion, previous functionalization studies focalized on modifying biomaterial surfaces have been developed.
