Liquid-liquid phase separation has been reported to play an important role for biological processes ranging from the formation of proteinaceous membrane-less organelles (PMLOs) [2], [3], [4], [5] and spindle assembly [6], to the assembly of underwater adhesives [7], [8], amyloid formation [9], and the assembly of biopolymeric materials [10], [11], [12], [13], [14]. Coacervation of biopolymers, such as elastin [12] and squid beak proteins [10], [11] is reported to have a role in assembling molecules as an intermediate step prior to the final transition from liquid to solid. Spider silk is an extraordinary example of the properties that a natural fiber can possess. It has high tensile strength yet it is very elastic, both properties leading to extreme toughness that one has so far escaped attempts at synthetic reproduction [15]. In addition, spider silk is biodegradable and causes low immunogenic response which makes it attractive for biomedical applications [16]. On a molecular level, spider silk consists of proteins with long highly repetitive regions capped by globular terminal domains [14], [17], [18]. Typical to biological materials, the properties of spider silk stem from weak inter- and intramolecular interactions and a precise molecular alignment of the constituent spider silk proteins [19]. Synthetic approaches to producing spider silk-mimicking fibers are attractive, but both the recombinant production of full-length spider silk and the assembly of the fibers have proven challenging [14]. Progress in recombinant DNA technologies allow the production of shorter spider silk-mimicking proteins in bacteria, but the molecular assembly of soluble proteins remains challenging and the biologically relevant mechanisms are at the moment not fully understood. In a previous study, we described that a silk-like triblock fusion protein self-coacervates in high protein concentration in water, yielding droplets that coalesce spontaneously, relax back to spherical structures after fusing together, and easily wet surfaces. Importantly, coacervation seems to be an important part of the early steps of assembly to various fibrous structures [20]. The coacervation occurred in solutions containing only the triblock fusion protein, and hence the system is classified as a self-coacervating one, as opposed to systems where polymers of at least two types form complexes, leading to complex coacervates [11], [21]. The triblock architecture was essential for achieving high solubility and functionality of the coacervates. Native terminal domains were not required, but could be replaced with for example unrelated folded domains such as cellulose-binding modules (CBMs) [22]. The exact nature of the terminal domains was not crucial for function but CBMs proved to function well for high solubility, good production levels, and coacervate formation [20], [23].', 'Natural polymer materials mainly include hyaluronic acid, collagen, polylactic acid [18, 19], etc., which have good biocompatibility and degradable absorption. However, they exhibit limited mechanical strength, rapid degradation [20], and the potential to produce acidic degradation products that can disrupt the local acid-base environment. Silk, as a natural protein fiber, has excellent mechanical properties comparable to synthetic polymers. Meanwhile, it displays high biocompatibility [21-23], does not elicit significant inflammatory responses [24]. Besides, it can be fully degraded and absorbed, and can regulate the degradation rate [25]. It has been employed as a novel biomaterial for tissue regeneration, including in tendon and rotator cuff repair [26-29]. There are two main categories of silk fibroin materials: natural silk fibroin materials (derived from raw silk degumming) and regenerated silk fibroin materials [30]. In terms of mechanical properties, the β-sheet structure plays an important role in the mechanical properties of silk [31], which is the main factor that endows silk fibroin with high strength and high elastic modulus [32]. However, the protein secondary structure of regenerated silk fibroin has been changed after dissolution, dialysis, and freeze-drying. The mechanical properties of regenerated silk fibroin are weak and brittle [33, 34]. The tensile strength of regenerated silk fibroin films is about 0.02 GPa, and the elongation at break is < 2% [35, 36]. Furthermore, the random coil and α-helix structures can be transformed into β-sheet structures through the application of specific external factors, including temperature, pH value, organic solvent, and shear stretching [37, 38]. This process can enhance the mechanical properties. Compared with the tensile strength of natural fibers about 0.5-0.6 GPa and the elongation at break of 10%-40%, there is still a huge gap. In terms of degradation rate, the degradation rate of regenerated silk fibroin materials is significantly faster than that of natural silk fibroin materials [39], which cannot match the tissue growth rate. Nevertheless, while natural silk protein materials exhibit superior mechanical properties and degradation rates compared to regenerated silk fibroin materials, natural silk fibroin materials have some limitations in processing and molding. The majority of studies currently concentrate on the utilization of electrospinning [40], freeze-drying, 3D printing [41, 42], self-assembly [43] and other technologies for the preparation of regenerated silk fibroin materials, which exhibit inadequate mechanical strength and are unsuitable for the repair of extensive soft tissue defects. Although the mechanical properties can be improved by producing composite materials with a multi-layer structure [44], this also increases the thickness and weight of the material. Concurrently, the cost is greater, and the capacity for large-scale production is limited.', 'Animal silks, especially spider dragline silks, have an excellent portfolio of mechanical properties, but it is still a challenge to obtain artificial silk fibers with similar properties to the natural ones. In this paper, we show how to extrude tough regenerated silk fibers by adding a small amount of commercially available functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (less than 1%) through an environmentally friendly wet-spinning process reported by this laboratory previously. Most of the resulting regenerated silk fibers exhibited a breaking energy beyond 130 MJ m−3, which is comparable to spider dragline silks (∼160 MJ m−3). The best of these fibers in terms of performance show a breaking stress of 0.42 GPa, breaking strain of 59%, and breaking energy of 186 MJ m−3. In addition, we used several advanced characterization techniques, such as synchrotron radiation FTIR microspectroscopy and synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, to reveal the toughening mechanism in such a protein-inorganic hybrid system. We believe our attempt to produce such tough protein-based hybrid fibers by using cheap, abundant and sustainable regenerated silkworm protein and commercially available functionalized carbon nanotubes, with simplified industrial wet-spinning apparatus, may open up a practical way for the industrial production of super-tough fiber materials. A carbon nanotube (CNT) is a fascinating material that is a one atom thick layer of graphite rolled into a cylinder with a 1 nm diameter and several microns in length. Although it is light and flexible, it is also the toughest material ever known as it has an elastic modulus of 1 TPa, a tensile strength of 100 GPa, and a breaking elongation of 30%.19-21 Therefore, CNTs are often used as nanofillers for the preparation of light weight and high strength composites,22-24 including, of course, for the enhancement of the mechanical properties of polymeric materials.25-29 There have been some reports on the combination of CNTs and silk fibroin to produce reinforced RSF composite fibers by electrospinning,30-32 but these are not conventional “fibers”, and their mechanical properties can hardly compete with natural silks (i.e. they are much worse). Considering we have a solid background on the wet-spinning of pure RSF fibers, we were eager to see if RSF fibers became much tougher after we introduced CNTs into them. Fig. 1A shows the appearance of our RSF-CNT hybrid fibers, which are fairly uniform and highly lustrous. The black color clearly indicates the presence of CNTs in the fibers. During the spinning process, we selected four different CNT/RSF mass ratios (i.e. 1/1000, 2/1000, 5/1000 and 10/1000), and performed a three stage post-draw (i.e. the draw-down ratios were 2, 6, and 9), as reported previously.16 It should be mentioned that in our former experiments, the pristine RSF fibers could only stand 6 times post-draw treatment,14,15 unless adding calcium ions to the spinning dope.16 Here we found that by incorporating CNTs, the fibers could easily stand 9 times post-draw treatment without the addition of calcium ions. Fig. 1B shows the SEM images of a typical RSF-CNT hybrid fiber, sample CNT2-9X. It shows a smooth surface and a dense cross-section, which are both homogeneous. There is no obvious aggregation of the CNTs on either the surface or in the cross-section, which could be evidence for the well-dispersed CNTs in the silk fibroin matrix. The cross-section is tabular, which is similar to the wild silkworm silks,4 with a long axis of 25-30 μm and a short axis of about 10 μm.', 'Artificial systems to spin silk into fibers. Macromol. 66, 319 (2014).60 Copyright 2014, Elsevier Ltd.', 'First published on 7th January 2011 Spider silk shows great potential as a biomaterial: in addition to biocompatibility and biodegradability, its strength and toughness are greater than native biological fibres (e.g.collagen), with toughness exceeding that of synthetic fibres (e.g.nylon). Although the ultimate tensile strength and toughness at failure are unlikely to be limiting factors, its yield strain of 2% is insufficient, particularly for biomedical application because of the inability to mimic the complex ultrastructure of natural tissues with current tissue engineering approaches. To harness the full potential of spider silk as a biomaterial, it is therefore necessary to increase its yield strain. In this paper, we discuss the means by which the mechanical properties of spider silk, particularly the yield strain, can be optimized through structural modifications.', 'The formation of β-sheet enhanced breaking strength and modulus of silk. Silk is used as a structural material in nature such as a lifeline and framework of spiders and the silkworm cocoon to protect larvae from predators [1]. The silk fibers are lightweight and show excellent mechanical toughness, thus being a candidate of bio-based materials for next generation [2]. Although the silkworm silk is used as surgical sutures for decades, the bulk-scale production of the natural silk is still limited especially in the case of spider silk [3]. Hence the artificial silk production has been reported using recombinant protein expression and chemical synthesis [4,5]. Furthermore, the artificial spinning of regenerated silk fibroin solution has been used to modify the diameter and physical properties of resultant silk fibers by varying the reeling speed and coagulation bath [6]. However, the mechanical strength of the resultant silk fiber is often inferior compared with that of the natural counterpart [6]. One of the causes of the inferior strength is the lower molecular weight of the synthesized silk [7]. In addition, the lack of knowledge on the mechanism of structural transition from random coil/helix to β-sheet retards the development of the artificial silk production [8]. Spiders and silkworms are thought to precisely and simultaneously adjust physiological conditions such as water contents and internal pressure in their glands to secret silk fibers with excellent mechanical properties [9]. In order to understand the mechanism of silk fiber formation in detail, it is important to investigate effects of each factor on structural transition of silk fibroin. Water molecules inhibit the intermolecular hydrogen bonds between silk molecular chains and cause the plasticization of silk fibroin, inducing the β-sheet structures of silkworm silk [10,11]. Dynamic mechanical thermal analysis demonstrated that water molecules interacted with the disordered structure of the silk fibroin and lowered the glass transition temperature [12]. Spider silk fibers are known to shrink when immersed in water, which is known as supercontraction [13]. The supercontraction of spider silk is triggered by an entropic relaxation mainly occurred in an amorphous region of the spider silk [14]. Accordingly, the mechanical properties of spider and silkworm silk are largely dependent on the environmental humidity [15].', 'Force-spinning at a controlled drawing rate. When silkworms are being immobilized, the silk can be artificially drawn by external force (i.e., force-spinning) to achieve superior mechanical properties, including strength, toughness and extensibility. Such force-spinning extrudes the silk at a constant speed and in a single direction, thereby eliminating any inconsistencies associated with the natural spinning (i.e., ‘Figure of eight’ spinning motion). Different force-spinning speeds were applied to obtain silk with greatly enhanced mechanical properties as compared to naturally spun counterpart (Fig. 11A) [54]. It was reported that slow force-spinning (e.g., 4 mm s−1) produced highly extensible silk with breaking strain comparable to that of Nephila spider silk, whereas fast force-spinning (e.g., 13 mm s−1) resulted in stronger and tougher silk with breaking stress and toughness approaching that of Nephila spider dragline silk. Modulated spinning in electric field. When silkworms spin in alternating electric field, the silk produced are stronger, tougher and more extensible than naturally spun silk, as shown in Fig. 11B. The enhanced silk fibers have β-sheet crystallites more oriented along the fiber axis, while the crystallinity and crystallite sizes are similar to that of naturally spun silk [73]. This strategy for enhancing the mechanical properties is based on the use of electric field to align the liquid-crystals (i.e., the water-soluble liquid crystalline state) of silk fibroin in the silk gland. Electric field has been shown to be able to align protein dipoles along the direction of the field [84]. The better oriented β-sheet crystallites are thus able to withstand the higher load applied along the fiber axis upon stretching during tensile test. The gene sequence of spider silk (e.g., Nephila clavata or Nephila clavipes) has been successfully transfected into silkworms via piggyBac vector, and this has enabled its co-expression in silk glands of the transgenic silkworms [85], [86]. Even at low expression level, the genetically-modified silk has an overall improved mechanical performance (Fig. 11C). It is noted that the favorable effect could also be observed through subsequent silkworm lineages, occasionally with highly enhanced effect. Successful incorporation of the guest proteins into the silk requires that their expression occurs in spatial and temporal proximity to the endogenous silk proteins [85], [86]. Besides, successful gene transfection relies greatly on environmental and genetic factors and thus explains the low rate of attaining the desired phenotypic expression [86].', 'The strength and stiffness of silk are dictated mainly by β-sheet crystallites (Table 1: experimental and simulation results of β-sheet crystallites of silkworm silk). In β-sheet crystallites, there are hydrogen bonds, together with intersheet van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions, that contribute significantly to the stability of the structure [58], [68]. On the other hand, the extensibility and toughness of silk are governed mainly by the semi-amorphous matrix [17], [64], [69]. Respectively, the semi-amorphous matrix and β-sheet crystallites of silk govern its mechanical behavior at small and large deformation during tensile loading. Upon tensile loading, the material undergoes homogeneous stretching until the onset of yielding, when the material ceases to behave elastically and starts to deform plastically. This is when the semi-amorphous components start to unravel, after which the load is transferred to the β-sheet crystallites, that subsequently handle the load up to the point of fracture [64]. Fundamentally, silk fibroin can form intramolecular/intermolecular β-sheet crystallites [67], [70], parallel/antiparallel β-sheet crystallites, as well as β-sheet crystallites of different sizes and orientations along fiber axis. Below, we discuss these structural aspects of the β-sheet crystallites pertaining to the mechanical properties of silk. Essentially, the splitting of intermolecular β-sheet crystallites leads to weakening of the overall molecular network in silk, and thus results in failure of the material. On the contrary, the splitting of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites leads to lengthening of silk as they split (i.e., unfold) [56], [65]. The content of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites significantly influences the mechanical properties of silk. Evidently, the superb mechanical strength and toughness of spider silk (Nephila pilipes) have been attributed to its high content of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites [56]. Spider silk has a content of about 57% of intramolecular β-sheet crystallites (of total β-sheet crystallites content), significantly above that of silkworm silk (18%). A possible explanation for the lower content in silkworm silk is that the H-chain has comparatively larger crystal-forming domains [55], that increase their likelihood of interactions with those from neighboring H-chains to form intermolecular β-sheet crystallites when the domains are well-aligned during spinning [71]. With this understanding, the mechanical properties of silkworm silk may be further enhanced if there is a way to increase the amount of the intramolecular β-sheet crystallites in silk fibroin. Different arrangements of β-strands in β-sheet crystallites have been proposed, i.e., parallel vs. antiparallel. When arranged in a parallel sense, adjacent β-strands form lengthier and non-linear hydrogen bonds, whereas antiparallel adjacent strands are able to form shorter and linear hydrogen bonds [42]. The arrangement of the β-strands thus influences the mechanical properties owing to the geometrical and energetic differences in the hydrogen bonding. Mechanical behavior of poly(GA) crystalline units, in both parallel and antiparallel arrangements, have been simulated to compare any difference in mechanical properties (Fig. 8A). It was found that antiparallel β-sheet crystallites outperform the parallel counterparts, in terms of rupture strength and stiffness, as shown in Fig. 8B. Experimental stress-strain data of silk fiber are also presented (green curve), presenting a lower strength and stiffness than the simulation data (i.e., antiparallel crystalline unit). This is because the experimental result was calculated using cross-sectional area of fiber, that includes also the area contribution from semi-amorphous region, in addition to the β-sheet crystallites. Meanwhile, it was also reported that the hydrogen bonds are stronger in the antiparallel arrangement [68].', 'Recent advancements in biomimetic materials have brought spider silk to the forefront of scientific attention. Its exceptional combination of Young′s modulus, tensile strength, and toughness makes it a highly versatile material with extensive potential applications.8 This remarkable performance originates from the unique molecular architecture of spider silk, characterized by stacked β-pleated crystallites surrounded by a disordered (amorphous) matrix rich in glycine.9 The amorphous polypeptide chains in silk are interconnected through β-sheet crystallites, which enhance the structural integrity of the protein strands under high strains as reinforcing elements. The presence of the amorphous region enhances the exceptional stretchiness of silk through the provision of entropic elasticity.10 Regenerated silk fibroin, mimicking this structure with anti-parallel β-sheet nanocrystals and an amorphous matrix composed of α-helices and random coils, offers a promising route for replicating the properties of spider silk in artificial materials.11 In this study, we presented a biomimetic approach through hydrogen bonding-induced self-assembly to enhance both the mechanical characteristics and self-repairing effectiveness of hyaluronic acid-based hydrogels, inspired by the heterogeneous structure of spider silk (Figure 1a). Specifically, the β-sheet crystallite domain of spider silk was simulated by the addition of tannic acid (TA) to induce the formation of a β-folded structure of silk fibroin (SF) through hydrogen bonds. Concurrently, the dynamic hydrogen-bonded amorphous domain of spider silk was emulated through acylhydrazone bond cross-linking between aldehyde hyaluronic acid (AHA) and a synthesized cross-linking agent 3,3′-dithiobis (propionohydrazide) (DTP), which contains hydrazide groups and disulfide bonds (Figure 1b). Additionally, the incorporation of TA provided the hydrogel with antibacterial and antioxidant properties. We comprehensively investigated the rheological properties, swelling kinetics, and morphology of the resulting hydrogel. Mechanical testing was used to quantitatively analyze the hydrogel′s mechanical properties, adhesion, and self-healing ability. This study presented a promising direction for the development of high-performance hydrogels with diverse biomedical applications. (a) Schematic diagram of the structure of spider silk; and (b) Diagrammatic representation of the ADS hydrogel fabrication process.', "Due to the limitations on the use of petroleum-based plastics as a solution to environmental problems in recent years, the increase in the number of studies on the use of renewable and environmentally friendly natural biopolymers such as chitosan, sericin, keratin, alginate, and cellulose obtained from animals or plants is remarkable. They are preferred because of their advantages, such as being suitable for changing the structure of many naturally occurring biopolymers by chemical modification techniques, structural compatibility with certain target regions of microbial cells, and economical, antibacterial, and not posing an ecological hazard. At the same time, it is clear that composites prepared from natural polymers in the form of fibers can be among the sustainable multifunctional textile materials of the future.[1] Silkworm silk, one of the natural fiber polymers included in the class of polypeptides and proteins (collagen, silk fibroin, and albumin), has superior physical properties such as luster, soft feeling, and mechanical strength,[2] physicochemical properties such as water absorbability, and microbial resistance after the degumming process removes the sericin component. The biochemical properties, such as oxygen permeability[3] and noninflammatory biocompatibility of its decomposition products,[2] also enable silk as a practical material in various fields ranging from biomedical to apparel applications.[4-9] The chain structure of silk, which predominantly consists of alanine-glycine amino acid units and also includes serine, threonine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, and tyrosine units that can be altered by chemical means,[2] makes silk fibroin an attractive material for application areas.[10] However, since these protein fiber surfaces are a good source of carbon and nitrogen for the growth of microorganisms, the deforming effect of microorganisms that can adhere to the surface causes the deterioration of its strength and changes in its original color, and a limitation to the use of silk in the practical applications.[11] Since the surface properties of polymers in direct contact with the environment are related to determining their usage areas, surface modification techniques are frequently applied to avoid the disadvantages mentioned above of silk. For example, many properties, such as wettability, adhesion, and reactions in biological environments result from the polymer surface's interaction with the environment.[12] One of the techniques frequently applied for the surface modification of silk is the graft copolymerization technique. While this technique is applied to the surfaces physically or chemically with the help of plasma in polymers with completely inert surfaces,[12] it is widely used in chemical bonding in polymer materials with surfaces that can interact chemically. For example, a hydrogel formation was performed on silk by co-grafting acrylamide and acrylic acid on fibroin fabric obtained from Tasar silkworm species and then crosslinking reaction with N,N'-methylene bisacrylamide in the literature. After coating the as-modified silk fabric surface with zinc oxide, it has been reported that the antimicrobial activity and cytocompatibility of the material were significantly improved compared to an untreated silk fibroin, making the silk a promising material for wound dressing.[13]", 'In the past decades, growing emphasis on environmental concerns and exhausting depletion of petroleum sources have triggered the exploration of natural fibers as a “green” alternative for synthetic polymer fibers in composites. Because of their advantages such as low cost, low density, renewability, biodegradability and acceptable specific strength etc., a bulk of natural fibers have been utilized for structural/semi-structural materials in various fields including aerospace, automotive, building, furniture, packaging and sports articles. However, most of them are originated from lignocellulosic fibers [1], [2], [3]. Bombyx mori silkworm silk, a representative animal fiber of luster and fineness, has been used in the textile industry for centuries. It structurally consists of a fibrous core protein named fibroin, and a family of glue-like proteins named sericin that surround the fibroin threads to cement them together. The high crystallinity of β-sheets (ca. 50%) as well as the well orientation of these nanocrystallites in the core filament [4] gives silkworm silk the remarkable mechanical properties, especially strength (0.4 GPa) and extensibility (20%) [5], [6]. In addition, the homogeneous physicochemical properties of silkworm silk as a continuous fiber allow for the fabrication facilities via filament winding and pultrusion processes. Recently, silkworm silk has received great interest as a filling material in composites. For example, chopped silk and commercial silk fabric have been used to reinforce biodegradable or synthetic polymers such as poly(butylene succinate) [7], [8], poly(ɛ-caprolactone) [9], poly(lactic acid) [10], or even polychloroprene rubber [11]. However, chopped silk loses the mechanical merits as a continuous fiber, and commercial silk fabric suffers from the wetting problem of twisted fibroin threads in the matrix, both of which may result in the uncompetitive mechanical performance of the reported silk composites. It is well known that the adhesion between components (e.g. the fiber phase and the matrix phase) is crucial for the mechanical performance of a composite. On one hand, Jin et al. [8] modified silk fabric with carbon nanotubes to improve its compatibility with poly[(butylene succinate)-co-(butylene adipate)], and obtained a composite with fairly increased mechanical properties. On the other hand, Li et al. [12] directly composed silk fabric with regenerated silk fibroin (RSF); however, the overall mechanical properties of the composite were still unsatisfactory. This was likely caused by the immiscibility between the different fine structures of silk fibroin, i.e., the well-ordered β-sheet in silk fiber [13] and either the amorphous state [14] or the randomly-aligned β-sheet [15] in RSF matrix. Furthermore, due to the highly-repeating GAGAGS (G = glycine, A = alanine and S = serine) motifs and the highly-ordered structure, silk fiber presents a water-resistant feature [16] that indicates its inadequate wettability with RSF solution. The resulting polymers were designated as poly(sorbitol citric sebacate) [p(SCS)] and poly(sorbitol tartaric sebacate) [p(STS)]. The synthesized polymers were characterized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, 1H-NMR spectroscopy, and differential scanning calorimetry analysis.     *   **POE IV specifically:** Degrades to yield **lactic acid (LA) or glycolic acid (GA)** ([2]).

    *   **Controlled Degradation Rate:** The LA or GA produced by **POE IV** further **autocatalyze the degradation**. This autocatalysis, combined with the initial acidity catalyzing the hydrolysis, allows the degradation rate to be **"tuned by the proportion of glycolic or lactic acid in the sequence to last from days to months"** ([2]). The drug loading capacity of PLGA microspheres is highly dependent on the drug's hydrophobicity. For **hydrophobic drugs**, PLGA microspheres achieve **high encapsulation efficiencies (>96%)** due to the polymer's hydrophobic nature, which facilitates effective loading and retention of hydrophobic payloads [1]. In contrast, **hydrophilic drugs** (e.g., peptides, proteins, small water-soluble molecules) exhibit **low encapsulation efficiency** in standard PLGA microspheres because the hydrophobic polymer matrix impedes water penetration and creates an acidic microenvironment that destabilizes hydrophilic compounds [2, 12]. 

To address this limitation, modifications such as copolymerization with hydrophilic blocks (e.g., PLGA-mPEG) or composite systems (e.g., PLGA-alginate core-shell structures) can enhance encapsulation efficiency for hydrophilic drugs by improving matrix hydrophilicity and reducing acidic degradation product accumulation [2, 3, 11]. For instance, PLGA-mPEG microspheres show improved water permeation and degradation kinetics, enabling better release profiles for hydrophilic drugs like vancomycin [2, 12]. Thus, while PLGA inherently excels at loading hydrophobic drugs, structural or compositional adjustments are required to optimize loading for hydrophilic agents.

The crystallinity percentage of neat polycaprolactone (PCL) is approximately **39–40%**, as reported in the literature and confirmed by DSC measurements (Contexts 1, 2). This crystallinity arises from PCL's inherent semicrystalline structure, where crystalline regions act as barriers to small molecules like gases.  

### Effect of Crystallinity on Permeability:  
1. **Reduced Permeability with Higher Crystallinity**:  
   Crystalline regions in PCL are less permeable than amorphous regions. Higher crystallinity decreases gas permeability because these regions restrict molecular diffusion (Contexts 1, 2, 5). For example, in PLA-PCL blends, increased crystallinity due to PCL incorporation enhances gas barrier properties (Context 5).  

2. **Role of Nanoparticles vs. Crystallinity**:  
   In PCL-ZnO nanocomposites, crystallinity remains ~40%, similar to neat PCL. The observed reduction in oxygen permeability (e.g., >60% with ZnO nanorods) is attributed to nanoparticle-induced mechanisms (tortuous diffusion paths and gas adsorption) rather than crystallinity changes (Contexts 1, 2).  

3. **Degradation and Crystallinity**:  
   During hydrolytic degradation, amorphous regions degrade preferentially, leaving a more crystalline residue. This process increases crystallinity over time, further reducing permeability (Contexts 9, 10, 12).  

In summary, while higher crystallinity in PCL inherently reduces permeability by limiting molecular diffusion, modifications in permeability in nanocomposites are primarily driven by nanoparticle effects rather than crystallinity changes.

Despite its versatility, PLA's low glass transition temperature (Tgl) and slow crystallization kinetics limit its mechanical and thermal properties. These characteristics result in poor heat resistance and limited load-bearing capacity under stress, restricting PLA's use in certain engineering applications [26,27]. Thermal annealing can enhance PLA's crystallization to address these limitations. By carefully controlling the annealing time and temperature, the crystal structure of PLA can be improved, leading to increased mechanical strength [28,29]. The final performance of PLA depends on crystal phase transitions and the degree of crystallization, as appropriate annealing conditions can transform PLA into a semi-crystalline polymer with higher strength [30,31]. For instance, annealing at 80 °C can significantly enhance PLA's crystal structure, while temperatures between 100 °C and 120 °C can optimize its mechanical properties by inducing the α′-α phase transition [32]. During annealing, PLA's amorphous regions are reorganized into more stable crystalline structures, which can significantly improve mechanical properties such as tensile and flexural strength, hardness, and impact resistance. This paragraph summarizes the studies in the literature on the thermal annealing and crystallization properties of PLA. The mechanical strength of FFF-printed PLA parts is **significantly influenced by build orientation** due to the **anisotropic nature** of the layer-by-layer deposition process. Key findings from the context include:

1. **Anisotropic Strength**:  
   - PLA parts exhibit **weaker mechanical strength along the build direction (Z-axis)** compared to directions perpendicular (X/Y-axis) due to **poor interlayer bonding** at weld interfaces. This is attributed to incomplete molecular diffusion and non-isothermal crystallization during printing, which weaken interfacial adhesion [[1], [3], [8]].  
   - For example, parts printed in the **X-direction (0°)** showed **64% higher ultimate tensile strength (UTS)** compared to raw PLA, while **Y and 45° orientations** had lower UTS values [[5], [6]].  

2. **Impact of Build Orientation**:  
   - **Optimal orientation** (e.g., 0° or aligned with the loading direction) maximizes strength by aligning deposited filaments with the stress path, enhancing interlayer cohesion [[3], [5]].  
   - Non-optimal orientations (e.g., **45° or 90°**) result in **reduced strength** due to weaker interlayer bonds and increased susceptibility to delamination [[3], [5], [8]].  
   - In tensile tests, **ZXY-ZYX orientations** (multi-directional layering) improved bending strength compared to unidirectional prints [[4]].  

3. **Interlayer Bonding and Fracture Behavior**:  
   - Parts printed at **0°** exhibit **brittle fracture** along layer lines, while thermal post-processing (e.g., low-temperature conditioning) improves interlayer bonding, reducing anisotropy and enabling **non-directional fracture** in conditioned samples [[3], [11]].  
   - **Fatigue resistance** is better for **45°-oriented parts** due to distributed stress, though their static UTS is lower than 0°-oriented parts [[5], [6]].  

4. **Mitigation Strategies**:  
   - **Thermal post-processing** (e.g., annealing) enhances crystallinity and interlayer diffusion, improving strength in non-optimal orientations (e.g., 28% UTS increase for 45°/90° prints) [[3], [11], [15]].  
   - **Material modifications**, such as polymer blends or nanofillers (e.g., carbon fiber, graphene), can reduce anisotropy by enhancing interfacial adhesion [[2], [9], [12]].  

In summary, FFF orientation directly impacts PLA part strength due to **interlayer adhesion quality**, with **0° alignment generally optimal for tensile strength** and **45° preferable for fatigue resistance**. Anisotropy remains a critical challenge but can be mitigated through parameter optimization, thermal treatments, or material engineering.

retrieved_contexts: ['Among PEG-based systems, self-assembled nanoparticles (NPs) based on block copolymers of PEG and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PEG-PLGA) have been demonstrated to be effective drug delivery systems to promote mucoadhesion or mucopenetration depending on the length and surface density of the PEG block.7,8 In terms of molecular weight, lower molecular weight PEG (<2 kDa) minimizes mucosal adhesion based on the inherent hydrophilic and electrostatically neutral properties of PEG while higher molecular weight PEG (>10 kDa) promotes mucosal adhesion based on physical interpenetration between the highly flexible PEG chains and the mucosal membrane and/or enhanced hydrogen bonding between the ether groups in the PEG backbone and sugars on glycosylated mucins.9 In terms of density, NPs with low coating densities cannot shield the NP from interactions with mucus and thus promote immobilization and entrapment within the mucin layer, while NPs with high PEG densities (particularly those achievable using low molecular weight PEG) can effectively shield the NP core from mucin interactions to promote mucopenetration.7 While linear PEG coatings have been primarily investigated in this context, changing the morphology of the PEG coating may also offer benefits for tuning NP mucoadhesion and mucopenetration. Herein, we report the mucoadhesion and mucopenetration properties of nanoparticles prepared via the self-assembly of amphiphilic block copolymers of poly(lactic acid) (PLA) and poly(oligo(ethylene glycol) methacrylate) (POEGMA) with various side chain lengths fabricated via atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP).18 We demonstrate that by tuning the length of the side chain we can optimize either mucoadhesion or mucopenetration of the self-assembled nanoparticles while also enabling easier preparation, modification, and/or functionalization of the nanoparticles based on the free radical synthesis approach in comparison to the ring opening synthetic method used for the fabrication of linear PEG-based blocks. We also demonstrate the biosafety and tissue tolerability of the self-assembled nanoparticles for ocular applications, in which optimal tuning of mucoadhesion/mucopenetration is essential to enhance nanoparticle retention in the eye while also ensuring drug transport to the cornea (Scheme 1).', 'In the field of biology, polyethylene glycol (PEG) has low toxicity; exhibits nonspecific adsorption of proteins, cells, and bacteria;16, 17 is resistant to degrading enzymes and mammalian cells;18 and possesses low antigenicity and low immunogenicity.19 PEG is a fascinating synthetic polymer that also has excellent water solubility and biodegradability. Acetic acid (CH3COOH), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), ethanol (C2H5OH), phosphate buffered saline (PBS), and all other chemicals were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Corp., St. Louis, MO, USA.', 'The use of polymers in biomedical applications is continuously increasing [1], [2], [3]. In spite of the recent development, poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is still one of the most preferable candidate [4], [5]. Moreover, the incorporated degradable linkages can generate some side products upon degradation, conditioning the application and the effectiveness of the polymer.', 'First published on 15th July 2015 This work evaluates the response of human aortic endothelial cells (HAECs) to thromboresistant collagen-mimetic hydrogel coatings toward improving the biocompatibility of existing “off-the-shelf” small-caliber vascular grafts. Specifically, bioactive hydrogels - previously shown to support α1/α2 integrin-mediated cell adhesion but to resist platelet activation - were fabricated by combining poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) with a 120 kDa, triple-helical collagen-mimetic protein (Scl2-2) containing the GFPGER adhesion sequence. The primary goal of the current study is to evaluate the capacity of a novel, thromboresistant biomaterial coating based on poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and collagen-mimetic proteins to support human endothelial cell adhesion, migration, and differentiation.', 'Biodegradable and biocompatible polyurethane (PU)-based thermoresponsive hydrogels have recently received increasing attention.6,7 PUs offer attractive mechanical properties and have been studied in regenerative medicine applications.8 They are synthesized from a variety of polyols, diisocyanates, and chain extenders or crosslinkers, offering the flexibility of tailoring their properties to match specific requirements. Drug encapsulation and release as well as temperature-induced actuation behaviour were studied. The potential of fabricating the PEU material into different forms such as microspheres and large 3D porous scaffolds was also demonstrated.', 'Biofouling is an extremely problematic issue for a wide variety of applications,47-49 and thus has generated rigorous interest in the literature for trying to mitigate its prevalence.50 For example, polyethylene glycols (PEGs) have long been used as an antibiofouling coating because it resists the adsorption of free proteins in serum.51, 52 Similarly, PEG can be used to create so-called “stealth” particles, which evade uptake by cells (especially macrophages) and thus have prolonged circulation.53 However, while there have been some studies that address the effect of PEGylation on the properties of responsive structures,54-56 there has been less focus on how PEG copolymers affect the performance of polyelectrolyte multilayers as responsive devices. In addition, the different processing strategies to produce the microcapsules lead to different pore structures, which play a critical role in determining the ultimate properties of the microcapsules.', 'Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) is a synthetic polyester. (35, 44-46) How to change the more common polyether- and polyester-based urethanes from a biodegradable form to a biostable form by incorporation of POSS (or other means) has not yet been reported.', "Crystallization kinetics and crystalline morphology of poly(ethylene naphthalate) and poly(ethylene terephthalate-co-bibenzoate) Bio-based and biodegradable polymers have received growing attention from both industry and academia during the past decades because of the increasing concerns of sustainable environment.1-5 Among them, aliphatic polyesters and poly(ether-ester)s are of high importance as they show widely potential applications in both biomedical materials and are general environmentally friendly.6, 7 Of all the biodegradable thermoplastics, poly(butylene succinate (PBS) is regarded as one of the most promising materials for its high mechanical strength, complete biodegradability, and renewability.8-10 In addition, as a commercially available aliphatic polyester, it has good thermal stability.11 Poly(ethylene glycol (PEG) is nontoxic and can be used in human body. The biocompatibility mechanism of Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) coatings involves several key factors derived from its physicochemical and biological properties, as outlined in the context provided:

1. **Hydrophilicity and Hydration Layer**: PEG's hydrophilic nature forms a hydrated surface layer, which sterically hinders nonspecific interactions. This reduces protein adsorption (preventing opsonization) and minimizes cellular or bacterial adhesion, thereby avoiding immune recognition and inflammatory responses ([1], [3], [6], [9]).

2. **Electrostatically Neutral Properties**: PEG’s lack of charge prevents electrostatic interactions with biological components, such as mucins or blood proteins, further reducing unwanted adhesion and immune activation ([1], [3], [6]).

3. **Stealth Effect**: PEG coatings create "stealth" particles that evade phagocytosis by macrophages and other immune cells. This prolongs circulation time in vivo by resisting recognition by the immune system ([3], [6], [8]).

4. **Low Immunogenicity and Antigenicity**: PEG exhibits minimal immune reactivity, reducing risks of antibody formation or allergic responses. This is critical for FDA approval and biomedical applications ([2], [3], [9], [11]).

5. **Biocompatibility via FDA Approval**: PEG’s safety profile, including low toxicity and biodegradability (when combined with degradable blocks like PLA or PLGA), supports its widespread use in drug delivery, hydrogels, and medical devices ([1], [3], [5], [7], [9]).

6. **Resistance to Biofouling**: PEG coatings prevent nonspecific adsorption of proteins, cells, and bacteria, enhancing biocompatibility in applications such as vascular grafts or ocular implants ([1], [4], [6], [12]).

7. **Tunable Properties**: PEG’s molecular weight and architecture (e.g., linear vs. brush-like structures) allow optimization of mucoadhesion/mucopenetration or degradation rates, balancing biocompatibility with functional requirements ([1], [7], [15]).

In summary, PEG’s biocompatibility arises from its ability to create a non-interactive, hydrated barrier that minimizes biological interactions, coupled with its inherent non-toxic, non-immunogenic nature, making it a versatile and safe choice for biomedical applications.

Meanwhile, surface roughness value measured by AFM is reduced after surface modification, as shown in Fig. 4. The actual total corrosion area of the multilayer-coated substrate is less than that of uncoated substrates, which attributes to the relatively smooth morphology of the modification layer. Nguyen et al. [39] found that the decreasing surface roughness of pure magnesium helped to decrease the corrosion rate in Hank's balanced salt solution, since the actual total surface area exposed to the testing media decreased in lower rough samples; and a lower corrosion rate was expected. The existence of cracks has a disadvantageous effect on corrosion rate for anodic dissolution at the crack tip [40]. Therefore, it is speculated that the morphology of the surface is another important factor to control corrosion rate and match bone regeneration. In previous studies [21], [26], it is also known that the degradation rate could be controlled by surface modification.", 'The introduction of permanent metallic stents was a major advance over balloon angioplasty in the treatment of arterial diseases, being highly effective in preventing acute vessel closure due to balloon-induced dissection, and in reducing the rate of restenosis [1]. However, it has been suggested that the role of the stent is temporary and limited to the intervention and shortly thereafter, until healing and re-endothelialization of the vessel wall is achieved [2]. In fact, after six months arterial remodeling typically enters a stable phase where substantial scaffolding is no longer needed to prevent recoil [3]. Afterwards, the presence of a permanent stent, besides requiring a lifelong anticoagulant therapy, can lead to late thrombosis and chronic inflammation, and can hinder the lumen expansion associated with late vessel remodeling. Biodegradable stents have therefore emerged as one of the most promising approaches in obstructive cardiovascular disease treatment due to their potential in providing mechanical support while it is needed and then, once they are bioabsorbed, leaving behind only the healed natural vessel. This would allow the restoration of vasoreactivity and possibly vessel remodeling as well as to avoid the aforementioned concerns related with the presence of a permanent metallic implant [2]. In addition, biodegradable stents are particularly needed in the case of pediatric cardiovascular treatments where a permanent stent usually requires a second surgery since the target vessel grows with the child [3]. A number of biodegradable stents made of metallic or polymeric materials have been investigated over recent years [4, 5]. Mg alloys are by far the most investigated biodegradable metallic materials for intravascular stent development [6, 7]. The first metallic bioabsorbable stent implanted in humans was the Mg alloy stent studied in the ‘Clinical Performance and Angiographic Results of Coronary Stenting with Absorbable Metal Stents’ trial [8]. Aliphatic polyesters, such as poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), poly(glycolic acid), poly(D,L-lactic-co-glycolic acid), and poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), have been widely investigated for biodegradable stents development due to their relatively long degradation rate and suitable mechanical properties [5, 9]. The Igaki-Tamai stent (Kyoto Medical Planning, Japan), the first biodegradable stent implanted in humans, consists of an extruded high molecular weight PLLA filament with a zig-zag helical coil design [10]. The stent received the CE marking in 2007 for the treatment of peripheral artery diseases, and recent clinical outcomes showed its long term safety as coronary scaffold that could disappear within three years [11]. The ABSORB Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffold based on PLLA (Abbott Vascular, CA) was the first bioabsorbable drug-eluting stent to have clinical outcomes similar to those following metallic drug-eluting stent implantation [12]. Other biodegradable stents that are currently under clinical investigation are the REVA Medical stent made of tyrosine polycarbonate (REVA Medical Inc., CA), the IDEAL stent made of a polyanhydride and salicylic acid (Bioabsorbable Therapeutics Inc., CA), and the novolimus-loaded DESOlve stent made of PLLA (Elixir Medical Corporation, CA) [8, 9]. Polymeric stents are generally composed by interconnected tubular elements with a zig-zag or sinusoidal structure. They are fabricated starting from a tubular body, obtained by injection molding or melt extrusion, whose wall is made porous by means of selective material removal through laser ablation, mechanical machining or chemical etching [3]. Alternatively, polymeric stents are made through melt extrusion of a monofilament that is then woven into a braid-like embodiment. Flege et al [13] recently reported on the development of stents made of PLLA or PLLA-co-PCL by means of a Selective Laser Melting technique. As highlighted by the authors, an additive manufacturing (AM) approach to stents fabrication allows achieving superior freedom in structural design and mechanical performance in comparison to conventional fabrication techniques. In fact, AM techniques allow fabrication of 3D objects with a predefined composition, geometry and size as well as a porous architecture characterized by a fully interconnected network of pores with customizable size, shape and distribution [14].', 'Among cardiovascular diseases, coronary artery disease is responsible for 18 million deaths around the globe [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. During various coronary artery treatments such as angiography, coronary stent implantation renders intra-arterial assistance [[5], [6], [7]]. For a stent to be ideal for clinical use, several fundamental merits are required such as mechanical strength, ductility, and biocompatibility [8]. Unfortunately, after stent implantation, a significant number of patients develop late restenosis [9,10]. Extensive anticoagulant medication is also not useful in the case of such patients. Non-degradable bare metallic stents (BMS) possess excellent mechanical properties with good biocompatibility but still, they cause late thrombosis and restenosis due to chronic inflammation and neointimal hyperplasia [11]. Drug-eluting stents (DES) are also employed which reduce thrombosis and restenosis in the early stages but in the latter stages due to the permanent implantation in the blood vessels, thrombosis and restenosis can occur after a year or two [[12], [13], [14]]. Biodegradable stents are a promising class to mitigate the shortcomings of the BMS and DES stents [15]. Magnesium and its alloys are an alluring class of metals for implants due to their biodegradable and mechanical properties [[16], [17], [18]]. After implantation, the spontaneous degradation and the resorption by the vascular tissue is a promising strategy. Despite the appreciable biocompatibility of the Mg stents, fast degradation hinders its vast clinical application [19,20]. For reducing the degradation rate, surface modification by surface coating is considered an efficient technique. Several surface coating techniques are used to achieve corrosion resistance, such as inorganic coating, chemical conversion, and organic coatings [[21], [22], [23]]. For a coating to be effective, it should be biocompatible and reduce the corrosion rate to an acceptable rate. Among the broad range of coatings, chemical conversion is considered an advantageous method offering simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency. Chemical conversion by treatment with hydrofluoric acid for the formation of magnesium fluoride (MgF2) improves the fast degradation of the Mg by reducing the corrosion rate [20]. Among the polymer coatings, Poly(l-lactide) (PLLA) and Polycaprolactone (PCL) are biodegradable polymers with good biocompatibility and excellent mechanical properties [20]. It has been reported previously PLLA has a better adhesion strength to the Mg substrate as compared to PCL [24]. However, the use of only polymer coating can have shortcomings such as acidic degradation products and undesired capillary pores that can limit the control of the degradation of Mg alloy. The acidic degradation products can also cause inflammation in the surrounding tissue environment of the implant [25]. The hydrophobicity of the polymer coating can hinder cell attachment [26]. HAp particles have high biocompatibility and due to the inorganic ions present in HAp, the degradation products are alkaline in nature. The hydrophilic nature of the HAp makes the cell attachment and proliferation favorable. If used alone on Mg substrate HAp coating can suffer fracture due to its brittle nature resulting in the lessen adhesion to the metal surface. Combining the polymer organic coating with inorganic HAp can assist to overcome the respective disadvantages while combining the advantages [18]. The inorganic alkaline degradation products can be neutralized by the polymeric acidic products and the intermolecular interactions between the different polymer layers and HAp can increase the adhesion strength of the coatings [27]. The degradation rate of the coating can be improved with increased bioactivity by combining polymeric organic coating with inorganic HAp.', 'In 2018, the US FDA reported that the design of the staples is the main crucial factor, and among the approximate 1 lakh cases of staple failure, more than ten thousand serious injuries occurred due to the abnormal deformation of the staple shape. (15) The design of Mg staples often references that of Ti staples. However, Mg staples, being biodegradable, are subjected to physiologically stressful environments, which may lead to stress corrosion cracking (SCC) during normal physical activities. (16) Studies have reported that Mg staples can degrade rapidly and break easily after deformation into a B shape due to their susceptibility to stress corrosion. (17−19) For instance, Gao et al. (20) found that applying tensile stress to a high-purity (HP) Mg bar will accelerate the corrosion process in vitro, resulting in severe pitting corrosion and SCC. After immersing the homogenized WE54 alloy in simulated body fluid (SBF), Asgharinezhad Baloochi et al. (21) found that corrosion pits and cracks are the primary causes of the initial fatigue crack formation. Generally, stress and strain distribution in biodegradable implants with plastic deformation can be finely regulated through structural design. (17,22) Wu et al. (23) designed staples in a U shape with interior angles of 90 and 100°. The finite element analysis (FEA) results indicated that the staple with a 100° interior angle was optimal as it effectively distributed residual stress at the staple’s tip upon closure, thereby reducing the risk of stress corrosion. The maximum incidence of staple failure is caused by deformation in the leg sections due to stress propagation and subsequent stress concentration. (15) The compression force of staples fired from the dispenser is greater than that in other regions. Staples in different open and closed stages may experience varying levels of stress concentration in the leg area. To prevent rapid corrosion or premature fracture at the bending points, the structure of Mg staples needs to be optimally designed to reduce stress and strain concentrations at the joints of the staple legs during the deformation process into a B shape. In this study, HP Mg (99.98 wt %) was adopted to develop biodegradable staples for intestinal anastomosis. Finite element numerical simulations were conducted to optimize the interior angle and height of the staple, aiming to minimize the stress concentration. Subsequently, Mg staples with optimized structures were manufactured, and the mechanical properties were characterized through tensile tests and burst pressure measurements, while the in vitro corrosion behaviors were evaluated using immersion tests and electrochemical measurements in modified simulated body fluid (m-SBF). At last, the effectiveness of biodegradable staples was verified, demonstrating that an optimized design could facilitate the accelerated clinical translation of magnesium-based anastomotic staples. Ten U-shaped Mg staples were designed according to ref (24), and as listed in Table 1, the interior angles and the height of the staple were the two factors to be optimized. After finite element numerical simulation, the staple with the optimized structure was chosen for the experimental studies. At the same time, a reference staple group was set up for comparison to verify the effectiveness of the structure optimization.', 'Metal matrix composites are chosen for orthopedic implants as compared to polymer and ceramic matrix composites due to their exceptional combination of properties, such as mechanical strength and fracture toughness. Numerous examples of current usage of orthopedic implants include joints (hip, knee, ankle, and so on), bone spacers, or bone filling materials. The progress on new biomaterials extends toward monolithic bulk materials and composites of different classes of materials in addition to coating. There are two types of implants for biomedical application, for example, permanent and temporary. For permanent implant SS316L stainless steel, titanium alloy and cobalt-chromium-molybdenum are widely used. (1) Most of the metallic implant is stiffer than the human bone. For biomedical application as a temporary implant, magnesium alloy has a considerable interest. Human bone is an example of a lightweight multiscale composite material, and for the long-term stability of the orthopedic implant, selecting suitable material plays an important role. The Mg-based biodegradable implant plays a significant role in orthopedic implant due to its good mechanical properties close to the bone, such as Young’s modulus and excellent biocompatibility. (2) The issue for stress shielding is reduced by the similarity of bone material to the human bone. The Mg-based biomaterial is used as a temporary fixation device as orthopedic fracture fixation due to its good biodegradability and biocompatibility. In the present day, the demand for orthopedic implants is increasing tremendously. Due to the higher occurrence of cardiovascular and orthopedic diseases, the speedy growth of bioimplant application takes place. Titanium alloy, cobalt-chromium, and stainless steel are the nondegradable bioimplant generally used for permanent application. However, this permanent implant releases toxic ions or wear debris; this damages the bone tissue and reduces the biocompatibility that limits its application. Moreover, the Young’s modulus of natural bone (3-20 GPa) is much lower to titanium alloy (110-117 GPa), stainless steel (189-205 GPa), and cobalt-chromium alloy (230 GPa), and due to this, the implant stability reduces and causing stress shielding. (3) After healing the fractured bone, the second time surgery is needed to remove the permanent implant because these alloys are non-biodegradable in nature. On the other hand, magnesium (Mg)-based biomaterial is of excessive interest due to its exceptional biocompatibility and biodegradability. In recent years, Mg-based biomaterial has received tremendous interest due to its excellent properties that are compatible with bone. There are several Mg alloys that have the potential for bioimplant applications, such as WE43, AZ91, (4) Mg-Zn, (5) Mg-Ca, (6) and Mg-Mn-Zn alloy. (7) Mg has low Young’s modulus (41-45 GPa), density (1.74-2.0 g/cm3), and mechanical properties that are parallel to the natural bone, that is: Young’s modulus (3-20 GPa) and density (1.8-2.1 g/cm3), whereas the density of other implantable materials are more (Ti alloy ∼4.5 g/cm3, stainless steel ∼8 g/cm3), and due to that, the stress shielding effect can be eliminated. (8) Mg also has greater stiffness than ceramic biomaterials. With time, Mg is biodegradable in a physiological environment, so the risk of a second surgery is also eliminated for implant removal.', 'Cardiovascular diseases currently stand as the leading cause of death and chronic disability [1]. There are over 500 million individuals worldwide affected by cardiovascular diseases, contributing to an estimated 18 million deaths annually [2]. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with stent implantation greatly reduces the risk of traditional open-heart surgery. This approach not only promotes postoperative recovery but also addresses acute elastic recoil often associated with balloon angioplasty [3]. It has emerged as one of the most efficacious treatments for cardiovascular diseases [4]. In comparison to non-degradable stents, biodegradable stents have the unique ability to gradually degrade and eventually vanish following vascular remodeling, effectively avoiding a series of immune rejection problems caused by the long-term persistent foreign body stimulation of permanent implants [5]. As a result, biodegradable stents have become a prominent research focus and development direction in the field of cardiovascular stents [6]. Among various biodegradable materials, magnesium (Mg) alloys are considered to be excellent candidates for biodegradable implants due to their appropriate mechanical performance, good biocompatibility and inherent bioactivity [6], [7]. However, in physiological environments containing large amount of polar corrosive media, Mg alloys exhibit excessively fast and uncontrollable degradation behaviors, leading to premature mechanical support loss and unpredictable structural damage [8], [9]. To enhance the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys, a series of anticorrosion strategies have been extensively explored, including impurity content reduction, alloy element regulation [10], [11], improvement of the forging process [12], surface deposition [13] and utilization of surface coating technologies [9], [14]. Unfortunately, this problem has not been effectively addressed so far due to the structural features of Mg and the stringent material requirements for biomedical implants. Compared with other anti-corrosion methods, polymer coating technology is easy to implement, and the degradation rate of Mg alloy substrate can be adjusted by optimizing the polymer structure and coating thickness [15], [16]. In addition, polymers can be conveniently biomodified or loaded with drugs to achieve anti-platelet, anticoagulation, anti-inflammation, enhanced endothelialization, inhibition of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) proliferation and so on. For biodegradable Mg-based stents, the polymer coating should possess commendable barrier properties against corrosion media, robust mechanical performance and adhesion strength to withstand the significant deformation arising from stent crimping and expansion [9], [17]. Moreover, it is imperative for the coating to be biocompatible and biodegradable.', "Compressive strength of FHA/PCL is higher than uncoated sample after immersion test. Magnesium (Mg) and its alloys have been considered a potential material for fabricating biodegradable metallic stents and several orthopaedic applications in recent years [1]. Magnesium possesses low density and high specific strength, and has an elastic modulus closer to that of natural bones when compared with other implant metallic materials such as stainless steel, titanium alloys and cobalt chromium alloys [2], [3], [4]. However, the use of magnesium is hindered by its poor corrosion resistance, which causes the mechanical properties of the implant to decrease significantly, resulting in the inability of tissue to heal [5], [6], [7]. Furthermore, the Mg corrosion process involves evolution of hydrogen gas, which accumulates in vivo adjacent to the implant. The H2 gas and subsequent formation of hydrogen bubbles can noticeably impair the clinical applications of Mg [5], [8]. Apart from alloying, surface modifications such as plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO), ion implantation, pulsed laser deposition, Ca-P coatings and polymer coatings have been widely applied in order to reduce the initial degradation rate of Mg alloys [9], [10], [11], [12]. Polymer-based biodegradable materials such as poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) and polycaprolactone (PCL) have been widely used in clinics to help with the repair of human tissues, for example as absorbable bone screws, plates and pins [13], [14]. Among these, PCL, (−[(CH2)5COO]n-) is a promising polymer because of its significant toughness and good biocompatibility as well as remarkable mechanical properties, such as 80% elongation at break point [15], [16]. PCL is a semicrystalline aliphatic polymer that has a slower degradation rate and higher fracture energy than most biocompatible polymers [15], [16], [17]. In addition, PCL is hydrophobic, which is desirable for a coating applied on magnesium because magnesium shows a high corrosion rate when exposed to physiological media containing Cl− [1], [16]. However, PCL has several disadvantages when used alone because of insufficient strength and a lack of the desired bioactivity [13]. To address this problem, fluorine-doped hydroxyapatite (FHA; Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2-xFx, where 0 < x < 2) films beneath organic coatings appear to have excellent potential to obtain both corrosion protection and surface stability without adversely affecting mechanical properties [18], [19]. FHA was reported to be a promising candidate for replacement of hydroxyapatite (HA) because of its low solubility and similar biocompatibility compared with HA [18], [20]. FHA coatings could provide lower dissolution, better apatite-like layer deposition, better protein adsorption and improved alkaline phosphatase activity in cell cultures [21]. Hence, it is reasonable to deduce that a composite material of polymer and calcium phosphate may combine the advantages of the two materials for the enhancement of corrosion resistance of Mg alloys [14]. In this study, a combination of two methods was used for the synthesis of fluorine-doped HA and PCL on the surface of Mg alloys. An initial electrodeposition (ED) was carried out to deposit a fluorine-doped HA layer on the surface of the Mg substrate. Subsequently, dip coating was performed to deposit a PCL film on the surface of the Mg substrate. These techniques have been selected because of their simple operation, ease of particle-size control, compact coating, low temperature processing and low cost [22], [23]. Various studies have reported that polymer and ceramic-polymer coatings can increase the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys in SBF [16], [24], [25], [26]. Abdal-hay et al. [27] reported a Ti-O/PLA composite coating on Mg alloy for adequate corrosion protection and the production of Mg-based implant materials with good biocompatibility. In this regard, HA-doped poly(lactic acid) porous film was coated on AZ31 Mg alloy for improvement of the bioactivity and corrosion behaviour of the alloy [28]. Zomorodian et al. [29] showed that a composite polymeric coating on biodegradable AZ31 Mg alloy can slow the corrosion rate of the alloys in Hank's solution. However, there are very few reports on the corrosion behaviour of ceramic (FHA)-polymer (PCL) coatings in simulated body fluid (SBF) and, in particular, dependence of mechanical properties on the degradation behaviour of composite coatings in orthopaedic implants. Thus, the main approach of the present study is the synthesis of a mono-layered PCL and bi-layered nFHA/PCL composite coating on Mg-Zn-Ce alloy by ED followed by dip coating. In addition, the degradation mechanism of the bi-layered nFHA/PCL composite in the SBF solution was evaluated. Magnesium alloys were prepared by melting 99.9% pure magnesium ingots, pure zinc (99.99%), and Mg-30 wt% Ce. The melts, with a constant concentration of Ce (3 wt%) and Zn (2 wt%), were then cast in a 300 °C preheated stainless steel mould to produce an ingot. In preparation for further experiments, several Mg-2Zn-3Ce specimens with composition of 0.047% Si, 0.034% Mn, 2.261% Zn, 0.021% Al, 0.012% Fe, 3.124% Ce and 94.501% Mg with dimensions of 15 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm, were cut from the ingot. The specimens were then mechanically wet ground with 320-2000 SiC grit paper until all visible scratches were removed.", 'The biodegradable implants which contain magnesium-based materials are used for temporary orthopedic and cardiovascular stent applications. The use of magnesium-based biodegradable implants avoids second surgical procedures and reduces the stress-shielding effect. So, it is more advantageous than compared to other metallic implants such as 316L steel, titanium alloys and Co-Cr alloys. Nowadays AZ31Mg alloy sheets that are coated with PCL nanofibers are used in designing biodegradable Mg-based implants and it has shown excellent corrosion resistance, wettability, bioactivity and degradation properties [130]. Most of the materials that are commonly used for bone fracture fixation are 316L stainless steel, cobalt-chromium-based alloys, pure titanium and its alloys, but all these are non-biodegradable. One of the important characteristics of an implant is its ability to degrade after the healing of bone. Since the implant is metallic, it is a foreign body to the tissue due to which local inflammation may take place, and in some cases, a second surgery may be required for the removal of that implant. To avoid such risks, biodegradable metallic implants came into use. One of the most commonly used degradable metallic materials is magnesium and its alloys. But again, there is an issue of corrosion and also it degrades rapidly with the release of hydrogen gas on degradation. To overcome this issue, several strategies like alloying, various surface treatments were tried to enhance the corrosion resistance of magnesium. To alter its original mechanical properties some of the rare earth metals like Zr, Ce is added into the Mg substrate, but they are toxic to the human cells and also the cytocompatibility of these elements is not known. To overcome all these drawbacks, the biodegradable polymeric membrane fabricated by dichloromethane and PCL onto Mg alloys is developed. By coating this controllable polymeric membrane on Mg alloy, the corrosion and degradation rate is reduced and also it provides good cytocompatibility of eGFP and SaOS-2 osteoblasts. The cell toxicity is also not observed. Now, these biodegradable polymeric membrane implants are extensively used in clinical use for orthopedic applications [131]. Some of the important parameters of ideal biodegradable implants are lower rates of biodegradability, to provide sufficient mechanical support until the healing process gets completed. Another parameter is biocompatibility which can be controlled by using bioinert elements, nutrients, etc. [132]. The organ which undergoes the most transplants/grafts every year is bone. Bone fracture is a common problem everywhere due to the increased rate of accidents/diseases. It is also estimated that every year over 3 million bone surgeries are performed worldwide. For this reason, the quality and efficiency of bone fracture treatments are more important for patients as well as for doctors [133].', 'Multilayer-coated ZEK100 magnesium alloy has a good biocompatibility. Compared with ceramics or polymeric materials, metals are superior for load-bearing applications, due to their high strength and fracture toughness [1]. Stainless steel, titanium-based alloys [2], [3], [4] and cobalt-based alloys are commonly used in the fixation of fractured bones [5], but these metals could not be degraded in the body; thus, a second surgery is needed to remove these metals after broken bones heal. In comparison, magnesium alloys possess excellent biocompatibility [6], [7], [8] and high primary stability to avoid the second surgery [9], [10]. Due to similar elastic modulus with human bone tissue [11], the mechanical properties of magnesium alloys such as tensile [12] and compressive strengths are close to natural bones [13]. Magnesium alloys have less undesirable effects of stress shielding that occur in conventional metallic implants [11], [14], [15]. It has also been confirmed that the initial mechanical strength of ZEK100 can be suitably used as a material for biodegradable implants in weight bearing bones [14], [15]. However, there are questions on whether these mechanical properties can remain to be satisfactory when the surface is modified and corrosion time is increased. High corrosion rate is the main reason that restricts the application of magnesium alloys in biology. The addition of a rare earth (RE) element into the magnesium alloy is known to slow corrosion rate and enhance the response of the surrounding bone [10], [16]. Although ZEK100 (0.1 wt.% RE) has been proven to be initially stable, positively biodegradable and suitable for implant applications [17], it continues to have a relatively rapid corrosion rate, compared with the healing process of fractured bones [10], [15], [18]. The main purpose of surface treatment on biodegradable magnesium alloys is to reduce its degradation rate [19]. Although the uncoated added RE element could reduce the corrosion rate of magnesium alloy [20], [21], [22], [23], results have shown that corrosion rate of modified magnesium alloys can be inhibited by the LBL method to some extent, but not satisfactorily. Currently used methods for measuring biodegradation rates in vivo such as magnesium ion changes in serum magnesium levels, hydrogen production rate and PH [13], [18], [24] are indirect and does not have enough precision. Thus, weight loss is chosen to measure corrosion rate. In order to achieve a satisfactory corrosion rate, the fabrication and surface modification process of magnesium alloy needs to be further investigated.']
response: The fatigue life of biodegradable magnesium (Mg) stents is notably shorter compared to stainless steel (SS316L). Context [1] highlights that pure Mg (HP Mg) failed after **1 day** in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) under corrosion fatigue testing, while stainless steel exhibits significantly higher fatigue strength. Although manufacturing improvements or physiological environments (less aggressive than PBS) may extend Mg's fatigue life, rapid degradation remains a critical limitation. Stainless steel's superior fatigue performance is attributed to its inherent corrosion resistance and mechanical stability, which ensures long-term structural integrity. Thus, Mg stents, despite surface modifications or alloying, generally have a shorter fatigue life than SS316L due to their accelerated degradation in physiological conditions.
reference: Magnesium alloys have lower fatigue strength than stainless steel (316L). While stainless steel has a fatigue limit of ~250-300 MPa, Mg alloys are often ~100-150 MPa. This necessitates careful stent strut design to ensure they can withstand the millions of cardiac cycles required before the stent degrades.
