retrieved_contexts: ['The rate of hydrolytic degradation of tissue-engineered scaffolds made from bioresorbable polyesters is dependent on several factors. Some are related to the properties of the degrading polymeric material, but others are related to the geometry of the porous structure and the operating environment. It is well known that the rate of hydrolytic degradation of a given object, porous or nonporous, is lower when it is exposed to dynamic conditions, a flowing medium, than when it operates in static conditions. The most likely reason is the more efficient removal of the acidic degradation products from the vicinity of the polymeric material when it is operating in a flowing medium. In this article, we present a new phenomenological reaction-diffusion model of aliphatic polymer degradation. The model can be used to predict the significance of various factors in in vitro degradation tests, with particular reference to the flow of the degradation medium, and the frequency of medium replacement in the case of static conditions. The developed model was used to simulate the degradation of poly(dl-lactide-co-glycolide) scaffolds with different porosities subjected to static and dynamic testing conditions. The results confirm that the porosity of the scaffold had a significant influence on the degradation rate. It was shown that the combination of dynamic conditions and high porosity effectively reduced the mass loss and molecular weight loss of the degrading polymer. However, the effect of changes in the velocity of the flowing medium had a negligible effect on the rate of degradation. © 2014 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J. Appl. Polym. Sci. 2014, 131, 40280. The degradation of polymeric materials is a very important issue, not only from the point of view of polymer science, but it is crucial in the context of the majority of applications, especially in the biomedical field.1, 2 The majority of biodegradable polyesters used for orthopedic implants, including polylactide, polyglicolide, and their copolymers, suffer from in situ hydrolytic degradation in aquatic environments.3, 4 The resulting changes in the biophysical and biochemical properties of the polymers have a significant effect on the behavior of tissue-engineered components. Hydrolysis is the dominant mechanism in the degradation of bioresorbable polyesters. Almost immediately after a polymer is placed into an aquatic environment, water molecules diffuse into the polymeric matrix. After some time, a large concentration of water molecules accumulates in the material. The water molecules reduce the strength of the chemical bonds of the polymeric chains. This causes them to divide into water-soluble shorter chains (oligomers and monomers) characterized by carboxylic ends, which are known to autocatalyze ester hydrolysis. These oligomers and monomers are able to diffuse inside the polymer matrix. The chain scissions inside the polymer matrix cause a reduction in the molecular weight of the polymer. The water-soluble monomers that are located near to the surface of the implant can leach out before total degradation occurs, whereas those that are located deep inside the polymer matrix remain entrapped and contribute to the autocatalytic effect.5, 6 This causes the degradation of large-size devices to proceed heterogeneously and to occur more rapidly internally than at the surface.', 'The degradation rate of a scaffold which is related to the properties of the degrading polymer, the porosity of the material and the operating medium must be in synchronization with the replacement of new matrix made from cells [41, 42]. Among them, the porosity had a significant effect on the degradation rate. All cryogels exhibited dissimilar degradation behaviors due to the different pore morphologies as shown in Fig. 5b. It was found that high porosity and large pore sizes resulted in high degradation rate. The apparent degradation rate for 40:60 chitosan/pectin cryogels was after 21 days. In addition to the pore structure of cryogels, chitosan which has a higher molecular weight with higher hydrophobicity than pectin degraded more slowly. Both natural polymers have been shown to degrade mainly by simple hydrolysis of the ester bond into acidic monomers, which can be removed from the body by normal metabolic pathways. The compressive strength and Young modulus of chitosan/pectin cryogel scaffolds were tested in their dry form. As listed in Table 2, the compression strength of the cryogels increased as the pectin ratio increased. This can be explained by the increased electrostatic interactions between chitosan and pectin with an increasing ratio of pectin up to 60%. The compression strength of the 40:60 chitosan/pectin sample was 2 times higher as compared with the 100:0 plain chitosan cryogel (112 ± 12 kPa vs. 52 ± 10 kPa). Higher pectin content increases the amount of ionic interactions occurring in composite cryogels and thereby enhances their compression strength. Chen et al. and Martins et al. found similar results due to the increased pectin content in chitosan/pectin composites [43, 44]. In addition, the Young’s modulus was much higher for the 40:60 chitosan/pectin scaffolds than for the 100:0 chitosan/pectin scaffolds. In the view of literature research, the Young’s modulus of the cryogels was on the level of smooth muscle and skeletal muscle [45, 46]. All the four types of cryogels exhibited a porous and interconnected structure as a result of cryogelation process. The gradual increase in pectin in the polymer composition enhanced the pore diameter, porosity and swelling ability of the cryogel. The inclusion of highest ratio of pectin resulted in significantly increased mean pore size, as well as porosity, compared to the plain chitosan cryogel (Fig. 4f). Swelling ability of the 40:60 samples was also higher compared to the other samples, which was in accordance with the porosity of the samples (Fig. 5a). High and interconnected porosity in addition to high swellability increase the performance of cryogels in guiding the cells for tissue regeneration. During fabrication of cryogel scaffolds, the first observations of the successful production of interconnected supermacroporous, spongy and mechanically stable matrices can be made by physical observational tests. As the swollen matrix is compressed/squeezed, it releases the water from its interconnected pores, and when the compression is removed, and the matrix is placed in aqueous environment, it absorbs the liquid rapidly and turns to its original shape without any deformation. This property of cryogels is excellent for tissue engineering applications. 1.  **Piezoelectric Property of PLLA:**
    *   PLLA exhibits **shear piezoelectricity**, primarily along the z-axis, characterized by the **d14 coefficient** reported in the range of **7-12 pC N⁻¹** [1,2,13,14].
    *   This piezoelectricity arises from the **aligned electric dipoles** of the **C=O bonds** branching out from the polymer backbone within its semi-crystalline structure [1,2,13,14].
    *   The piezoelectric properties depend critically on **crystallinity and molecular orientation** [1,2,13,14].
    *   The thermodynamically stable α-crystalline form has randomly oriented dipoles and negligible piezoelectricity. Processing (e.g., stretching, electrospinning) transforms it into the β-crystalline form where C=O dipoles align along the chain, imparting piezoelectricity [4,5,13,14].
    *   **Stretching** (drawing ratio ~2.5-4.5) aligns C=O dipoles uniaxially, enhancing shear piezoelectricity [1,2].
    *   **Electrospinning** aligns chains and dipoles, resulting in macro piezoelectricity [1,2]. It can also induce **longitudinal piezoelectricity (d33)** along the fiber direction for the first time [3,6,8], with a reported d33 of ~3 pm V⁻¹ [8].
    *   Piezoelectricity can be enhanced by increasing orientation and crystallinity (e.g., via nano-confinement improving crystallinity by 70%) [1,2].

2.  **Biomedical Relevance:**
    *   **Biodegradable Sensors:** PLLA films/nanofibers are used to fabricate fully **biodegradable piezoelectric sensors**, often sandwiched between biocompatible electrodes (like molybdenum), for measuring physiological pressures (e.g., 0-18 kPa), diaphragmatic contraction pressure, and blood pulse [1,2,7,3]. These sensors function reliably even during degradation [7].
    *   **Ultrasonic Transducers:** PLLA-based devices function as biodegradable **ultrasonic transducers** for applications like assisting drug delivery, opening the blood-brain barrier, and underwater structural health monitoring [1,2]. Its intrinsic shear mode avoids the need for electrical poling [1,2].
    *   **Air Filtration:** Piezoelectric PLLA nanofiber membranes generate surface charges, enabling highly efficient, reusable, humidity-resistant, and **biodegradable air filters** (e.g., face masks) for capturing small particulate matter (PM1.0, PM2.5) and preventing pathogen penetration [1,2,11,12].
    *   **Tissue Engineering Scaffolds:** The **bioelectric signals** generated by piezoelectric PLLA scaffolds improve the physiological electric environment, regulating cell action for effective **bone regeneration and repair** [11,12].
    *   **Physiological Monitoring:** Electrospun PLLA nanofiber membranes are used in **flexible, wearable piezoelectric biosensors (PBio-e-skin)** for non-invasive monitoring of vital signs (muscle movement, joint motion, arterial pressure, pulse) without external power [8,9].
    *   **Medical Devices:** Examples include PLLA fiber-based medical tweezers/catheters for tasks like grasping and eliminating thrombosis [9].

retrieved_contexts: ['In this work, the influence of melt compounding and incorporation of talc on a commercial grade of poly (lactic acid) was studied. The apparent viscosity of the PLA decreases with compounding time, as the material is subject to thermo mechanical degradation. Concerning the incorporation of talc, it was found that it increases the viscosity measured during the compounding, but it also enhances the stability of the material viscosity during the mixing. The relative viscosity of the as-received PLA is 2.5, in agreement with the datasheet provided by the supplier. The formulations #1, #2, and #3 that involve talc behave in the same fashion. The formulation #2 that involves talc and maleic anhydride (MAH) grafted PLA (PLA-MA) has the greatest relative viscosity after extrusion compounding. This result can be attributed to the effect of the expected interactions of the PLA-MA chain extender with the talc and Poly(Lactic Acid) (PLA). Weight crystallinity content (Xc, %) of each material after the first and second scan was also calculated.', 'XRD diffractograms for PLA and PLA/CH-g-OLLA nanocomposite films have demonstrated well resolved peaks at 14.7°, 16.4°, 18.9° and 22.1°, which corresponds to the various crystallographic planes i.e. [010], [200/110], [203] and [015] respectively as displayed in Fig. 2c. A sharp peak at 2θ =16.4° confirms α crystalline structure and exhibits orthorhombic crystal structure of PLA matrix. A peak positioned at 22.1° in all the samples also represents the presence of α form of crystals. The existence of a β crystalline form of PLA is approved by the availability of two peaks at 14.7° and 18.9°, which is less stable crystalline form than α form. It is noteworthy to mention that the sharpness and intensity of all the crystalline peaks reduce continuously with an increase in CH-g-OLLA loadings, which gives a clear indication about the decrement in crystallinity% from 37% to 27.4%. The phenomena of shifting of peaks are absent in PLA/CH-g-OLLA nanocomposite films, which suggests that the ordered crystal structure is unaffected with the addition of nano-filler. From XRD data, the calculated values of crystallinity of PLA decreases with the addition of filler due to the effect of processing of composites. During melt extrusion technique, the material comes out from the die and further passes through the chilled rollers, which provides the sudden cooling of the extruded material. Hence, the quenching of polymer will result in the reduction in crystallinity. The values of Mn and Mw of pristine PLA are observed as ~155,000 Da and ~264,000 Da respectively. The effect of various loadings of CH-g-OLLA copolymer on the values of Mn, Mw and polydispersity index (PDI) of pristine PLA during melt extrusion technique is demonstrated as shown in Fig. 3. According to Fig. 3, the values of Mn and Mw of PLA are continuously reduced up to ~23% and ~15% respectively with an increment in the loading of CH-g-OLLA up to 5 wt%. This may be attributed to the alteration of long PLA chain lengths due to the increment in chitosan content. The technique ‘melt extrusion’ of PLA/CH-g-OLLA nanocomposite films may also be one of the dominant reason for the reduction in Mn and Mw values of PLA due to applied mechanical stresses between the screws during processing. It is noteworthy to mention that the hydrolysis reactions occur preferentially in the amorphous phase of PLA matrix during processing, which is responsible for initiating the degradation of polyester chains. Similar results have been observed by Tenn et al. [36] for PLA/montmorillonite-based nanocomposites prepared by melt processing. The values of PDI for PLA and its nanocomposite films are calculated as 1.7, 1.76, 1.76 and 1.89 after the addition of 1%, 3% and 5% (wt/wt) of nano-filler respectively as shown in Fig. 3, which suggests that the non-uniform distribution of PLA chain lengths due to the presence of CH-g-OLLA in various amounts. Molecular weight distribution in melt extruded PLA and its nanocomposite films', "Molecular weight decrease caused by thermal, hydrolytic, and mechanical degradation of PLA is a major concern during melt processing. Modeling and predicting degradation is essential to minimize material deterioration and material property changes. Current kinetic degradation models show potential to describe degradation, but they are limited to rheometry and focus on thermal and/or hydrolytic degradation only. There is no model yet that describes degradation during melt processing techniques such as injection molding or extrusion. The aim of this work is to establish a degradation model that predicts the molecular weight decrease of PLA throughout single-screw extrusion. A combination of experimental extrusion data and numerical simulations is used to establish the model. Subsequently, the model is experimentally validated to check its predictive quality. The results show good similarity between predictions and measurements for multiple process variables. The maximum deviation between both was found to be 5%. Combining experimental data with numerical simulations allows us to describe the extrusion process in an equipment-independent way, which is essential to use the model for different extruders or dies. Overall, minimizing degradation during processing will avoid the loss of valuable resources, materials, and time, and will result in obtaining high quality products. The sensitivity of the ester bonds in poly(lactic acid) or PLA is a major concern during processing, since polymer chains of molten PLA have the tendency to degrade [1]. The potential presence of moisture in the granules, combined with high shear stresses and temperatures during extrusion or injection molding, may result in hydrolytic, thermal, and mechanical degradation. Chain scission of the polymer chains, caused by the three types of degradation, leads to a decrease in molecular weight, depending on the applied process parameters [2-5]. The selection of process parameters is crucial to minimize polymer degradation, which is nowadays often based on experience by the process operator, recommendations on the technical data sheet of the material supplier or by trial-and-error. Generally, it is not investigated or known whether the selected process parameters result in degradation. Nevertheless, degradation may strongly affect PLA's material properties [2]. In the work of Teixeira et al. [6], the complex viscosity was reported to decrease from 2680 Pa s to around 1300 Pa s at the die end due to degradation during processing. A similar conclusion was reported by Benvenuta-Tapia and Vivaldo-Lima [7], where a decrease from 2300 Pa s for neat PLA to 330 Pa s was observed after processing PLA. Aside from rheological properties, also thermal properties are affected by processing PLA. Due to a decreasing molecular weight caused by degradation, the mobility of the polymer chains increases and allows faster crystallization. A decrease of the cold crystallization temperature from 103.0°C to 97.1°C and an increase of the crystallization temperature from 96.8°C to 100.2°C was reported in the work of Lv et al. [8]. Other researchers [9, 10] confirmed a change in the crystallization behavior. Also the mechanical properties are affected by degradation, such as a reported decrease in the stress at break from 66 to 25 MPa after repeated injection molding cycles [10], explained by a lower number of entanglements due to chain scission. The impact strength was also affected by degradation, as shown in the work of Zenkiewicz et al. [11] where a decrease of 0.19 kJ m−2 (7.4%) occurred in the first reprocessing cycle. Yellowing of PLA can also occur due to degradation, as reported in the work of Agüero et al. [12] by an increase of (blue-yellow value in LAB color space definition) from 10.75 to 20.59. In order to limit the change of PLA's properties and to obtain high quality products after extrusion or injection molding, it is essential to understand the severity of degradation during processing.", 'In this work, bio-based products composed of blends of a star-shaped poly(d,l-lactide) (star-PDLLA) and a conventional linear poly(l-lactide) (linear-PLLA) are produced by typical large-scale manufacturing techniques for thermoplastic blends. In the first case, the two polymers are blended through melt extrusion, producing pellets that are subsequently compression-molded into the final bio-based polymer films. Alternatively, the star/linear poly(lactide) (PLA) materials are developed by direct blending through injection molding, a process that generally applies after a preblending extrusion step to ensure proper mixing. Thermomechanical degradation induced by the different processes is evaluated, and the performances of the final star/linear PLA products are thoroughly compared. The effect of the short-branched, amorphous, star polymeric component on thermal, mechanical, and rheological properties of the conventional PLLA is comprehensively investigated, revealing that the star-PDLLA incorporation promotes the formation of a more flexible and tougher material with reduced capability of crystallization. Most importantly, star-PDLLA decreases the melt viscosity of the final material, while increasing the shear-thinning behavior, hence facilitating melt flow during manufacturing. Such properties lead to enhanced material ductility and processability, with respect to typically brittle and viscous conventional PLLA-based materials. Moreover, the tuning of final material performances can be achieved by simply varying the star-PDLLA content. Poly(lactide) is one of the most extensively investigated and utilized bio-based polymers of the last decades. This biodegradable thermoplastic polyester is now subject of significant industrial and commercial development by numerous manufacturing companies around the world, also thanks to recent advancements enabling its production from renewable stocks.[1] PLA exhibits many interesting properties compared to existing oil-derived commodity polymers, such as discrete tensile strength, stiffness, and biodegradability.[2, 3] However, although much progress has been made on PLA performances, its applicability on flexible products, both for packaging and biomedical field, is still limited due to several inherent drawbacks, such as brittleness, high melt viscosity, and poor impact resistance.[4] Conventional semicrystalline PLA (linear poly(l-lactide) (linear-PLLA)) is commonly processed at temperatures close to 200 °C, where chain scission and transesterification phenomena become significant.[5-7] PLA may also exhibit resistance to flow and color change through an injection-molding process due to the elevated melt viscosity at the applied manufacturing conditions.[8-10] Indeed, it has been demonstrated that bio-based polyesters, like PLA, undergo drastic degradation for every processing step they are subjected to, before getting to the market (i.e., from batch compounding of the raw material to the molding of the final commercial item).[9, 11] These complications generally cause loss of mechanical performances. Although a lot of research has been conducted on improvement of PLA performances through extensive use of both small molecules and macromolecules (e.g., plasticizers,[12, 13] polymeric tougheners,[14, 15] or nucleating agents[16, 17]), such modifications often drastically affect thermal stability, mechanical resistance, and, above all, biodegradability of the final material.[18] Indeed, in order to solve PLA disadvantages and maximize its applicability, it is essential to optimize its processing at high shear rates.[4, 9] Therefore, finding a proper green modifier to enhance ductility and ease the melt flow of conventional PLA would represent a versatile tool to improve its processability, preventing its typical deterioration during manufacturing, as well as final PLA-based product performances. An interesting industrially employed method to modify rheological properties of polymeric materials is the introduction of branching.[19, 20] This strategy has widely been used in the past for implementation of polyolefins processing[21, 22] and is now attracting attention for bio-based polyesters.[23-25] However, the information regarding combinations of different PLA architectures, which would ensure maximal compatibility between the blend components, is very limited, especially at relatively high-scale processing levels.[20, 26, 27] It has been shown that short-branched polymers present lower viscosities and improved melt elasticity than corresponding linear structures with comparable molecular weight (MW).[19, 28, 29] In particular, star-shaped macromolecular architectures, which consist of branched polymers with only one branching point, are characterized by very low capability of forming entanglements and extremely compact structures.[29, 30] Such well-defined polymer architectures can drastically enhance ductility and melt flow of conventional PLA, without altering the chemical nature of the material.[31] However, a high-molecular-weight PLLA is generally required to ensure sufficient structural strength.[32] Therefore, the incorporation of a star-shaped PLA with relatively short-chain branches to a conventional linear PLA matrix would decrease the overall melt viscosity, yet preserving the good original properties of the latter.[27, 33-35]', 'Figure 7a illustrates the variation of torque over time during the melt mixing process, which indirectly reflects the plasticization process and rheological properties of the samples. During the melting process of TPS, glycerol as a plasticizer diffuses into the inside of starch granules causing granules to expand; thus, the torque continues to increase, reaching the plasticization torque. Subsequently, the starch granules gradually fuse and evenly plasticize under the influence of shear force, leading to a gradual decrease in torque, which tends to be gentle.21, 36 The incorporation of PVA leads to higher plasticization torque and equilibrium torque compared with TPS, as PVA and starch molecular chains form strong hydrogen bonds. The addition of DAS causes the torque of samples fluctuate up after reaching the plasticizing torque, due to crosslinking. However, after reaching the second peak torque, the torque of S/2DAS75 decreases again, possibly due to the degradation of starch molecules.22 This indicates that the introduction of DAS may cause reactions other than crosslinking to occur in the melt mixing process, leading to the degradation of starch molecules, and thereby reducing the torque of S/2DAS75. For S/P/2DAS75, the introduction of DAS and PVA increases the equilibrium torque of the sample due to the dominant role of crosslinking. As shown in Figure 7a, the introduction of DAS and PVA increases the equilibrium torque of the samples, reflecting the enhancement of the melt viscosity, since the torque can be used as a quantitative assessment of polymer melt viscosity. It is noteworthy that the changes in melt viscosity can have an impact on the processability of TPS-based materials. Research has revealed that there is a critical shear viscosity in the extrusion blown film processing of TPS. When the melt viscosity is lower than the critical shear viscosity, the melt is prone to breaking, making film blowing difficult.37 Therefore, the introduction of DAS is expected to improve the processing performance of TPS-based materials during extrusion blown film processing and reduce the processing difficulty. PVA has limited effect on the mechanical properties of S/P compared to TPS. This finding is consistent with previous studies on TPS/PVA blends, which suggest that blends with higher starch content demonstrate minimal changes in mechanical properties due to the partial compatibility of starch with PVA.38, 39 The addition of DAS affects the mechanical properties of the materials, and the TS of the blend with DAS is significantly higher than those without DAS. The TS of S/2DAS75 increases to 2.09 MPa compared to TPS due to crosslinking between DAS and cassava starch, and the EB of DAS is also increased. In connection with the analysis of the plasticization process of S/2DAS75, it is inferred that the increased EB may stem from the degradation of cassava starch. In contrast to other samples, the TS of S/P/2DAS75 increases to 3.60 MPa, while its EB decreases to 70.58%. Therefore, hydrolysis reactions of the PLA matrix could be taken place because of the PLA moisture absorption in the feed hooper of the extruder, although the PLA and its blends and composites were dried before blending. Without thermo-mechanical degradation of PLA in the extrusion process, the viscosity ratio of the blend components (ηPP1/ηPLA) should be lower than 1 at 200 °C and higher shear rates (kneading elements in the extruder) because of the higher pseudoplastic character of the PP1 dispersed phase than that of PLA. But this viscosity ratio should lower than 1 at high shear rates in the blends with PP2 as dispersed phase. Nonetheless, the reduction of the PLA viscosity by thermo-mechanical degradation and/or hydrolysis reactions in the extruder increases these viscosities ratios along the extruder sections. The influence of processing conditions during melt extrusion on the degradation of poly (lactic acid) has been already investigated [16, 27-31]. This degradation is influenced by the temperature, residence time in the extruder (screw rotation speed and mass flow rate), and the moisture content. Taubner and Shishoo [31] found a reduction in shear viscosity of about 50% at 230 °C and 120 rpm for the samples conditioned at 65% of relative humidity (RH) before measurements. In polymer blends research, the drop breakup phenomenon has been study extensively but the effect of the degradation (chain scission reactions) of the continuous phase (PLA) during the mixing process has not been fully explored [4, 5, 16]. In the extrusion process, the shear viscosity of PLA (matrix) is reduced and a negative effect on the dispersion of the minority phase (PPs) should be expected. Then, there is an enhancement of the viscosities ratios (ηPP1/ηPLA and ηPP2/ηPLA) and a reduction of the matrix shear stress with time. Consequently, an increase of the droplet sizes of the dispersed phase should be obtained. This explains the large sizes of the dispersed phases in the blends without sepiolite clay (Table 6). On the other hand, it has been reported that SEBS-g-MA is an efficient emulsifying agent in PP/PA-6 blends and number-average diameters of the dispersed phases lower that 1 μm have been found in these blends These results have been explained by the emulsifying process where the SEBS-g-MA compatibilizer agent migrates to the melted dispersed phase and a copolymer is formed at the interface that reduces the coalescence of the dispersed phase droplets [4, 5, 32-36]. In that sense, the thermal properties of the blend components should have some influence in the morphology of these blends [35].', 'This work investigates the effect of cellulose nanocrystal (CN) loading on the properties of polylactide/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PLA/PCL) (70/30) blend processed in a twin-screw extruder as a potential material that can be utilized in various applications where biodegradation is highly desired. The morphological analysis revealed a reduction in droplet size of dispersed PCL phase upon addition of CN at low concentrations (1 and 2 wt %) with maximum reduction at 2 wt % which led to maximum improvement in mechanical properties. Sci. 2019, 137, 48665. Blending of polymer materials to attain systems with enhanced properties has been a feasible strategy to improve properties that individual polymers possess and thus widening their utilization in various applications.1 Polylactide/poly(ε-caprolactone) (PLA/PCL) blend is a type of biodegradable blends that has received lots of attention because of the superior properties that the two polymers exhibit; in particular, both polymers are biodegradable-a property which makes them favorable for packaging and biomedical applications, and so forth.2-4 In this blend, PCL is mostly dispersed inside a continuous PLA phase to enhance its properties. These include enhancing its toughness, a reduction in brittleness, slow crystallization and biodegradation rates, poor thermal stability, and low melt strength, which restricts its foamability. PLA is a promising biodegradable polymer that is already available in the market to replace most currently used fossil-derived polymers such as polyolefins due to its environmental friendliness and biodegradability; hence, it is crucial to improve the mentioned properties by blending it with ductile and fast crystallizing polymers such as PCL.4-8 However, PLA/PCL blend has been shown to be thermodynamically immiscible over a wide range of composition, whereby both matrices exist in separate phases due to factors such as differences in molecular weights and viscosities, among others, and this usually leads to phase separation and thus poor properties and performance of the final system.9 Among the strategies mostly employed to improve interfacial adhesion between blend matrices, the addition of nanofiller materials becomes an effective route compared to utilization of copolymers which are expensive and only specific to individual blend systems.10-12 Even so, the localization of nanofiller materials in the blend matrices is still a challenge as they tend to localize either at the interface or selectively localize in one of the phases or reside in both phases depending on both thermodynamic and/or kinetic factors. The thermodynamic factors dictate localization when the filler has high affinity to either of the polymers while the kinetic factors control filler localization based on processing strategies employed during preparation, and also the viscosity differences whereby filler will localize in low viscosity phase.12, 13 Therefore, depending on their localization, the final morphology and properties would differ from one composite system to another. For instance, Kelnar et al.14 noticed localization of graphite nanoparticles (GNPs) in the PCL phase in PLA/PCL (80/20) blend. Selectively localized GNP in PCL phase could be the result of kinetic effects; that is, processing strategy employed during composite preparation whereby all the components were added simultaneously in the batch mixer; therefore, PCL that has lower viscosity and melts first masked GNP before it can disperse in PLA. Apart from the PLA/PCL blend system, the selective localization of filler particles has also been noticed in other immiscible blend systems such as PLA/PHBV blend. Mofokeng and Luyt5 observed titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanoparticles mostly dispersed in the PLA phase and also at the interface in 50/50 PLA/PHBV blends. In their case, although TiO2 was expected to localize in PHBV due to its low viscosity estimated from melt flow index, the localization in PLA phase was attributed to factors including crystallinity difference between PLA and PHBV and also high affinity of TiO2 to PLA as determined from surface energies. Filler materials typically localize in low viscosity phase to bring balance between the viscosities of blend polymers; however, such behavior was not observed in their case indicating that thermodynamic compatibility was predominant in controlling the localization of TiO2.', 'Processes of PLA melt blending and molding require high operating temperatures above the polymer melting point (up to 200°C) and/or high pressures.16, 19, 22, 24, 39, 56-68 After being melted, PLA is shaped into the desired form by molding (with or without a mechanical press) and cooled down to stabilize its dimensions.23The resulting material can be shaped into a film, fiber, or monolith, but it is non-porous form. Drawbacks of these processes include high-energy consumption and the use of high temperatures that can lead to thermal degradation of PLA leading to the formation of LA monomers.23 On the other hand, PLA degradation is also related to a residence time.23 Schematic presentation of these processes can be seen in Figure 3a,b. Huda et al.59 reported the preparation of PLA films (thickness 0.1-0.2 mm) by compression molding at temperature 180°C. The film showed a clear transition in dynamic mechanical properties. Its recovery of elasticity was faster as process temperature was higher. Alias et al.69 and Klinkajorn & Tanrattanakul62 processed PLA via melt mixing using an internal mixer at 180°C followed by compression molding. Obtained films showed elongation at break of 5%. Rojas-Lema et al.16 exposed PLA beads to thermo-compression at 180°C with a pressure of 40 MPa tons for 3 min by two hot plates and air-cooled at room conditions. Films with a thickness of approximately 250 μm, elongation at break 3.5%, and elastic modulus 2846 MPa were obtained. Melt spinning of PLA was one of the first method used for the preparation of textile fibers.23, 41, 70 After PLA is melted (usually at 185-240°C), it is pumped through a spinneret (die) with numerous holes (one to thousands).     *   **Surface modification/coating:** Creating a diffusion barrier (Context 1, Context 15).
    *   **Polymer composition:** Using specific polymers or blends (e.g., PCL/PEO, Context 1; PLGA, Context 11) or adding inorganic particles (e.g., MCS, Context 10).

Blending chitosan (CS) with poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) significantly enhances the electrospinning process and fiber properties through the following mechanisms:

1. **Improved Spinnability**:  
   - CS alone is challenging to electrospin due to its polycationic nature, rigid structure, and strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which hinder chain entanglement. PEO acts as a **co-spinning agent**, improving solution viscosity and elasticity, enabling continuous fiber formation without beads. For instance, CS/PEO blends (e.g., 6.7:0.3% w/v) in trifluoroacetic acid/dichloromethane (TFA/DCM) yield smooth fibers (average diameter: 272 ± 56 nm) [1, 8].

2. **Rheological Modifications**:  
   - PEO increases solution **viscosity**, preventing jet fracturing during electrospinning. Higher PEO content (e.g., 90:10 CS:PEO) enhances viscosity, while lower ratios (e.g., O-CS/PEO = 1/3) balance conductivity and viscosity for stable fiber formation [3, 5].  
   - High molecular weight PEO (e.g., 2000 kDa) contributes to **elasticity**, critical for smooth fiber formation, whereas lower MW PEO (600–1000 kDa) results in beaded fibers [11].

3. **Solvent Compatibility**:  
   - PEO enables electrospinning with less toxic solvents (e.g., 50% acetic acid) instead of harsh solvents like TFA. This improves biocompatibility for biomedical applications [4, 8].

4. **Post-Spinning Stability**:  
   - PEO can be **removed post-electrospinning** via water washing, stabilizing CS fibers in aqueous environments. This step reduces residual acidity and enhances fiber stability [2].

5. **Morphological and Functional Benefits**:  
   - PEO reduces CS crystallinity and promotes hydrogen bonding, creating defect-free fibers with uniform morphology [7, 9].  
   - Blends with PEO improve mechanical flexibility (e.g., 150% elongation increase with 20% glycerol) and antimicrobial efficacy, as quaternized CS/PEO derivatives show superior antibacterial activity [1, 12].

6. **Phase Separation and Structure Control**:  
   - Immiscible CS/PEO blends form **core-shell** or **microphase-separated structures** during electrospinning, influenced by phase separation mechanisms (nucleation vs. spinodal decomposition). These structures enhance functionality for drug delivery or tissue engineering [6].

In summary, PEO enhances chitosan’s electrospinnability by modifying solution rheology, enabling benign solvent use, stabilizing fiber formation, and tailoring structural/functional properties for diverse applications.

As can be seen from Table 1, owing to its very low tensile yield strength and tensile modulus (7.67 and 62.6 MPa, respectively), coupled with a high elongation at break (>1000%), neat PBAT showed a very soft and ductility behavior. While introducing PGA with high tensile strength (>68.9 MPa) and tensile modulus (6.9 GPa)23 into PBAT matrix, the mechanical properties of the PBAT/PGA samples could be changed significantly. With an increase in PGA content, the tensile yield strength and modulus of PBAT/PGA samples gradually increased. While PGA content increased to 35 wt%, the tensile yield strength increased from 7.67 MPa of neat PBAT to 12.05 MPa. Meanwhile, the tensile modulus increased from 62.6 MPa of neat PBAT to 158.9 MPa. Compared with neat PBAT, the tensile yield strength and tensile modulus of PBAT/PGA (65/35) sample were increased by 57% and 153%, respectively. As we known, the tensile modulus and tensile yield strength are two important parameters for evaluating the resistance to deformation of polymer materials. Compared with neat PBAT, the enhancement in tensile modulus and tensile yield strength will allow the PBAT/PGA blend to meet wider application requirements while it is used as biodegradable packaging materials. However, it has to be mentioned that the tensile ductility of PBAT/PGA samples (in terms of elongation at break) decreased drastically with an increase in PGA content. For example, the elongation at break of PBAT/PGA (65/35) sample decreased from 1082.1% (neat PBAT) to 88.7%. Due to the significant reduction in tensile ductility, the stress enhancement effect caused by the orientation of macromolecule segments during the tensile stretching process was restrained greatly, as shown in Figure 1. As a result, the tensile fracture strength of PBAT/PGA (65/35) sample also decreased significantly from 25.74 MP (neat PBAT) to 13.17 MPa. SEM observation was conducted to research the microscopic morphologies of PBAT/PGA samples. The SEM photographs of cryo-surfaces for PBAT/PGA samples were shown in Figure 2. The sizes of PGA particles were measured using the particle size statistics software (Nano Measurer). Thus the ranges of particle size distribution and apparent number average particle sizes (app) of PGA for all the PBAT/PGA samples were shown in Figure 3. As can be seen from Figure 2, the PBAT/PGA blends exhibited a two-phase microstructure, where the PGA particles dispersed in PBAT matrix. The SEM observation confirmed that PBAT/PGA blends were incompatible. As PGA content increased from 5 to 15 wt%, the app of PGA particles increased from 1.77 to 2.59 μm. While further increasing the PGA content, the app of PGA particles remained almost unchanged along with an increase in number of PGA particles. For many incompatible polymer blends, the size of the dispersed phase tends to increase with the increase of the dispersed phase content, because the main mechanism that determines the shape development of the dispersed phase is the balance between breakdown and coalescence of the dispersed phase droplets. After reaching this balance, the trend that the dispersed phase size increases with the increase of dispersed phase content become less obvious.25, 26 For the PBAT/PGA blending system, when PGA content reached the threshold value of 15 wt%, the balance between breakdown and coalescence of PGA droplets could be achieved. According to SEM observation, with an increase in PGA content, more and more PGA particles formed in the PBAT matrix, which could greatly restrict the movement of PBAT chains and segments. Thus, it was beneficial to improve the tensile modulus and tensile yield strength of PBAT matrix. However, due to the poor interface compatibility between PBAT matrix and PGA domains, the elongation at break decreased significantly from 1082.1% (neat PBAT sample) to 88.7% with an increase in PGA content from zero to 35 wt%. Similar behavior was also reported previously for PBAT blends with other polymers, such as PLA, and EVOH etc. For example, Li et al.11 prepared PBAT/stereocomplex polylactide (sc-PLA) blends using sc-PLA as a reinforcing modifier. Gamma sterilization increases the glass transition temperature of polymers with high PEG content. Materials and devices intended for in vivo applications are either aseptically processed or terminally sterilized before use to avoid any implant-related infection. Aseptic processing of medical devices is rarely practical or economical.6 Therefore, terminal sterilization, where a device is sterilized within its final sterile barrier package, is preferred for medical device sterilization.6 Clinical success of polymeric biomaterials thus depends on the ability of the polymers to be sterilized while retaining their essential physical and chemical characteristics.', "The standard gamma-irradiation sterilization dose used in the industry for most combination devices that come in contact with skin or tissue is 25 kGy. This dose is considered sufficient for gaining a minimum of 10−6 sterility assurance level (6 log reduction). Use of an irradiation dose lower than the standard 25 kGy is of special interest in sterilization of medical devices, because of the damaging effect that this dose might have on physical-mechanical properties. During gamma irradiation at room temperature, the product temperature is elevated as a result of gamma ray absorption. For the sterilization of bioresorbable polymers, temperatures must be kept below the temperature at which changes occur in the polymer's molecular weight, in order to prevent degradation. For this reason, cooling the product to 0°C or less during irradiation is advised. This requires the use of cooling agents in the irradiation container to prevent heating to the critical temperature where molecular weight is affected. Various combinations of doses and temperatures can be employed to achieve product sterility without adversely affecting the product. Careful design principles are employed to impart specific characteristics (such as stiffness, bioactivity, biodegradation, 3D printability) in GelMA biomaterials for targeted tissue engineering applications [6-9]. Ideally, the sterilization treatment should not alter the carefully designed biomechanical and biochemical properties of the GelMA prepolymer and scaffolds, ensuring that the scaffolds perform as intended after sterilization [10, 11]. This requirement renders the sterilization of the GelMA scaffolds a formidable task, as the hydrogels are more sensitive and prone to undergo chemical modifications during terminal sterilization process. Filtration is one of the commonly used methods of sterilization; however, as the concentration and/or the molecular weight of the biopolymer increase, filtration becomes gradually more difficult. Therefore, for different applications, other methods of sterilization are under investigation for biopolymers. Unfortunately, limited attention has been paid to the characterization of the effects of terminal sterilization on the GelMA prepolymer and scaffold properties. For example, heat-based sterilization such as autoclaving has good penetrability to allow for complete sterilization [10]. These studies emphasize the importance of studying the effects of the sterilization methods on GelMA properties, which could ultimately affect cellular adhesion, growth, and differentiation in GelMA scaffolds. Therefore, the effects of sterilization on the properties and printability of the GelMA prepolymer are critically important, yet unstudied to date.', "Based on differential counts of surface areas and volumes, there is at least a 3× reduction in pore dimensions between untreated control samples and the sterilized samples. The sterilization method of choice for heat-sensitive biodegradable polymers depends on their chemical composition and the need to minimize physicochemical degradation. Based on the provided contexts:  

1. **Gamma (γ) irradiation with cooling** is a viable option when applied at controlled doses (e.g., ≤25 kGy) and temperatures (≤0°C). Cooling mitigates heat-induced degradation, preserving molecular weight and structural integrity, as demonstrated for bioresorbable polymers like PDLGA-collagen hybrids (Contexts 2, 3).  

2. **Ethylene oxide (EtO)** is an alternative for heat-sensitive polymers but may cause esterification of carboxylic acid groups (Context 1), leave toxic residues, and reduce cell viability (Contexts 8, 12). Post-sterilization degassing is critical, though impractical in clinical settings.  

3. **Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma** (e.g., H₂O₂ plasma) is highlighted as a safer chemical method compared to EtO, with fewer toxic byproducts and minimal impact on mechanical properties (Contexts 8, 12).  

4. **Vaporized hydrogen peroxide (VHP)** causes hydroxylation and hydrolytic degradation (Context 1) but is less thermally damaging than autoclaving.  

**Conclusion**: Gamma irradiation with controlled cooling is often preferred for heat-sensitive biodegradable polymers due to its efficacy and adaptability (Contexts 2, 3). For polymers sensitive to radiation, hydrogen peroxide gas plasma or VHP may be better alternatives, while EtO requires careful handling to address toxicity concerns. The choice ultimately hinges on the polymer’s chemical stability and the clinical feasibility of post-sterilization treatments.

For the sake of clarity, to the best of our knowledge, the superior hydrophilic structure of SC could enhance the conductivity and electrical performance of LIBs, similar to the properties of ceramic materials.', "A sustainable and low-cost separator is highly required for electrochemical energy storage systems. As with other transient technologies, scalability, mass production energy demands, and sourcing impacts remain to be fully considered for broader environmental evaluation.', 'Aqueous Zn-ion batteries have emerged as one of the best candidates for efficient and safe energy storage systems; however, they are severely restricted by the formation of uncontrolled Zn dendrites. The accumulated Zn dendrites can pierce the separator and cause short circuit, which greatly reduces the life span of ZIBs and restricts the practical applications.', 'In addition to hydrolytically degradable systems, several studies have explored for truly biodegradable battery systems─including those using inorganic electrodes─where the degradation occurs through microbial or enzymatic processes. This work highlights the balance between degradable polymer structures and electrochemical performance, advancing sustainable organic electrode materials for next-generation batteries.', '(a) Process of converting cellulose fibers to metallic paper and applying it to create flexible supercapacitors.141 (b) Schematic illustration of the transient supercapacitor, photographs showing the transient behavior of the supercapacitor during dissolution in water.142 (c) Illustration of the preparation process for a CNF separator derived from rice straw,143 (d) Schematic illustration for the fabrication of biomimetic CNF/CNT/MXene aerogels by a facile bidirectional freezing strategy.144 (e) Schematics for the preparation of Ti3C2Tx/CNF hybrid dispersion and Ti3C2Tx/CNF nanopapers.145 Cellulose-based conductive materials have become essential in battery fabrication due to their unique properties, such as excellent mechanical strength, flexibility, and biocompatibility.146 These qualities make them ideal for various battery components, including electrodes, separators, and binders. It is anticipated that novel synthesis methodologies, like holographic lithography, direct dispensing, and 3D printing, could assist in developing biocompatible secondary batteries encompassing three-dimensional architectures [42].', 'Over the past decade, increasing attention and efforts have been focused on the development of alternative energy sources and energy storage devices to alleviate the impacts of climate change and fossil fuel depletion. This work sheds light on a simple method to prepare an environmentally friendly separator with a better and safer performance for LIBs and paves the way to the transformation of raw materials from petroleum to biomass resources.', 'Currently, the most commonly used commercial separator for ZIBs is the glass fiber (GF) separator, possessing high porosity and electrolyte wettability. However, its large pore size (micron scale) and irregular pore structure accommodate a large number of SO42− and H+ ions, triggering side reactions and non-uniform Zn2+ flux, thereby accelerating dendrite formation.9 Its poor mechanical strength renders it susceptible to penetration by Zn dendrites during repeated cycling, leading to internal short circuits and safety risks.10 Moreover, the production process of GF separators is relatively complex, raising environmental concerns. Finally, the remaining challenges and future development directions of biomass-based separators for ZIBs are summarized and analyzed to promote further research and development for large-scale applications.', "AbstractAqueous zinc ion batteries (AZIBs) have attracted increasing attention because of their high energy density, excellent safety features, and environmentally friendly properties. IntroductionThe increasing need for dependable power sources with substantial energy storage capacities is driven by the rapid development in the fields of electric vehicles and portable electronic devices. The performance requirements of the ZIB separator and various strategies to improve the performance of the separator are reviewed. Finally, the challenges and future development directions of cellulose-based zinc-ion battery separators are proposed.", 'In recent years, the issue of population aging has promoted significant interest in the development of implantable biomedical devices.1,2 However, conventional batteries in these devices have introduced challenges, such as limited battery life and the need for secondary surgical extraction, imposing risks and financial burdens to patients.3,4 Consequently, the quest for an alternative solution has led to a burgeoning interest in implantable solid-state biodegradable energy storage devices.5 Although implantable biomedical devices powered by conventional batteries are highly reliable and convenient, they are not without drawbacks:6-8 (1) their rigid and bulky nature occupies considerable space within implantable devices, (2) non-biodegradability necessitates a second surgical procedure, and (3) the presence of toxic substances in electrodes and electrolytes poses severe safety hazards. The most glaring example is PLA, which releases acidic LA that could drop the surrounding pH to levels that could even cause cell necrosis [225]. Based solely on the provided context, the differences between alkaline and acid hydrolysis for polyesters are:

1.  **Mechanism & By-products:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Involves attack by hydroxyl ions (OH⁻). For PLA, this leads to intramolecular transesterification, releasing dilactide dimers and decreasing molecular weight ([1]). For PET, it hydrolyzes into terephthalic acid (TPA), forming salts (e.g., terephthalate potassium salt) and ethylene glycol (EG) ([2], [6]).
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Involves protonation. For PLA, protonation of the hydroxyl end-group forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond, leading to hydrolysis of ester linkages to produce lactic acid (LA) ([1]). For PET, it hydrolyzes into TPA and EG using acids like H₂SO₄, HNO₃, or H₃PO₄ ([2], [6]).

2.  **Degradation Rate:**
    *   Polyesters generally undergo **faster hydrolytic degradation under alkaline (basic) conditions** compared to acidic conditions ([1], [224]).
    *   Specifically for PGA, degradation kinetics are accelerated under alkaline conditions (pH > 10) ([1], [230]).
    *   Hydroxyl anions (in alkali) act as a **reagent** consumed in the reaction, meaning higher alkali concentration promotes hydrolysis. Protons (in acid) act as a **catalyst** for both hydrolysis and esterification, so concentrated acid is needed to favor hydrolysis over re-esterification ([6]).

3.  **Environmental Concerns & Limitations:**
    *   Both acid and alkaline hydrolysis of PET generate **corrosive** reaction systems and produce **large quantities of inorganic salts** and highly acidic or basic wastewater ([2]). Acid hydrolysis specifically uses concentrated acids like H₂SO₄ ([2]).
    *   Neutral hydrolysis is seen as more environmentally friendly but suffers from long reaction times and potential purity issues with the TPA product ([2]).

4.  **Catalyst Role:**
    *   **Alkaline Hydrolysis:** Hydroxyl anions function as a **reagent** rather than a catalyst, meaning they are consumed in the reaction. A high alkali concentration is therefore needed to drive the hydrolysis ([6]).
    *   **Acid Hydrolysis:** Protons function as **catalysts** for both the hydrolysis reaction and the reverse esterification reaction. Concentrated acid solutions are required to favor the hydrolysis step ([6]).

The conventional plastics commonly used in electronic components are petroleum-derived, exacerbating challenges related to their disposal and degradation. Consequently, biodegradable plastics have emerged as a promising solution for tackling pollution linked with e-waste. These materials have the inherent ability to undergo natural decomposition through microbial action, ultimately converting into carbon dioxide and water within a timeframe of 20-45 days, contingent upon sufficient levels of humidity, oxygen, and microbial activity [4]. Polylactic acid (PLA) is highly notable for its biodegradability, synthesis from renewable resources, and classification as an aliphatic thermoplastic polyester [5, 6]. Additionally, it is extensively employed as one of the leading bioplastics in commercial applications, effectively replacing conventional non-biodegradable plastics [7]. In recent years, there has been a study of research focused on exploring the dielectric behavior of biodegradable polymers. For instance, Wu et al. investigated the dielectric properties of polylactic acid (PLA) were enhanced through the incorporation of titanium dioxide (TiO2) decorated carbon nanotubes. The research suggested that the resulting biodegradable PLA nanocomposite, characterized by a high dielectric constant and low dielectric loss, could potentially facilitate the development of disposable electronics [1]. Therefore, we selected biodegradable polylactic acid as the matrix to prepare the composite film intended for use in electronic products. Dielectric materials based on polymers exhibit attractive properties, making them potential alternatives to widely used inorganic and ceramic-based dielectric materials. Numerous studies have explored the use of polymer dielectrics, evaluating their feasibility for various applications due to their higher flexibility, easy processing, chemical stability, and adjustable properties [8]. However, a primary drawback of polymer dielectrics is their comparatively low dielectric constants when compared to inorganic materials. Therefore, the incorporation of inorganic fillers into the polymer structure, forming polymer nanocomposites, emerges as a preferred solution to achieve higher dielectric constants [6]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of cellulose fiber-reinforced composites. These materials not only enhance mechanical properties but also prove effective as insulators, making them well-suited for applications in the electrical and electronics fields [9]. Furthermore, the combination of polymer and cellulosic materials also contributes to the development of unique dielectric properties [10]. With the development of social industry, the waste of electronic products causes serious global environmental pollution problems. In this context, the use of renewable resources to develop biodegradable dielectric materials to reduce environmental pollution and fossil resource depletion is a promising and sustainable method [1-4]. In this regard, poly(lactide) (PLA) has attracted wide attention from business and academia due to its excellent biocompatibility, good mechanical properties, low cost, and being completely derived from renewable biological resources [5-8]. PLA is a sustainable and environmentally friendly petroleum-based polymer substitute, which is widely used in medical supplies, industry, agriculture, and electronic products [9-13]. However, its poor dielectric properties and poor heat resistance limit its application in electronic fields such as micro-storage capacitors and integrated circuits [14, 15]. Currently, blending with other polymers with high dielectric constant such as polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) is one of the easiest ways to improve the dielectric properties of PLA. Mishra et al. [16] found that PLA and PVDF allow electrons to migrate between conductive paths at a specific mixing ratio, thereby increasing the electric field strength and leading to an increase in polarization, ultimately resulting in an increase in dielectric constant. Meanwhile, it has been reported that the filler with a high aspect ratio is the best candidate for the preparation of dielectric nano-polymer materials [17, 18]. CNTs are composed of hexagonal ring carbon atoms with a special one-dimensional hollow structure. They have the advantages of a large aspect ratio, low density, large specific surface area, and good mechanical properties. The aspect ratio can reach 104-106 [19, 20]. Therefore, carbon nanotube fillers have received extensive attention in charge storage or capacitor applications [21-24]. CNTs in the polymer matrix can be used as electrodes for nanocapacitors, resulting in a significant increase in space charge polarization. In addition, the high conductivity of CNTs increases the interfacial polarization between the CNTs and the polymer interface layer [25, 26]. Moreover, it is demonstrated that carbon nanotubes can also act as nucleating agents for the polymer, which is beneficial for improving the crystallinity and enhancing the heat resistance of the polymer materials [27]. Ahmad et al. [28] introduced MWCNTs as a new nano-reinforcing filler into the PLA/PEG polymer matrix by melt blending. The results showed that the introduction of MWCNTs improved the dielectric properties of PLA/PEG blends. Chen et al. [29] introduced MWCNTs into PLA, which has improved the crystallinity and heat resistance of PLA composites. However, due to the weak interaction between MWCNTs and the polymer and the poor dispersion of MWCNTs in the polymer matrix, it is difficult to prepare high-performance PLA/MWCNTs composites with high dielectric constant and heat deflection temperature (HDT). So, it is possible to construct high-performance PLA/PVDF/CNTs composites with enhanced dielectric properties and high HDT. In our previous work, a chain extender containing epoxy functional groups (ADR) was employed to control the interfacial properties of incompatible PLA/PVDF blends, and it was found that ADR can obviously enhance the interaction between PLA and PVDF. So, on the basis of our previous work, a high content of carboxylated MWCNTs was introduced into PLA/PVDF/ADR blends. PVDF/MWCNTs masterbatch was first prepared by solution blending, because the CNTs tend to disperse in the PLA phase with low viscosity, which was blended with PVDF by solution blending to prepare the masterbatch, and then PVDF/MWCNTs-COOH masterbatch, PLA, PVDF, and ADR were melt blending [31, 32]. The effects of MWCNTs-COOH on the microstructure and macroscopic properties of PLA/PVDF/ADR blends were systematically studied. Scaling down generates problems such as interconnect signal delay (RC delay) that gives rise to propagation delay, crosstalk noise, and power dissipation.1-4 These problems have become an obstacle to further development within the microelectronics. The use of interconnect materials with low dielectric constant is one effective way to reduce RC delay.5-8 Therefore, the development of materials with low dielectric constant has received widespread attention.1-8 One method for decreasing the dielectric constant is to prepare porous materials because the dielectric constant of air is approximately 1. However, high porosity will decrease the mechanical strength and increase water absorption, thus increasing the dielectric constant.2 Additionally, Long et al. synthesized polymers using ring-opening olefin metathesis polymerization of strained cyclic olefinic monomers.9 The material was found to have a low dielectric constant from free volume theory. An alternative method is to use intrinsically low-k polymers, such as SiLK, poly(benzoxazole)s, and polyimides.10-13 Among these, benzocyclobutene (BCB) resins, as one family of low-k polymers, have attracted much attention in recent years.14-17 The monomer BCB could exhibit a ring-opening reaction in certain circumstances, yielding a cured resin.14, 16-23 No catalyst is required and no volatile compounds are released during the curing process. Unfortunately, the main problem in this case is the preparation of larger volumes of these materials. Fig. 3 illustrates fracture surfaces of the alloys after tensile tests. On the other hand, in the case of the Mg-5Sn alloy there is only an indication of shallow dimples on the fracture surface (Fig. 3b) corresponding to the low elongation of this alloy (Fig. 2).", 'Population aging is a significant global social issue that cannot be ignored, as it has increased bone and cardiovascular diseases incidence, leading to a growing demand for biomaterials. For the in vivo tests, three kinds of implants were inserted into rabbit femurs for 4, 8 and 16 weeks to evaluate their biocompatibility, corrosion rate and bone forming ability.', 'Bone metal implants are currently made from stainless steel or titanium alloy. retrieved_contexts: ['The abuse of traditional plastic food packaging has caused severe food safety and environmental pollution, urgently necessitating the development of green and sustainable biodegradable packaging materials. Chitosan (CS) belongs to an inexpensive and readily available biopolymer; however, the poor mechanical properties and weak resistance to UV light and water make it unsuitable for the food packaging industry. In this study, a layer-by-layer (LBL) assembly of CS decorated with anthocyanins as a polycationic electrolyte and carboxylated graphene oxide (GO-COOH) as a polyanionic electrolyte is used to fabricate bio-based films with the aim of improving comprehensive properties of CS-based films. The results indicate that the LBL assembly extremely enhanced the UV-blocking ability (the average transmittance in the UV-B region drops to 1.68%), tensile strength (TS) (53.52 MPa), toughness (71.81%), thermal stability, water resistance, hydrophobicity (the water contact angle is up to 109.5°), and antioxidant activities of the films, attributed to hydrogen bonds among CS, anthocyanins, and GO-COOH and electrostatic interactions between GO-COOH and CS along with anthocyanins. In addition, the LBL films show exceptional advantages in the storage application for fresh-cut apples. In general, the study demonstrates that a novel and sustainable CS-based film can be fabricated by the LBL technique for food packaging. The carboxylated graphene oxide and chitosan decorated with anthocyanin are deposed by a layer-by-layer assembly to fabricate the bio-based films for food packaging. The films exhibit enhanced mechanical properties, UV-blocking ability, water resistance, and antioxidant as well as unique potential in preserving fresh fruits, thereby providing new strategies for the future development of food packaging.', 'First published on 24th February 2025 Dual functionalization of polyurethane (PU) foam to achieve both flame-retardant and antibacterial properties is crucial for meeting stringent fire safety and hygiene standards. Herein, an efficient dual-functional coating, PDA@CS-POM, is developed by combining a transition metal-substituted polyoxometalate (POM), [Co4(H2O)2(PW9O34)2]10−, with a catecholamine-tethered polycation (PDA@CS(+)) prepared with polydopamine (PDA) and chitosan (CS), through a straightforward layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly method. The catecholamine groups in PDA@CS enable effective LbL assembly on hydrophobic silicon wafers and flexible PU foams without substrate pre-treatment. In particular, the PDA@CS-POM coating achieves a growth rate of 11.3 nm per BL, more than twice that of the reference CS-POM coating without PDA. Compression-recovery cycles demonstrate that the PDA@CS-POM coating increased the toughness of the PU foam while maintaining its inherent resilience. Assessments including limiting oxygen index (LOI), cone colorimetry, zone of inhibition, and colony culture tests confirm the efficient flame-retardant and antibacterial properties of the PDA@CS-POM coated PU foams. These dual-functional properties of the PDA@CS-POM coating positively correlate with the effects of the POM in inhibiting foam degradation, improving graphitization/aromatization of char barrier, and disrupting bacteria redox processes or cytoskeleton dynamics. Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly is a highly facile and attractive method to impart multiple functional properties to polymeric materials. In contrast to modifying PU foams by incorporating functional groups or additives into the bulk matrix, employing functional coatings through LbL assembly can augment and alter the performance of the polymeric material without compromising its bulk properties.5-7 A diverse range of functional molecules shows promise in the LbL construction of flame-retardant and antibacterial coatings. Examples include phosphorus-, silicon-, halogen-, and transition-metal-containing compounds, as well as renewable biomass-based materials (e.g., chitosan, phytic acid, and lignin) for flame retardancy,8-14 and silver nanoparticles, quaternary ammonium compounds, and metal oxide nanoparticles for antibacterial efficacy.15-18 Of particular interest are polyoxometalates (POMs), which are anionic molecular metal-oxide clusters known for their rich redox chemistry, diverse structures, and tunable chemical compositions.15,19 Sustained research has highlighted the great potential of POMs in enhancing both flame retardancy and bacteriostasis. Various types of POMs, such as Keggin- (e.g., [PMo12O40]3−, [PW12O40]3−),20-22 Anderson- (e.g., [MnMo6O18{(OCH2)3CNH2}2]3−),23 and transition-metal-substituted POMs (e.g., [Cu4(H2O)2(PW9O34)2]10−, [Ni4(H2O)2(PW9O34)2]10−, PMoNi),24,25 have been identified as effective flame retardants or flame-retardant synergists due to their superior catalytic activity in promoting char formation. Moreover, the electrostatic nature of POMs has been demonstrated to induce POM-associated biological activities, such as POM-protein and POM-enzyme interactions, thereby contributing to their efficiency against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria.15', 'Research and development of smart nanostructured materials governed by their surface properties is a rapidly growing field [1]. Layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly is a simple bottom-up technique to modify surfaces, synthesize nanocomposites and thin films of different materials [2,3]. This method consists of alternating physisorption of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes, whereby electrostatic is one of the most critical interactions between molecules [4]. Due to its simplicity, cost-effectivity and versatility to tailor the physicochemical properties and structure of several materials [2,3], the LbL technique has been used in a wide range of applications such as adhesives [5,6], separation [7,8], catalysis [9,10], sensing [11,12], food industry [13], bioelectronics [14,15], drug delivery [16,17], biomineralization [18,19], cell adhesion [20,21], tissue engineering [22,23], blood vessel models [24], and many others. Notably, in the last decade, hyaluronan (HA, a polyanion) and chitosan (CHI, a polycation), two biocompatible and biodegradable polyelectrolytes, have been assembled by LbL for the synthesis of antibacterial coatings: HA provides compression strength and lubrication, whereas CHI presents the antimicrobial properties. Most of the representative works were performed by Richert et al. these authors characterized HA/CHI films, which reduced the population of E. coli bacteria by 80% after 30 min of culture [20]; Chua et al. functionalized Ti with HA/CHI films and immobilized RGD peptides on the surface, obtaining a 80% reduction of S. aureus after 4 h of culture [25]; Cui et al. synthetized HA/CHI microcapsules and could reduce by around 100% the population of E. coli bacteria after 4 h of incubation [26]; Hernandez-Montelongo et al. showed the antibacterial effect of HA/CHI nanofilms against X. fastidiosa, one of the top 10 plant pathogenic bacteria in molecular plant pathology, for up to 8 days [27]; Hernandez-Montelongo et al. optimized the synthesis of HA/CHI nanofilms obtaining around 100% reduction of S. aureus after 8 h of culture [28]; and Nascimento et al. studied the influence of pH and ionic strength on the antibacterial effect of HA/CHI nanofilms against S. aureus, obtaining almost 100% of reduction after 24 h of incubation [29]. In spite of the extensive studies regarding the formation process of the LbL films and their diverse applications, there are few theoretical and experimental investigations that analyze the dynamic scaling of surface growth, which can provide evidence for the mesoscopic behavior of LbL films assembly. Dynamic scaling theory is a well-known and proven formalism to assess the growth mechanism of thin films [30]. This theory has also been applied to LbL films: De Souza et al. [31] characterized the surface morphology of poly (o-methoxyaniline) (POMA) alternated with poly (vinyl sulfonic acid) (PVS) films, and Spera et al. [32] analyzed carboxymethylcellulose (CMC)/CHI films. In that sense, this work deals with the fractal analysis of polyelectrolytes assembled by LbL into nanofilms. We used HA and CHI as models to investigate the impact of pH and ionic strength (IS) on synthesis, two of the most critical variables of this technique [29]. The thickness and topography measurements were obtained from films with a different number of HA/CHI bilayers, and dynamical scaling analysis was used to characterize the growth process [33]. In that sense, this work is useful for the understanding of the driving force behind nanofilm formation.', 'Oxidation of alginate is a promising method that creates aldehyde groups, which can form stable cross-links with amine groups on chitosan. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the pH-responsiveness of the multilayer films can be regulated by the choice of pH at which the layer-by-layer assembly is conducted. Multilayer films of chitosan (CHI) and alginate (ALG) have drawn increasing attention due to their nontoxicity, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and tunable physicochemical properties.[1-3] These films are produced using the layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly method, in which a charged substrate is alternately immersed in CHI and ALG solutions.[4] The electrostatic interactions between the oppositely charged components promote LbL deposition and film growth. LbL assembly itself is a facile, efficient, versatile, and tunable method.[5] Considering these advantages, CHI/ALG multilayer films are promising candidates for multiple biomedical applications ranging from tissue engineering to drug delivery.[6-8] The interior part of the polyelectrolyte multilayer films maintains charge-neutrality at the pH where the LbL assembly is conducted.[9, 10] In other words, the number of positively charged amine groups on CHI and negatively charged carboxyl groups on ALG are roughly identical, showing an ≈1:1 charge stoichiometry.
